article_title: Vocabulary Instruction for Middle School Students with Learning Disabilities: A Comparison of Two Instructional Models
citation: Fore III, C., Boon, R. T., & Lowrie, K. (2007). Vocabulary Instruction for Middle School Students with Learning Disabilities: A Comparison of Two Instructional Models. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 5(2), 49-73. https://www.ldworldwide.org
title: Teach content-area vocabulary to students with learning disabilities through explicit concept-model instruction rather than definition-only methods
description: Because students with learning disabilities acquire vocabulary poorly through independent word-learning strategies and definition lookup, the article recommends direct, explicit concept instruction: "the concept model, as a method of direct instruction, should be explicitly taught to students to facilitate independent word learning." The structured diagram format gives teachers and students a concrete outline of the word, its definition and characteristics, and examples and non-examples.
requirements: Direct and sequential teaching of target words, since students with LD take longer to learn new strategies
Words should be unfamiliar to most students (screened by a pretest of prior definitions)
constraints: Evidence base in this article is six seventh-graders with LD in one resource setting; the authors call for replication across more students, grade levels, content areas, and disability categories, and note maintenance and generalization were not measured
target_learning_goals: content-area vocabulary acquisition and reading comprehension
examples: The study implemented the principle by replacing dictionary lookup and sentence writing with teacher-led concept-diagram lessons for mathematical terms
key_sources: Fore III, C., Boon, R. T., & Lowrie, K. (2007). Vocabulary Instruction for Middle School Students with Learning Disabilities: A Comparison of Two Instructional Models. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 5(2), 49-73. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ797664

article_title: AARP Foundation Experience Corps Tutoring (Book Buddies)
citation: AARP Foundation Experience Corps. (2021). AARP Foundation Experience Corps. Evidence for ESSA program summary. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Staff Experience Corps programs with a Project Director, Site Coordinators, and Volunteer Team Leaders
description: The page states that although staffing structure varies, "best practice indicates that programs with a Project Director, Site Coordinators, and Volunteer Team Leaders are the most successful". The Project Director oversees day-to-day operations; Site Coordinators maintain relationships with schools, principals, teachers, and volunteers and can manage up to 5 schools; Volunteer Team Leaders handle daily communication with and data collection from volunteers.
requirements: Number of Site Coordinators and Volunteer Team Leaders scaled to the number of volunteers and schools served
constraints: Site Coordinators can manage up to 5 schools with assistance from Volunteer Team Leaders
examples: The Project Director oversees day to day operations and implementation of the program within the schools
key_sources: AARP Foundation Experience Corps. (2021). AARP Foundation Experience Corps. Evidence for ESSA program summary. https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Graspable Math — From Here to There (FH2T)
citation: From Here to There (FH2T): Program Description and Evaluation Evidence. (2023). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au/the-toolkit/from-here-to-there/
title: Expression-transformation puzzle: match a starting expression to an equivalent target form via valid operations
description: The core design pattern of FH2T is a transformation puzzle: "The program presents a starting expression and a mathematically equivalent target expression. Students manipulate the original expression to match the target form." Because moves must be "mathematically valid operations," students practice algebraic manipulation by direct interaction with notation rather than by answering discrete items. The pattern embeds practice of distribution, factoring, inverse operations, and order of operations inside the game's goal structure.
requirements: A starting expression paired with a mathematically equivalent target expression
An interface allowing students to drag and transform expressions using mathematically valid operations
constraints: Applied in the article to algebraic expressions and equation solving for introductory prealgebra/algebra
target_learners: Middle and high school students learning introductory prealgebra or algebra
target_learning_goals: Fluency with algebraic manipulation operations, including distribution, factoring, inverse operations, and order of operations
examples: FH2T tasks ask students to transform a given expression into a target form using operations such as distribution and factoring.
key_sources: From Here to There (FH2T): Program Description and Evaluation Evidence. (2023). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au/the-toolkit/from-here-to-there/

article_title: Reading Edge
citation: The Reading Edge. (2008). https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/the-reading-edge/
title: Teach metacognitive reading skills explicitly within cooperative team reading instruction
description: Within the Reading Edge approach, cooperative team activities are paired with direct instruction in self-regulatory reading strategies: "Instruction focuses on explicit teaching of metacognitive skills, such as clarification, summarization, predication, and graphic organizers." The principle is that peer team structures and explicit strategy teaching operate together, with teams using these strategies as they prepare for assessments.
requirements: team structures in which students prepare themselves and teammates for individual assessments
explicit lessons on clarification, summarization, predication, and graphic organizers
examples: Reading Edge students engage in partner reading, story retelling, story-related writing, word mastery, and story-structure activities alongside explicit metacognitive instruction.
key_sources: The Reading Edge. (2008). https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/the-reading-edge/

article_title: What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?
citation: Neil Seftor. (2016). What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Education decision-makers should examine what a null-effect study means before making program decisions
description: This principle holds that practitioners considering a program change, such as "switching curricula or implementing a new schoolwide intervention aimed at behavior," should not take a null finding at face value. The brief advises readers on "what to look for in a study that finds no effect and how you can think about what to do next," treating interpretation of null results as a necessary step before acting.
requirements: Access to the study of the program under consideration, so its null finding can be examined rather than accepted at face value
constraints: The brief addresses school or district decision-makers weighing program choices; its guidance is framed for that audience
target_learners: school and district decision-makers evaluating education programs
target_learning_goals: informed interpretation of evaluation evidence when choosing or continuing education programs
examples: The brief opens with the scenario of a school or district staff member picking up a study of a program and reading that there is no effect, then asks what caused the result and what it means
key_sources: Neil Seftor. (2016). What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels
citation: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935
title: Integrate explainability into predictive LADs to build trust and support uptake
description: The article argues that predictive LADs should expose how models work and why specific predictions were made, since students engage more when they understand outputs. It notes that "detailing the reasons why students receive a particular recommendation has been shown to increase their trust in the system and the likelihood of them following the advice." SensEnablr implements this via SHAP feature-importance visualizations and Anchors rule-based explanations presented in simplified form on the dashboard.
requirements: Explanatory technologies (e.g., SHAP, Anchors) must be integrated alongside predictive models; explanations should be simplified for student comprehension
constraints: When a model produces unexpected or erroneous output, trust is further eroded and could result in rejection by the end user
examples: SensEnablr displays a simplified SHAP feature-importance plot showing top features and their relative strengths, plus Anchors-based IF-ELSE rule explanations for individual predictions
key_sources: Gomathy Ramaswami, Teo Susnjak and Anuradha Mathrani. (2023). Effectiveness of a Learning Analytics Dashboard for Increasing Student Engagement Levels. Journal of Learning Analytics, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2023.7935

article_title: Meeting Families' Needs
citation: Ehrlich, S.B., Allensworth, E.M., & Tansey, J. (2021). Meeting families' needs: Attendance rates in full-day vs. half-day pre-k. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Expand access to full-day pre-k, prioritizing students and families facing the greatest logistical and economic barriers to attendance
description: The article recommends that policymakers increase full-day pre-k availability because it better fits families' daily lives and raises attendance, particularly for groups with historically lower attendance. It states that "Increasing opportunities for full- day programs is especially beneficial for these families" with fewer economic resources, and that districts should consider which students benefit most when deciding program location and enrollment processes.
requirements: Full-day pre-k is more expensive for districts to offer than half-day pre-k, so expansion requires additional investment in teachers and classes.
constraints: The article states full-day programs address some, but not all, logistical barriers; families with limited economic resources still face challenges such as childcare, transportation, and healthcare access.
target_learners: Black students and other groups with historically lower attendance
examples: CPS opened new full-day classrooms in under-enrolled, high-priority neighborhoods and where elementary schools had space; enrollment in full-day pre-k grew from roughly 1,700 students in 2012-13 to more than 6,000 in 2015-16.
The NLCI funded four elementary schools' transition from half-day to full-day pre-k, where the most consistently significant effects of the initiative were found.
key_sources: Ehrlich, S.B., Allensworth, E.M., & Tansey, J. (2021). Meeting families' needs: Attendance rates in full-day vs. half-day pre-k. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/meeting-families-needs

article_title: A Community Effort to Support the Transition from Pre-K to Kindergarten
citation: Spain, A.K., Ehrlich, S.B., Cowhy, J.R., Dasgupta, D.K., & Lockaby, T. (2018). A community effort to support the transition from pre-K to kindergarten. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Provide an external facilitator for multi-school transition programs to sustain collaboration and communicate a consistent vision
description: The report recommends that programs bringing together staff from multiple schools use an external facilitator and coordinator. Planning professional learning community meetings, field trips, and family learning activities took substantial time, and "Having BPI as an external facilitator and coordinator provided leadership around these responsibilities" that teacher ownership would have been hard to sustain. An external facilitator is also positioned to reflect on designing future meetings to better meet the needs of all teachers and families.
requirements: An external facilitator with capacity to plan meetings, field trips, and family learning activities and to communicate a consistent vision of the work
constraints: Especially relevant in the context of teacher and administrator turnover from one year to the next
target_learners: pre-K and kindergarten teachers and families across multiple schools and centers
target_learning_goals: sustained cross-school collaboration supporting children's transition to kindergarten
examples: BPI, a public interest law and policy center, staffed PKTP and provided leadership around planning and coordination across the six Altgeld-Riverdale sites.
key_sources: Spain, A.K., Ehrlich, S.B., Cowhy, J.R., Dasgupta, D.K., & Lockaby, T. (2018). A community effort to support the transition from pre-K to kindergarten. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research and Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/community-effort-support-transition-pre-k-kindergarten

article_title: NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools
citation: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Exclude insufficiently engaged examinees when building assessment norms to protect validity
description: This norming principle holds that test events from examinees who did not engage with the assessment should be removed before estimating norms, because disengaged responses distort the score distributions that norms are built from. The report states: "To improve the validity of norming results, examinees who were not sufﬁciently engaged during the test were not included in the analyses." The 2020 MAP Growth norming study applied this screening as part of its data eligibility criteria.
requirements: A operational way to flag insufficiently engaged test events in the assessment data
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of achievement and growth scores
examples: The 2020 MAP Growth norming study excluded insufficiently engaged examinees from its analyses
key_sources: Thum, Y. M., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). NWEA 2020 MAP Growth Achievement Status and Growth Norms for Students and Schools. NWEA Research Report. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/nwea-2020-map-growth-achievement-status-and-growth-norms-for-students-and-schools/

article_title: A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. NWEA Research presentation, National Council on Measurement in Education 2020 virtual conference. https://www.nwea.org
title: Exclude rapid guesses from scoring because they represent a test taker's choice to opt out of the measurement process
description: The principle holds that because rapid guesses do not reflect what a test taker knows and can do, they do not contribute to measurement and should be excluded from scoring. The authors base this on the belief that "rapid guessing on an item represents a test taker's choice to 'opt out' of the measurement process." The presentation supports the principle through data analyses and previous research findings.
requirements: Response-time data from computer-based test administration must be available to identify rapid-guessing behavior.
constraints: Applies to computer-based tests where disengaged item responses can be identified as rapid-guessing behavior.
target_learners: Test takers on computer-based achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of knowledge, skills, and abilities
examples: The authors contend rapid guesses should be excluded from scoring and provide evidence through data analyses and previous research findings.
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. NWEA Research presentation, National Council on Measurement in Education 2020 virtual conference. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-cessation-of-measurement-identifying-test-taker-disengagement-using-response-time/

article_title: Rapid‐guessing behavior: Its identification, interpretation, and implications
citation: Steven Wise. (2017). Rapid‐guessing behavior: Its identification, interpretation, and implications. Educational Measurement Issues and Practice 36 (4) 52-61. https://doi.org/10.1111/emip.12189
title: Exclude rapid guesses from scoring because they do not contribute to measurement
description: The article recommends that rapid guesses not be counted in scores: "because rapid guesses do not contribute to measurement, it makes little sense to include them in scoring." The rationale follows from the conceptualization of rapid guessing as a momentary opt-out and from the finding that inclusion tends to negatively distort scores and diminish validity. Implementing the principle requires identifying rapid guesses from very short response times before scoring.
requirements: A method for identifying rapid guesses from item-level response time data before scoring occurs
constraints: The article notes there are misconceptions regarding the dynamics of rapid guessing that must be handled for proper interpretation; the supplied text does not print those details
target_learners: Test takers taking computer-based multiple-choice assessments
examples: The article argues that rapid guesses identified via very short response times should be removed from the scored record
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2017). Rapid‐guessing behavior: Its identification, interpretation, and implications. Educational Measurement Issues and Practice 36 (4) 52-61. https://doi.org/10.1111/emip.12189

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Explore existing platform data before fully specifying a research plan to inform questions, design, and sample selection
description: The report advises that DLPs offer access to data on large numbers of users or full user populations, usable for secondary analysis or to refine hypotheses and run power calculations. The stated consideration is "taking time to explore this available data before fully specifying a research plan," because existing data reveal available data structures and user behavior and help relate a planned experimental contrast to current platform activity.
requirements: Access to existing datasets on platform users, or prior-study data providing context on sample sizes and dependent measures
constraints: The depth of existing data varies across platforms; some data may only support school-level covariates rather than individual demographics
target_learners: Education researchers planning studies in DLPs
target_learning_goals: Designing feasible, well-powered studies grounded in real platform data
examples: Platforms may offer data from similar prior studies that provide context on sample sizes and statistics on built-in dependent measures for power calculations
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades
citation: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Provide high-quality vocabulary instruction throughout the day, teaching essential content words in depth and addressing common words, phrases, and expressions not yet learned
description: The guide recommends vocabulary instruction throughout the school day for English learners, graded Strong. Teachers should "Teach essential content words in depth" and also "use instructional time to address the meanings of common words, phrases, and expressions not yet learned." The checklist adds adopting an evidence-based vocabulary approach, developing districtwide lists of essential words drawn from the core reading program and content-area textbooks, and emphasizing everyday words native speakers know that are not necessarily part of the academic curriculum.
requirements: Adopt an evidence-based approach to vocabulary instruction
Develop districtwide lists of essential words drawn from the core reading program and key content-area textbooks
target_learners: English learners in the elementary grades
target_learning_goals: Word meanings, including essential academic content words and everyday words, phrases, and expressions
examples: Districts develop essential-word lists from the core reading program and from textbooks in science and history.
key_sources: Gersten, R., Baker, S.K., Shanahan, T., Linan-Thompson, S., Collins, P., & Scarcella, R. (2007). Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades: A Practice Guide (NCEE 2007-4011). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/6

article_title: Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices
citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Provide explicit vocabulary instruction in reading, language arts, and content-area classes
description: The guide's first recommendation is that teachers "provide students with explicit vocabulary instruction both as part of reading and language arts classes and as part of content-area classes such as science and social studies." It spans two complementary approaches: direct instruction in word meaning (definitions, semantic maps, recitation) and strategies for independent word learning (semantic, syntactic, and context clues). Implementation steps include dedicating lesson time, repeated exposure in multiple contexts, varied use through discussion and writing, and teaching word-analysis strategies.
requirements: Dedicate a portion of regular classroom lessons to explicit vocabulary instruction
Provide repeated exposure to new words in multiple contexts with sufficient practice sessions
Give opportunities to use new vocabulary through discussion, writing, and extended reading
Teach strategies that make students independent vocabulary learners
constraints: Only some studies show effects on standardized reading comprehension measures; the panel states additional research is needed on that relationship
Words appearing only once or twice in a text are typically not targets for explicit instruction
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students, including struggling readers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of academic and content-area vocabulary
examples: The panel rates the evidence strong based on six randomized controlled experimental studies and three well designed quasi-experiments demonstrating group equivalence at pretest, plus a single subject design study.
key_sources: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/8

article_title: Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices
citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Provide opportunities for extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation
description: The guide's third recommendation calls for structured, extended small- and large-group discussion of what texts mean and how they should be interpreted. "There is evidence that encouraging high-quality discussion about texts, even in the absence of explicit instruction in reading comprehension strategies, can have a positive impact on reading comprehension skills." Discussion also gives teachers a window into students' thinking that can inform future instruction. Implementation includes preparing engaging materials and questions, using follow-up questions, and developing a specific discussion protocol for small groups.
requirements: Carefully prepare by selecting engaging materials and developing stimulating questions
Ask follow-up questions that provide continuity and extend the discussion
Provide a task or discussion format students can follow in small groups
Develop and practice the use of a specific discussion protocol
constraints: The evidence base is rated moderate rather than strong by the panel
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students in content-area classes
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and interpretation of texts
examples: The guide notes one study in which discussion improved knowledge of word meanings and relationships for students reading biology texts.
key_sources: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/8

article_title: Preparing Young Children for School
citation: Burchinal, M., Krowka, S., Newman-Gonchar, R., Jayanthi, M., Gersten, R., Wavell, S., Lyskawa, J., Haymond, K., Bierman, K., Gonzalez, J. E., McClelland, M. M., Nelson, K., Pentimonti, J., Purpura, D. J., Sachs, J., Sarama, J., Schlesinger-Devlin, E., Washington, J., & Rosen, E. (2022). Preparing Young Children for School (WWC 2022009). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://whatworks.ed.gov/
title: Strengthen children's executive function skills using specific games and activities
description: The guide recommends planning games and activities that build paying attention, following directions, thinking flexibly, and self-control. It defines the construct directly: "Executive function skills include paying attention, following directions, thinking flexibly, and exhibiting self-control and self -regulation." Teachers can use games where rules change or children move from follower to leader, increase challenge over time, and embed executive function activities in literacy, mathematics, and arts-and-crafts routines.
requirements: Games and activities planned to create practice opportunities
Progressive increase in challenge over time
constraints: The guide assigned this recommendation a moderate, not strong, level of evidence
examples: Games to practice following directions, thinking flexibly, and controlling impulses
a game where rules are changed
a game where children go from being a follower to being a leader

article_title: Deepening Science Engagement With Challenge Based Learning: Research Report
citation: Iwatani, E., Means, B., Romero, M. R., & Vang, M. C. (2020). Deepening Science Engagement with Challenge Based Learning: Research Report. San Mateo, CA: Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Professional learning for student-centered science instruction should be experiential, sustained, and relationship-based rather than sporadic half-day sessions
description: The report argues that transforming teachers' values and behaviors toward student-centered instruction requires professional learning that builds on existing expertise, is experiential and affective, professionally relevant, organized around value-laden goals, provides sustained critical reflection, and is founded on authentic relationships. Sporadic half-day sessions are deemed insufficient to overcome over-reliance on teacher-directed transmission.
requirements: Significant experiential component
Leadership support
Modeling of the target instructional approach
Ongoing learning community
Multiple iterations with feedback and reflection
constraints: Not all professional development can or should be as extended and participant-centered as this project's model
examples: The project used two multi-day design workshops with participatory observation, reflection opportunities, and district-level instructional and emotional support

article_title: Foundations for Young Adult Success: A Developmental Framework
citation: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). A Framework for Developing Young Adult Success in the 21st Century: White Paper — Defining Young Adult Success. University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research Working Paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/framework-developing-young-adult-success-21st-century
title: Taxonomy of existing competency models: 21st century skills, MHA Labs building blocks, NRC three domains, CASEL five competencies, Conley four keys
description: Section 2 organizes the landscape of models the authors reviewed (over 20 existing models and frameworks) into named exemplars: the 21st century skills framework (the 4 Cs, media/information/technology skills, life and career skills); MHA Labs' six building blocks comprising 35 core skills; the NRC classification with "the cognitive domain... the intrapersonal domain... and the interpersonal domain"; CASEL's five interrelated SEL competencies; and Conley's four keys to college and career readiness. The framework positions itself as extending these toward a broader definition of success.
requirements: The framework builds on this body of work by articulating relationships among critical factors and adding a developmental, settings-spanning lens
constraints: The authors note the broader definition poses challenges for measurement and adds ambiguity
target_learners: K-12 and post-secondary students transitioning to young adulthood
target_learning_goals: mapping competencies, mindsets, and skills needed for college, career, and civic success
examples: CASEL's five competencies (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, responsible decision-making) are presented as one reviewed model the new framework extends
key_sources: Nagaoka, J., Farrington, C. A., Ehrlich, S. B., with Johnson, D. W., Dickson, S., Heath, R., & Mayo, A. (2014). A Framework for Developing Young Adult Success in the 21st Century: White Paper — Defining Young Adult Success. University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research Working Paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/framework-developing-young-adult-success-21st-century

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Two discourse types — exploratory and explanatory — comprise English learners' interactional opportunities
description: The brief organizes collaborative interaction into two discourse types. It states that "Exploratory discourse supports students to speculate, imagine, and conjecture about what might be and to jointly construct new understandings," while explanatory discourse supports sharing what they know, developing arguments, constructing explanations, and providing descriptive accounts. The two types carry different language requirements for vocabulary and sentence structure, so teachers can scaffold disciplinary language, for example by role-playing conversational moves. The brief cites Legare (2014) and Bunch (2014) for this distinction.
requirements: Teachers call attention to and provide scaffolding for how to achieve the purposes of exploratory or explanatory discourse through disciplinary language.
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge and language development through academic discourse
examples: Teachers design regular opportunities for academic discourse based on meaningful prompts and tasks with well-structured routines and appropriate linguistic support.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/

article_title: AI-Driven Educational Reform: Enhancing Talent Cultivation in Computer-Related Majors for the Digital Era
citation: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916
title: Expanded AI competency framework adding technological adaptability and cross-cultural collaboration sub-competencies
description: Building on Huang's AI competency framework of knowledge, team, and learning competence with six sub-competencies, the authors extended it for the AI era. As printed, "we further expanded upon this framework by incorporating two additional sub-competencies: Technological Awareness and Adaptability Competence and Cross-cultural Collaboration Competence." The first emphasizes staying informed about emerging technologies and adapting to unforeseen technological change; the second equips students to communicate, collaborate, and problem-solve in diverse, multicultural teams as AI technologies are developed and deployed globally.
requirements: The expansion responds to fast-paced developments in AI requiring students to adapt quickly to new tools and technologies
constraints: Derived from Huang's framework as applied in China's AI education reforms
examples: Knowledge Competence combines technical skills such as programming, algorithms, machine learning, and data analysis with understanding of social, cultural, and ethical implications
key_sources: Wang J and Li P (2026). AI-driven educational reform: enhancing talent cultivation in computer-related majors for the digital era. Front. Psychol. 17:1790916. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1790916

article_title: Large Scale AI Grading of Handwritten Physics Assessments: Score Agreement and Olympiad Team Selection Outcomes
citation: Praveen Pathak, Siddharth Tiwary, Charudatt Kadolkar, Vijay Singh, David Rakestraw, Shirish Pathare, and Anwesh Mazumdar. (2026). Large-scale AI grading of handwritten physics assessments: Score agreement and Olympiad team selection outcomes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20521
title: Before AI grading is attempted, rubrics should state as explicitly as possible the conditions for awarding marks, common deductions, acceptable alternatives, and carried-forward-error rules
description: The article finds that rubric detail was central to strong AI–human agreement and that disagreements arose where rubrics stated a broad goal while leaving the required physics implicit. It recommends that "the rubric should state as explicitly as possible the conditions for awarding marks, common deductions, acceptable alternative solutions, and carried-forward-error rules." Focused refinements making such conditions explicit reduced AI–official differences on the tested questions.
requirements: Access to the official rubrics and model solutions used for human grading
constraints: Refined-instruction gains were demonstrated on the specific refined questions and should be confirmed on a holdout set, per the article
target_learners: Examination bodies and examiners grading handwritten physics responses
target_learning_goals: Reliable AI-assisted partial-credit grading aligned with official examiner standards
examples: The refined OE2 T–S graph rubric stated required branch shapes and temperature ordering, after which AI stopped awarding shape credit in incorrect-curvature cases
key_sources: Praveen Pathak, Siddharth Tiwary, Charudatt Kadolkar, Vijay Singh, David Rakestraw, Shirish Pathare, and Anwesh Mazumdar. (2026). Large-scale AI grading of handwritten physics assessments: Score agreement and Olympiad team selection outcomes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20521

article_title: Child Safety in Generative AI: An Expert-Guided and Incident-Grounded Evaluation Framework
citation: Haein Kong. (2026). Child Safety in Generative AI: An Expert-Guided and Incident-Grounded Evaluation Framework. HEAL@CHI, April 2026, Barcelona. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00395
title: Child-centered AI safety evaluation framework integrating expert guidelines with real-world AI incident data
description: The article introduces an evaluation framework for child safety in generative AI that combines two resources: expert-proposed child safety guidelines and AI incident databases. It first constructs "a taxonomy of child safety risk categories informed by expert guidance," then leverages incident data to build a synthetic test set reflecting realistic harmful scenarios. The framework is designed to be flexible and extensible so it can respond rapidly to real-world AI incidents, addressing the gap that most existing safety benchmarks focus on general adult user populations.
requirements: Requires expert-proposed child safety guidelines and AI incident databases as its two source resources
constraints: The study applies the framework only to education-related risks and evaluates only Llama Guard models
target_learners: children and adolescents using generative AI
target_learning_goals: safe educational use of generative AI systems
examples: Applied as a case study to the education domain, generating a 130-prompt test set and evaluating three Llama Guard models on it
key_sources: Haein Kong. (2026). Child Safety in Generative AI: An Expert-Guided and Incident-Grounded Evaluation Framework. HEAL@CHI, April 2026, Barcelona. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00395

article_title: Collaborative Making of a Boundary Object for Classifying Generative AI Learning Activities
citation: Dohn, N. B., Markauskaite, L., Huber, E., Wardak, D., Yang, H., Zeivots, S., Casey, A., van Diggele, C., Dohn, N. B., Mannix, K., Mantai, L., Pressick-Kilborn, K., Spence, N., Vallis, C., & Wilson, S. (2026). Collaborative Making of a Boundary Object for Classifying Generative AI Learning Activities. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00671-3
title: Extend epistemic engagement categories beyond cognitive terms to include social and emotional engagement
description: The article argues that describing Epistemic Engagement "in what appear to be purely cognitive terms" is problematic because "other kinds of engagement, particularly social and emotional engagement, are inseparable from cognitive engagement." Emotions form an integral part of learning, especially when GenAI outputs are unpredictable, and group interaction helped students draft prompts and evaluate outputs. The entwinement of cognitive, social and emotional aspects was closely related to critical stance and identity formation, and the terms understanding, critiquing, using, and creating are interconnected and iterative.
requirements: Recognition that students' emotional states affect their reactions, especially when introducing new technologies
Attention to social settings, where interaction success or breakdown amplifies emotional engagement
constraints: Distinctions between screen-based and paper-based, human and non-human elements were blurred in the tested examples
examples: In Example 3, a GenAI law client responded helpfully when students displayed professional empathy, foregrounding emotional engagement
In a cited study by Yang and Markauskaite (2025), group discussion helped student teachers draft prompts and evaluate GenAI outputs

article_title: Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing
citation: Li, H. and Zhang, W. (2026). Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1871022. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871022
title: Newly developed three-item External Mandate scale
description: The External Mandate (EM) measurement scale was "specifically developed for this study" as a unidimensional, three-item construct operationalizing mandated technology adoption and external regulation within SDT. Items capture instructor-required AI use, AI revision being a mandatory grading requirement, and using AI because the teacher forces it. Its Cronbach's alpha was 0.880, with CR = 0.932 and AVE = 0.822.
requirements: Wording explicitly emphasizes the mandatory nature of the grading policy, revised after pilot feedback that general suggestions and grading requirements were ambiguous.
target_learners: University EFL students subject to instructor-mandated generative AI use
target_learning_goals: Measuring perceived externally mandated AI use in academic writing
examples: Sample item: "My instructor explicitly requires me to use generative AI tools to complete my English writing assignments".
key_sources: Li, H. and Zhang, W. (2026). Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1871022. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871022

article_title: Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills
citation: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864
title: The Executive LLM as a computerized adaptive test of complex behaviors
description: The Executive LLM is a single LLM that generates responses for all AI teammates, has access to the pedagogical rubrics, and is prompted to "create situations that will allow the subject to demonstrate their skill, so that their skill level can be quantitatively inferred". The article frames it as analogous to a computerized adaptive test: whereas traditional CAT varies only item difficulty in a narrow domain, the Executive LLM varies the flow of a group conversation — heightening or softening conflicts, creating project-management needs, or eliciting creative ideas — to maximize information about the test-taker while keeping the interaction naturalistic.
requirements: Access to the scoring rubrics as prompt input so steering targets the dimensions under assessment
constraints: Replacing human teammates with AI trades some authenticity for comparability and reliability
A completely unconstrained conversation likely will not efficiently provide the evidence of interest
target_learning_goals: Collaboration, creativity, and critical thinking proficiency measurement
examples: In the Debate task, the Executive LLM reasoned internally and responded as teammate Leo to steer toward conflict resolution evidence
key_sources: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Know why you are acting: explicit goals should guide technology use at every level of educational practice
description: Principle 0 of the framework holds that "Know why you are acting -- whether at the highest level or specific class activity" — the goals one prioritizes ought to inform the actions one takes and how one leverages new technologies. The article treats this as the foundational move that makes the later role-allocation principles coherent, noting goals can be multifaceted and potentially contradictory.
requirements: Practitioners must articulate their goals, from institutional mission down to individual class activities, before deploying technologies
constraints: The article acknowledges that goals in education systems are regularly contradictory, so no single prioritization is prescribed
target_learning_goals: alignment of educational practices with explicitly chosen goals
examples: The article asks whether technologies will support the development of more self-realized, empathetic, community engaged, rational, civic, and artistic individuals
key_sources: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01467

article_title: Transforming Curriculum Design with Generative AI: A Model for Assessing Teacher Digital Competence
citation: Guillén-Gámez, F. D., Tomczyk, Ł., Habibi, A., & Díaz Vargas, B. L. (2026). Transforming curriculum design with generative AI: a model for assessing teacher digital competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10647-6
title: Extended Technology Acceptance Model for GenAI integration in curriculum planning
description: The article proposes an extended version of Davis's Technology Acceptance Model applied to GenAI tools in curriculum design. "The model included factors such as Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Enjoyment, Self-Efficacy, Attitude of Use, and Behavioural Intention, analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM)." Self-efficacy is the only exogenous factor; PU, PEOU, PE, AOU, BI and digital competence are endogenous. The novel contribution is the explicitly modelled path from behavioural intention to pedagogical digital competence, which "in the traditional TAM model... had not previously been explicitly demonstrated".
requirements: Measurement of all seven latent factors as reflective constructs on a 7-point Likert scale, with reliability (α, CR > .70) and convergent validity (AVE > .50) established
constraints: Digital competence is operationalized as self-reported pedagogical competence, "rather than objective performance-based competence"; the model was tested only at the overall sample level in the Dominican Republic
target_learners: In-service teachers across early childhood, primary, secondary and higher education in the Dominican Republic
target_learning_goals: Developing teachers' pedagogical digital competence for planning and integrating GenAI tools (text, image, multimedia, video) into curriculum design
examples: The instrument was validated with 434 in-service teachers using a three-round expert review and PLS-SEM in Smart-PLS 4, with all twelve hypothesised paths supported
key_sources: Guillén-Gámez, F. D., Tomczyk, Ł., Habibi, A., & Díaz Vargas, B. L. (2026). Transforming curriculum design with generative AI: a model for assessing teacher digital competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10647-6

article_title: Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment
citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Rubric design pattern: interaction-scale D1 (0–4) plus expert-anchored evaluation-scale D2 (0–3) with the expert answer key as external calibration standard
description: Across both tasks, one rubric captures Physics-Driven AI Interaction and one captures Physics-Grounded Evaluation. "The D1 rubric is a 0–4 scale that captures the degree to which students use disciplinary physics knowledge to structure and drive their AI interaction," evaluating the entire interaction rather than the initial prompt alone. "The D2 rubric is a 0–3 scale that captures the accuracy and depth of students' physical judgment about AI-generated content," with the expert answer key as the external calibration standard for the highest performance levels.
requirements: An expert answer key identifying key errors and assumptions is needed to calibrate the highest D2 performance levels
constraints: Rubrics are task-specific in their examples and physical conditions, though the underlying scoring logic is shared within each dimension
target_learning_goals: Physics-driven AI interaction and physics-grounded evaluation
examples: The highest D2 score requires the student to independently identify at least one expert-anchored error with physical justification, without having been prompted by AI output
key_sources: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24837

article_title: Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning
citation: Fathima Ameen, Tasmia Shahriar, Aditi Mallavarapu, Shiyan Jiang, Noboru Matsuda. (2026). Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning. Behaviormetrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-026-00294-9
title: ExpectAdapt: an expectation-tailored adaptive questioning framework of three stacked LLMs for teachable agents
description: ExpectAdapt (Expectation-tailored Adaptive Questioning Framework) generates adaptive follow-up questions after a tutor answers a static focal question. It consists of "three stacked Large Language Models (LLMs)": an Expected Response Generator, an Alignment Detector, and a Follow-up Question Generator, all using GPT-3.5-turbo via the OpenAI API. The Alignment Detector compares the tutor's response to an expected response and, in the study, "classified 69% of KBR and 63% of KTR as aligned"; the generator targets uncovered conceptual stems, with a maximum of three follow-ups per focal question.
requirements: Requires an expected-response generator supplied with domain-specific conceptual assertions and an expert role prompt to minimize mathematical errors
Requires the follow-up generator to stop once all stems from the expected response have been addressed
constraints: A follow-up question is generated only when the response is classified as aligned, to avoid being out of context or overly corrective
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8) learning algebraic equation solving
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge and procedural skill in algebraic equation solving
shifting tutors from knowledge-telling to knowledge-building responses
examples: In the study, ExpectAdapt was integrated into APLUS so SimStudent posed follow-up questions such as "Are all equations with no coefficient done?" after shallow tutor responses
key_sources: Fathima Ameen, Tasmia Shahriar, Aditi Mallavarapu, Shiyan Jiang, Noboru Matsuda. (2026). Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning. Behaviormetrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-026-00294-9

article_title: Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents
citation: Lan Anh Do, Hanling Jiang, Shuchin Aeron, Ayanna K. Thomas. (2026). Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28651
title: Extended 7-point ICAP framework for cognitive engagement in collaborative discourse
description: The article extends the ICAP framework (Passive, Active, Constructive, Interactive) into a 7-point ordered scale with intermediate levels between adjacent modes, to "capture differences in participation when instances did not align cleanly with a single mode". Level 1 is passive listening, Level 3 active participation such as agreement, Level 5 constructive proposals with reasoning, and Levels 6–7 sustained two- or three-plus-turn interactive exchanges. It was used to code trial-level engagement of individuals in three-person collaborative problem solving.
requirements: Trained annotators and a codebook with criteria for each level; turn boundaries defined as all utterances by one speaker until another begins
constraints: Developed and validated on a single logical inference task (letters-to-numbers) with undergraduate three-person groups; mid-level categories (3–5) showed the greatest ambiguity
target_learners: undergraduate students working in three-person groups
target_learning_goals: characterizing cognitive engagement during collaborative problem-solving discourse
examples: Annotators labeled each trial's expression and guess phases; Criteria Version 2 added detailed rules such as counting simple corrections as Level 3 and random guesses as Level 5
key_sources: Lan Anh Do, Hanling Jiang, Shuchin Aeron, Ayanna K. Thomas. (2026). Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28651

article_title: A Semi-Automated System for Generating Dialogue-Based TTS Lessons Using Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study of Educational Potential
citation: Gendo Kumoi, Fumie Watanabe, Tota Suko, Takashi Ishida, Yuko Kuma, Manabu Kobayashi, and Shigeichi Hirasawa. (2026). A Semi-Automated System for Generating Dialogue-Based TTS Lessons Using Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study of Educational Potential. Preprint, under review at IEEE Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12235
title: Expert–Novice dialogue narration design inspired by cognitive apprenticeship theory
description: The article adapts cognitive apprenticeship theory to author fixed Expert–Novice dialogue narration in advance, rather than as live interaction. The Expert "is responsible for providing accurate knowledge, offering explanations through metaphors and concrete examples", while the Novice "acts as a proxy for the learner by asking naive questions", rephrasing in their own words, and confirming understanding. Table 2 maps dialogue elements to cognitive apprenticeship: modeling as verbalization of the Expert's thought process, coaching as Expert responses to the Novice, and scaffolding as stepwise support via the five-stage pattern. The design aims to preemptively resolve learners' latent questions and provide vicarious experience.
requirements: Two distinct TTS voices assigned to the personas (Enceladus for Expert, Autonoe for Novice) with prompt-engineered speaker characteristics
constraints: Fading (gradual reduction of support) is not realized; the system borrows only the inspiration of the Expert–×–Novice dialogue structure
What learners receive is a fixed artifact rather than an interaction, which the authors state is what makes it deliverable at curriculum scale and also what limits it
target_learning_goals: understanding of lesson concepts through vicarious dialogue and self-explanation
examples: The dialogue TTS lesson on a framework for data-driven decision-making was generated with this structure and delivered as a 22 min 14 s video
key_sources: Gendo Kumoi, Fumie Watanabe, Tota Suko, Takashi Ishida, Yuko Kuma, Manabu Kobayashi, and Shigeichi Hirasawa. (2026). A Semi-Automated System for Generating Dialogue-Based TTS Lessons Using Large Language Models: An Exploratory Study of Educational Potential. Preprint, under review at IEEE Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12235

article_title: 'I can''t read your mind": A Study of Neurodivergent Computing Students'' Experiences with Collaborative Active Learning'
citation: Cynthia Zastudil, Srishty Muthusekaran, Rayhona Nasimova, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). “I can’t read your mind”: A Study of Neurodivergent Computing Students’ Experiences with Collaborative Active Learning. Proceedings of the 31st ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 1 (ITiCSE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3803400.3809386
title: Design collaborative active learning with explicit expectations and predictable guardrails for neurodivergent computing students
description: The article recommends designing collaborative active learning around explicit, predictable structures for neurodivergent students. It argues its survey and interview results "provide evidence to support recommendations from previous position papers" for "explicit and unambiguous instructions and expectations for assignments", and proposes building "guardrails to assignments that promote consistency and predictability" such as team contracts, regular schedules, and consistent feedback loops.
requirements: Assignments must carry explicit, unambiguous guidelines and expectations, including what is expected at the end of each iteration and what counts as done; the article also names consistent feedback and predictable team structures as supports.
constraints: The authors present these as preliminary results from small samples and caution that findings are not meant to be generalized to the broader ND computing student population, as neurodiversity is a highly individual experience.
The article notes self-disclosure of access needs can be uncomfortable, emotionally taxing, and expose students to bias and stigma, motivating anonymous disclosure as an alternative.
target_learners: neurodivergent computing students, specifically autistic students and students with ADHD
target_learning_goals: comfort and sense of belonging in collaborative active learning
computing coursework completed through collaborative team activities
examples: Interview participants suggested introducing low-stakes collaborative activities earlier and more frequently, adding consistent feedback, and designing projects that incorporate personal interests or real-world applications.
The discussion proposes anonymous disclosure of access needs to reduce the burden of self-disclosure while helping ND students receive accommodations.

(2026). “I can’t read your mind”: A Study of Neurodivergent Computing Students’ Experiences with Collaborative Active Learning. article_title: From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education
citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: Exercise coverage must match content coverage in self-paced quantum courses
description: Drawn from the dead zone finding, this principle holds that students treat exercises as the operational definition of required material in a self-paced course. The article states that "Any quantum concept without a corresponding implementation exercise risks being skipped regardless of its importance". In the pilot, students stopped watching the Module 2 lecture where exercise coverage ended, and the instructor closed the gap by adding multi-qubit checkpoints. Designers should map every lecture concept to at least one implementation exercise.
requirements: A checkpoint or exercise should exist for each lecture concept instructors expect students to engage with
constraints: Evidence comes from a single pilot deployment with five graduate students and no control group
target_learners: graduate students in self-paced quantum computing courses
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement with full curriculum content, including multi-qubit and entanglement topics
examples: The instructor revised the Module 2 exercise set to include multi-qubit checkpoints after the analytics agent identified the coverage gap
key_sources: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Extended Strobel taxonomy of five student–GenAI entanglement types organized by degree of creativity and degree of modification
description: The paper extends Strobel et al.'s (2024) taxonomy of GenAI applications — originally derived from 100 commercial and professional applications — into a classification lens for educational settings. The five types are Generator, Reimaginator, Synthesizer, Assistant, and Enabler, differing along two dimensions: "the degree of creativity — the extent to which GenAI output aims to innovate rather than improve, and 2) the degree of modification — the extent to which the GenAI output departs from the input." Each type is operationalized for higher education (e.g., Enabler reinterpreted as a competence-scaffolding role targeting higher-order competences), enabling classification of how epistemic work is distributed between student and GenAI in a learning activity.
requirements: Each study is assigned one primary category, since the analytical question of which entanglement type a study foregrounds is single-valued
constraints: The taxonomy was originally designed to describe commercial GenAI applications, and the Enabler category required substantial reinterpretation for educational settings
target_learning_goals: literacy in student–GenAI entangled academic practices
examples: A nursing student prompting GenAI to draft a patient care plan from a brief case description exemplifies Generator; a structured argumentation exercise with GenAI to strengthen critical thinking exemplifies Enabler
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: The Competence Paradox: Negotiating Ease, Risk, and Creative Identity in Text-to-Image Generative AI Use Among Art and Design Students
citation: Liu Y, Meng M and Zhang Y (2026) The competence paradox: negotiating ease, risk, and creative identity in text-to-image generative AI use among art and design students. Front. Psychol. 17:1858187. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1858187
title: Extended UTAUT framework with creative competence for T2I GenAI adoption in studio-based creative education
description: The article builds a contextualized extension of UTAUT for text-to-image generative AI in art and design education. It retains the four canonical constructs and adds novelty value, perceived risk, and a new domain-specific construct: "we conceptualize Creative Competence (CC) as a domain-speciﬁc self-eﬃcacy construct" capturing the ability to translate ideas into prompts, steer outputs via advanced controls, iteratively revise generations, and critically evaluate alignment with creative vision. The framework treats adoption as shaped by risk interpretation and creative identity, not solely utilitarian predictors.
requirements: Requires instructor-informed, context-specific model building: Study 1 focus groups identified the extension constructs before the survey
constraints: The article states the SEM showed acceptable but not optimal fit (CFI = 0.873, TLI = 0.849) and explained limited variance in use behavior and perceived risk
Sample drawn from a single national context and relatively well-resourced institutions, interpreted as context-sensitive rather than universally generalizable
target_learners: Higher education art and design students (undergraduate and graduate)
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting students' adoption and selective use of text-to-image generative AI in studio coursework
examples: Study 2 tested the model with a questionnaire of 417 students (400 retained) across three Chinese universities using two-step SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects
key_sources: Liu Y, Meng M and Zhang Y (2026) The competence paradox: negotiating ease, risk, and creative identity in text-to-image generative AI use among art and design students. Front. Psychol. 17:1858187. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1858187

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Extended Taxonomy Design Process (ETDP) as an iterative method for building taxonomies
description: The ETDP, described by Kundisch et al. and adopted as this article's method, is an iterative, user-centered taxonomy design methodology with six phases: problem specification, objective definition (including a meta-characteristic and ending conditions), development, demonstration and analysis, evaluation, and communication. The article emphasizes that "the ETDP is inherently iterative, allowing taxonomy designers to continuously update, extend, and refine existing taxonomies without restarting the entire design procedure". It supports both empirical-to-conceptual and conceptual-to-empirical building approaches.
requirements: Designers must determine the meta-characteristic, objective and subjective ending conditions, and evaluation goals upfront
constraints: Taxonomies should be judged by suitability for their intended purpose, not as right or wrong
target_learners: taxonomy designers and computing education researchers
target_learning_goals: structuring and classifying phenomena such as student difficulties
examples: This article applies the ETDP with a conceptual-to-empirical start, justified by the existing substantial body of research on student difficulties
key_sources: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966

article_title: Can students identify AI? – A cross-sectional quantitative study about AI recognition in tablet-based MCQ assessment among fifth-year undergraduate medical students at Saarland University, Germany
citation: Vogt P, Wolf N, Jordan S, Volz-Willems S, Jäger J, Dupont F. (2026). Can students identify AI? – A cross-sectional quantitative study about AI recognition in tablet-based MCQ assessment among fifth-year undergraduate medical students at Saarland University, Germany. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10410-8
title: Expert-panel human-review workflow for AI-generated MCQ drafting in a high-stakes exam
description: A structured workflow in which LLMs (ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro) received the full blended-learning curriculum and generated MCQs via sequential prompting, followed by expert-panel review. The panel "accepted 82% of the questions", applied "limited expert refinement" to retained items, and excluded items needing substantial revision; 30 AI questions (18 ChatGPT, 12 Gemini) entered the exam. The authors position it so "AI-generated MCQs serve as template, while humans remain responsible for quality control".
requirements: Human expert panel review of all generated items before exam use
Provision of the full curriculum and learning materials to the LLMs for generation
constraints: 18.2% of initially generated MCQs had to be eliminated, showing the necessity of human oversight
A visible bias underestimating FM competency was observed during human evaluation, e.g. distractors suggesting referrals for abdominal ultrasound, a common FM task
target_learning_goals: Family Medicine clinical decision-making and clinical reasoning assessment
examples: In the 2024 FM examination, 44 LLM-generated MCQs were reviewed, 36 (81.8%) accepted, and 30 used alongside 30 NLE questions under a 90-minute time limit

article_title: Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency
citation: Sverrir Thorgeirsson, Theo B. Weidmann, and Zhendong Su. 2026. Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791666
title: Expert-vetted assessment suite of GUI-oriented vibe-coding tasks with scoring criteria
description: A curated set of natural-language programming tasks for measuring GUI-oriented vibe-coding proficiency, produced via a two-stage Delphi-style consensus process with eight subject-matter experts from four countries. The article states it offers "an expert-designed set of natural-language programming tasks produced via a structured consensus process with eight subject-matter experts", accompanied by clear scoring criteria and predefined rubrics, intended to support replication, cross-cohort comparison, and possibly instructional use. Tasks were rated on interdisciplinarity, authenticity, challenge, purpose clarity, and culture fairness, with selected tasks reaching median ratings of at least 4.
requirements: Tasks must meet the panel's seven criteria, including that the topic "should resonate beyond computer science, engaging at least one other domain" and be implementable end-to-end in roughly 10–15 minutes of iterative prompting.
constraints: The suite targets "pure" or no-code vibe coding and captures only a limited subset of more algorithmic-centric vibe coding.

target_learning_goals: vibe-coding proficiency: iteratively specifying, refining, and debugging program behavior through text prompts and observed behavior alone
examples: Selected tasks included an exam scheduler, a meal planner, and a course registration platform; a third, deliberately decontextualized toy application was added to stress expressive specification without LLM-helpful task labels.

article_title: Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course
citation: Dang, C. T., & Nguyen, A. (2026). Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course.
title: Issue AI-generated study materials only after checking by a named expert who is disclosed to students
description: The article defines expert-verified AI study materials by "three jointly necessary features": generation "by a source-grounded model from the course’s own documents", checking "by a named expert before release", and a label disclosing "both their AI origin and their verification". Verification screens errors, signals a low-cost reason to engage, and relocates rather than removes labour. The article recommends assigning verification to staff with subject expertise and a teaching relationship with students, counting it in workload allocations, and keeping a log of verification time and changes per item.
requirements: A named verifier with subject expertise and a relationship with the students, since trust attached to a verifier students knew from tutorials
constraints: Source-grounding reduces but does not eliminate hallucination, which is why named verification is required; a label naming an unknown or anonymous checker may not carry the same weight, and a label can keep signalling after checking becomes cursory
target_learners: undergraduate students in large introductory courses where prior preparation varies most
target_learning_goals: examination performance on core course content, particularly for lower-attaining students
examples: In 2024/25 the Part 2 lecturer generated podcasts, FAQs and study guides in Google NotebookLM from course documents; the GTA checked definitions, terminology, examples and quiz answers against sources, revising prompts or regenerating sections rather than accepting first drafts; producing and verifying each weekly set took about 30 minutes.

article_title: AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education
citation: Linus Brunnström & Lisa Palmqvist. (2026). AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261
title: Teachers should explicitly teach AI-interaction literacy, with particular attention to students with lower academic self-efficacy or less developed study skills
description: The article proposes that higher education teachers develop an explicit strategy for teaching students how to use GenAI in self-regulated learning, treating productive GenAI use as a learned competence rather than an intuitive one. This means teaching "how to formulate productive prompts, how to recognise when a response is too abstract or too broad, and how to structure a learning session around small, manageable goals". The responsibility for cultivating this competence, the authors argue, cannot rest with the student alone.
requirements: Teachers need an explicit strategy for teaching GenAI-supported self-regulated learning, not only disciplinary content.
constraints: Without such instruction, the article states GenAI risks becoming a tool that widens rather than narrows the performance gap between students.
target_learners: higher education students, particularly those with lower academic self-efficacy or less developed study skills
examples: The demonstration's own calibration work — requesting simplification, narrowing scope, and condensing an overwhelming plan into a three-step loop — illustrates the competence the principle says should be taught.

article_title: AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought
citation: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013
title: Expanded versus novel epistemic practices when students form hybrid minds with AI as an external memory system
description: The article's organizing taxonomy distinguishes expanded (or transformed) epistemic practices, where AI substitutes or augments existing tools and sequences of steps, from genuinely novel epistemic practices, where AI enables processes previously impossible without external human input — particularly theoretical and empirical reflection. It builds on Säljö's hybrid minds account, in which "Hybrid minds operate in environments of external symbolic storages where human reasoning is located at the intersection of the human mind and external, technological resources", and on Salomon et al.'s cognitive partnership concept. Figure 3 summarizes expanded and novel practices of reflective thought using AI.
requirements: Students must engage with AI as a cognitive partner within learning processes rather than merely outsourcing tasks
constraints: Novel practices of examination or construction may only emerge under certain conditions, whereas theoretical and empirical reflection reveal distinct novel components
target_learning_goals: epistemic practices of learning and knowledge construction with generative AI
examples: Customized overviews of a subject area and co-generated idea catalogues are given as cases where novel examination or construction practices may emerge

article_title: Towards trustworthy and explainable-by-design large language models for automated teacher assessment
citation: Li, Y.; Yang, H.; Fang, Q. (2025). Towards Trustworthy and Explainable-by-Design Large Language Models for Automated Teacher Assessment. Information 2025, 16, 882. https://doi.org/10.3390/info16100882
title: Explainable-by-design framework coupling dual-lens hierarchical attention, trust-gated inference, and on-the-spot explanation generation
description: The framework is an LLM-based teacher assessment architecture in which trustworthiness and explainability are built into inference rather than appended afterward. It couples "a global lens aligned to curriculum standards and a local lens aligned to subject-specific rubrics" with a Trust-Gated Inference module combining Monte-Carlo-dropout calibration and adversarial debiasing, and an On-the-Spot Explanation generator that shares the same fused representation and predicted score used for decision making, so explanations are decision-consistent and curriculum-anchored. Trust gating exposes uncertainty and bias alerts and can output Reject with reason.
requirements: Training data with human-annotated rubric scores and expert explanations
A learnable key/value memory of curriculum standards and rubric descriptors for the global attention lens
constraints: Experiments primarily evaluate text and ASR transcripts due to dataset availability, not full multimodal input
Monte Carlo dropout and layered attention increase inference latency by 18.3% relative to BERT
target_learning_goals: Rubric-aligned evaluation of pedagogical practices such as formative questioning, feedback quality, and cognitive demand
examples: In a mathematics lesson case study the model noted insufficient formative questioning, aligning with rubric criterion 4.2 and matching expert annotations
