article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect
citation: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4
title: The expertise reversal effect: the reversal of cognitive load effects with increasing learner expertise, explained by schema-based guidance replacing instruction-based guidance
description: The article names and substantively describes the expertise reversal effect as "the reversal of cognitive load ef- fects with expertise": instructional techniques highly effective for inexperienced learners lose effectiveness or become negative for experienced learners. Its cognitive-load explanation is that novices lack schemas, so instructional guidance acts as a substitute, while experts' activated schemas provide full guidance, and redundancy between the two causes cross-referencing that "will require addi- tional working memory resources and might cause a cognitive overload." The review traces the effect's interaction with split-attention, redundancy, modality, worked-example, isolated-interacting elements, and imagination effects.
requirements: Instructional designs must be tailored to the level of experience of intended learners, without which "the effectiveness of instructional designs is likely to be random."
constraints: In the isolated-interacting elements studies the review reports no full reversal, only elimination of the effect with increased expertise.
target_learners: learners at all levels of domain-specific expertise, from novices to experienced learners
examples: The review cites experiments on electrical circuit diagrams, industrial machinery instruction, mechanical trade apprenticeship, spreadsheet learning, and database use in which effects reversed or disappeared with increased expertise.
key_sources: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4

article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect
citation: Chen, O., Kalyuga, S. & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9359-1
title: Unified cognitive load account: the expertise reversal effect as a variant of the element interactivity effect
description: The article proposes, within cognitive load theory, a unifying account in which the expertise reversal effect is subsumed under the element interactivity effect. It argues that "the two effects may be intertwined with the expertise reversal effect constituting a particular example of the element interactivity effect." On this account, both effects reflect the same underlying mechanism — changes in the number of interacting elements that must be processed in working memory — triggered by different factors. The article supports the contention with empirical evidence from prior studies.
requirements: Both effects must be interpreted within the framework of cognitive load theory, where element interactivity determines working memory load
constraints: The article presents this as an argued contention supported by empirical evidence, not as a directly tested new hypothesis
target_learners: Learners across levels of expertise in cognitive load theory instructional contexts
target_learning_goals: Managing cognitive load when learning novel or complex material
key_sources: Chen, O., Kalyuga, S. & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9359-1

article_title: THE EXPERANTO EXPERIMENT
citation: Rick de Graaff. (1997). The Experanto Experiment: Effects of Explicit Instruction on Second Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19(2). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002064
title: Computer-controlled self-study course in the artificial language Experanto
description: The article's instructional element is a "computer-controlled self-study course in an artificial language" (Experanto), used to deliver L2 input and explicit instruction to university students under controlled conditions. Two groups of 27 students differing in exposure to explicit instruction worked through the course, and "computer-controlledposttests" measured acquisition of four L2 structures. The computer control of both instruction and testing is what allowed the presence or absence of explicit instruction to be manipulated experimentally.
requirements: Learners work through the course in self-study mode under computer control, with exposure to explicit instruction varied between groups.
constraints: The course teaches an artificial language rather than a natural second language, which limits generalization to natural L2 acquisition.
examples: Two groups of 27 university students, differing in the exposure to explicit instruction, followed the computer-controlled self-study course in the artificial language.

article_title: IMPLICIT AND EXPLICIT CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK AND THE ACQUISITION OF L2 GRAMMAR
citation: Rod Ellis, Shawn Loewen and Rosemary Erlam. (2006). Implicit and Explicit Corrective Feedback and the Acquisition of L2 Grammar. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060141
title: Synergy account: explicit corrective feedback in communicative activity can foster implicit as well as explicit knowledge
description: The article frames corrective feedback via the implicit/explicit learning and knowledge distinction, drawing on connectionist models in which "conscious and unconscious processes are dynamically involved together in every cognitive task and in every learning episode." Metalinguistic time-outs from communicating are proposed as a context for melding conscious and unconscious processes, so explicit feedback caters to implicit as well as explicit learning. The study's delayed-posttest gains in oral imitation are presented as consistent with this account.
requirements: Feedback must be recognized by the learner as corrective and the error located, per Carroll's autonomous induction theory as cited in the article
constraints: The article notes no single exchange can guarantee that the targeted form will enter implicit memory; repeated exchanges directed at the same form might be expected to do so
target_learning_goals: acquisition of L2 grammar (regular past tense -ed), implicit and explicit L2 knowledge
examples: The study operationalized explicit feedback as metalinguistic explanation and implicit feedback as partial recasts during communicative tasks

article_title: Exploring the Factors Influencing Artificial Intelligence Adoption among Gen Z University Students: the Role of Self-Efficacy and Perceived Trust

title: Extended UTAUT framework for Gen Z AI adoption integrating self-efficacy and perceived trust
description: The article proposes an extended UTAUT conceptual framework in which behavioural intention to adopt AI among Gen Z university students is modelled from performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, self-efficacy and perceived trust, with behavioural intention predicting usage behaviour. The authors state the study "has provided an improved and tested theoretical framework to enhance understanding of AI adoption in the field, with an R² value of 0.751". Facilitating conditions were deliberately excluded from the framework on demographic and theoretical grounds.

Findings may reflect Gen Z's intention to adopt technology beyond the academic sphere, as the authors note

article_title: Differential benefits of explicit failure-driven and success-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction.
citation: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(3), 530–555. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000483
title: Explicit failure-driven scaffolding via problematizing to facilitate problem-space exploration
description: The article describes a scaffolding design that explicitly pushes student problem-solving toward failure by nudging students to generate suboptimal solutions. The stated rationale is that such scaffolding facilitates problem-space exploration, giving students opportunities to entertain exploratory hypotheses and experience initial failures before instruction. This operationalizes failure in preparatory problem-solving as a designed, scaffolded experience rather than an incidental one.
requirements: Problem-solving must occur before instruction so that exploratory hypotheses and initial failures can prepare students to learn from follow-up instruction.
constraints: The article's rationale for explicit failure scaffolding is rooted in facilitating problem-space exploration; its measured benefits were higher constructive reasoning quality, not higher posttest conceptual understanding.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of the target learning concepts
Quality of constructive reasoning during problem-solving
examples: The intervention designed scaffolds to explicitly push student problem-solving toward failure via problematizing, nudging students to generate suboptimal solutions.

article_title: Differential benefits of explicit failure-driven and success-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction.
citation: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(3), 530–555. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000483
title: Explicit success-driven scaffolding via structuring with low-specificity heuristics
description: The article describes a contrasting scaffolding design that explicitly pushes student problem-solving toward success by nudging students to generate optimal solutions through heuristics with low specificity. Structuring supports successful initial problem-solving attempts before instruction, providing a comparison point for the failure-driven approach. The low specificity of the heuristics is the design feature that keeps the support from fully solving the problem for students.
requirements: Heuristics provided must have low specificity so that students still generate the optimal solutions themselves rather than being given them outright.
constraints: Success-driven scaffolding matched failure-driven scaffolding on posttest conceptual understanding but did not produce the higher constructive reasoning quality seen under failure-driven scaffolding.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of the target learning concepts
Generating optimal solutions during preparatory problem-solving
examples: The intervention designed scaffolds to explicitly push student problem-solving toward success via structuring, giving students heuristics with low specificity.

article_title: Differential benefits of explicit failure-driven and success-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction.
citation: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(3), 530–555. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000483
title: Design preparatory problem-solving scaffolds that explicitly engineer either success or failure before instruction
description: The article recommends designing scaffolds that explicitly push student problem-solving toward success via structuring or toward failure via problematizing, rather than leaving preparatory problem-solving unscaffolded. Both routes prepared students to learn from follow-up instruction with similar posttest conceptual understanding, while failure-driven scaffolding additionally raised constructive reasoning quality. Choice of scaffold can therefore be tuned to the targeted outcome.
requirements: Problem-solving must precede instruction, and scaffolds must explicitly push students toward either suboptimal (failure) or optimal (success) solutions.
constraints: The pedagogical value of success versus failure in initial problem-solving was still unclear in prior work; the differential benefits were more salient for the more difficult learning concept.
target_learners: Classroom students learning concepts through problem-solving prior to instruction
examples: In the classroom intervention (N = 221), scaffolds were designed to explicitly push problem-solving toward success via structuring and toward failure via problematizing, followed by instruction and posttests.

article_title: Where science starts: Spontaneous experiments in preschoolers’ exploratory play
citation: Cook, Claire, Noah D. Goodman, and Laura E. Schulz. (2011). Where Science Starts: Spontaneous Experiments in Preschoolers' Exploratory Play. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2011.03.003
title: Expected-information-gain framework: integrating prior knowledge about causal hypotheses with knowledge about possible actions
description: The article frames exploratory play with probabilistic models of expected information gain. On this account, learners integrate "prior knowledge about causal hypotheses" with "knowledge about possible actions that might generate data relevant to those hypotheses"; the action side is captured by affordances, or "action possibilities", in the environment. The article uses this framework to predict when preschoolers' play will be selective versus indiscriminate, testing it by manipulating stimulus properties and cause base rates.
requirements: The framework requires integrating prior knowledge about causal hypotheses with knowledge about possible actions that might generate relevant data
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills such as variable isolation
examples: The article manipulated the physical properties of stimuli and the base rate of candidate causes and observed children's exploratory play under ambiguous and unambiguous evidence.
key_sources: Cook, Claire, Noah D. Goodman, and Laura E. Schulz. (2011). Where Science Starts: Spontaneous Experiments in Preschoolers' Exploratory Play. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2011.03.003

article_title: Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review
citation: Den Heijer, A. E., Groen, Y., Tucha, L., Fuermaier, A. B. M., Koerts, J., Lange, K. W., Thome, J., & Tucha, O. (2017). Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review. J Neural Transm 124(Suppl 1):S3–S26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00702-016-1593-7
title: Three-axis categorization framework for exercise effects in ADHD: exercise type, effect duration, and outcome measure
description: The review organizes the exercise-in-ADHD literature along three axes: "exercise type (cardio versus non-cardio), duration of effects (acute versus chronic), and outcome measures (cognitive, behav- ioral/socio-emotional, and physical/(neuro) physiological)". Cardio exercise raises heart rate and oxygen use over relatively long durations (running, cycling, swimming); non-cardio exercise is performed at lower energy levels (yoga, walking, playground activity). Acute effects are those measurable up to 24 h after exercise; chronic effects persist beyond 24 h after interventions of one to ten weeks. All 29 tabulated studies are classified within this framework.
requirements: Studies must describe some form of exercise, include an ADHD group, and be written in English, with outcomes classifiable into the three outcome-measure categories.
constraints: The review deemed it unjustified to reliably compare effect sizes across studies because of profound variation in samples, medication use, tests, and designs.
examples: The review tabulated 29 studies (25 in children, 4 in adults) within this framework, calculating Cohen's d effect sizes where possible.
key_sources: Den Heijer, A. E., Groen, Y., Tucha, L., Fuermaier, A. B. M., Koerts, J., Lange, K. W., Thome, J., & Tucha, O. (2017). Sweat it out? article_title: Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review
citation: Den Heijer, A. E., Groen, Y., Tucha, L., Fuermaier, A. B. M., Koerts, J., Lange, K. W., Thome, J., & Tucha, O. (2017). Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review. J Neural Transm 124(Suppl 1):S3–S26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00702-016-1593-7
title: Offer physical exercise as a promising alternative or additional treatment option for patients with ADHD, especially cardio exercise
description: The review concludes that "physical exercise represents a promising alternative or additional treatment option for patients with ADHD", with acute and chronic beneficial effects of especially cardio exercise on cognitive, behavioral, and socio-emotional functions. It suggests exercise "could be combined with other treatment approaches of ADHD" rather than replacing them. The recommendation is explicitly provisional: the authors call for "more well-controlled studies on this topic, in both children and adults".
requirements: Exercise programs should be deliverable alongside existing ADHD treatment approaches; effects are best supported for cardio exercise.
constraints: Non-cardio exercise effects remain more questionable; the evidence base needs more well-controlled studies in both children and adults before firm implementation conclusions.
examples: Reviewed interventions included treadmill running, cycling, aerobic and motor-skills programs of 30–90 minutes several times weekly over 5–12 weeks.

article_title: Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants
citation: Pixner, S., Leyrer, M., and Moeller, K. (2014). Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1479. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01479
title: Give children with cochlear implants extra time on arithmetic and provide focused teaching of the base-10 place-value system
description: Based on the finding that children with CI are generally slower yet qualitatively similar in arithmetic, and specifically weaker when place-value demands rise, the authors draw two educational implications: "children with CI may perform equally well than their hearing peers provided they are given some extra time to solve arithmetic problems" and they "may require more focused teaching of the Arabic base-10 place-value system". This targets the general slowing and the circumscribed place-value difficulty respectively.
requirements: Extra time addresses the observed general response slowing; focused place-value instruction addresses the borrow-subtraction and wide-range number-line difficulties
constraints: Recommendations rest on a single matched-group study of third- to fifth-graders in Austria; the dyscalculia indications may partly reflect the speeded HRT format
target_learners: children with cochlear implants in elementary school
target_learning_goals: place-value understanding of the Arabic base-10 number system
examples: In the study, CI children's latencies were longer across multiplication and subtraction tasks, and their error increase was specific to borrow problems and the 0–1000 number line range

article_title: A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment
citation: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844
title: Use exemplars of good and poor work in peer assessment so students can calibrate against a yard-stick
description: The review identifies exemplar exposure as a recurring design mechanism across tools. It states that "the use of exemplars can help students to identify what is good or bad in a given assignment" and that these exemplars "can act as a 'yard-stick' by which students can measure their own performance and that of others." Several tools operationalise this: OASYS distributes scripts across good, intermediate and poor categories; Web-SPA uses multiple review cycles exposing best and worst cases; SWoRD publishes all drafts and ratings; OPAS displays top-ranked assignments.
requirements: A mechanism for exposing students to a diversity of assignments, ideally spanning quality levels
constraints: Aropa does not systematically provide best and worst reviews, only a seeded sample solution
target_learning_goals: identifying strengths and weaknesses in assignments
examples: Web-SPA randomly presents each individual with exemplars of the best and worst cases chosen by other groups to review
key_sources: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844

article_title: Expert blind spot: When content knowledge eclipses pedagogical content knowledge
citation: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali
title: Expert Blind Spot hypothesis: advanced content knowledge leads experts to assume learners will find formal representations most accessible
description: The Expert Blind Spot (EBS) hypothesis holds that people with greater content expertise "tend to make assumptions about student learning that turn out to be in conflict with students' actual performance and developmental propensities." Experts believe learners, like themselves, find symbolic formalisms most accessible because of their parsimony, while novices actually acquire knowledge through informal and concrete representations. The article develops EBS through mathematics education examples (New Math, teacher difficulty rankings) and language arts case studies.
requirements: Advanced content knowledge in a domain, unaccompanied by well-developed pedagogical content knowledge
constraints: The article frames EBS for mathematics and language arts education settings
target_learners: middle school, high school and college students
target_learning_goals: mathematical reasoning and algebra problem solving
examples: The New Math movement of the 1950s, which the authors attribute to mathematicians designing curricula around set theory and number theory with little regard to how the domain was to be learned or taught
key_sources: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali

article_title: Western science and Islamic learners When disciplines and culture intersect
citation: Ian Robottom and Sharifah Norhaidah. (2008). Western science and Islamic learners: When disciplines and culture intersect. Journal of Research in International Education 7(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/1475240908091302
title: Expanded constructivism: faith- and culture-based dissonances exceed alternative conceptions and should not be treated as misconceptions to be taught out
description: The article proposes that constructivist theory in science education must expand to embrace dissonances rooted in epistemology, ontology and religious commitment. It argues that some constructivist research treats personally constructed meanings that differ from taught science as "misconceptions" to be eliminated, overlooking that for many learners these constructions rest on "much deeper cultural and faith-related beliefs, convictions and commitments." The data from Islamic learners show dissonances "exceed the kind of factors usually referred to in constructivist explanations of the formation of alternative conceptions."
requirements: Recognition that learners' personal biographies continuously shape knowledge acquisition, and that some dissonances are not amenable to change by a well-intentioned teacher
constraints: The article frames this as an interpretation grounded in its Islamic-context studies, not a tested model of conceptual change
target_learners: Islamic-background learners of western science in secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Reconciling faith-based and scientific knowledge claims
examples: The article reports Malaysian and Australian studies of discord among Muslim science students as the empirical basis for expanding the constructivist concept
key_sources: Ian Robottom and Sharifah Norhaidah. (2008). Western science and Islamic learners: When disciplines and culture intersect. Journal of Research in International Education 7(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/1475240908091302

article_title: Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs
citation: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org
title: Expectation-Misconception Tailored Dialogue framework adapted for assessment rather than tutoring
description: The AutoTutor-based Expectation-Misconception Tailored Dialogue framework structures agent responses around a main question with a pre-programmed complete expected answer. When the student cannot fulfill the answer, the agent provides a pump such as "can you tell me more", then hints (open-ended clues), then prompts (single-word clues), followed by an assertion; stated misconceptions are corrected and correct answers receive an assertion. CBAs adapt this framework but provide less scaffolding information, because the goal is to probe what the student already knows rather than give away the answer, so assertions are often withheld. The framework also defines response categories the agent must recognize: correct, incomplete, irrelevant, meta-communicative, meta-cognitive, and no response.
requirements: Identification of student speech acts, which is integral in determining an appropriate agent response
Expert definition of correctness for the main question in the domain at hand
constraints: CBAs deliberately provide less information in follow-up scaffolding moves than tutorial dialogues, since eliciting evidence rather than teaching is the goal
examples: In the RegExp/LSA CBA, an irrelevant response prompted the agent to say the remark was not relevant to the conversation and continue with a closing statement and the next scaffolding move
key_sources: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org

article_title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity
citation: Benedek Mathias, Jauk Emanuel, Sommer Markus, Arendasy Martin, Neubauer Aljoscha C. (2014). Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity. Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007
title: Executive nature of creativity: controlled top-down processes (updating and inhibition) support creative thought
description: The article advances an executive account of creativity, arguing that creative idea generation "does not solely depend on spontaneous thought processes, but strongly relies on controlled top-down activity". Inhibition is thought to suppress dominant, obvious responses so that remote concepts can be retrieved, while working memory supports controlled search of memory and active maintenance of task goals and strategies during idea generation. The study's latent variable findings (updating and inhibition predicting creativity; shifting not) are presented as direct support for this account.
requirements: Measurement of both executive abilities and divergent thinking ability within the same individuals
constraints: Interpretation limited by latent EF factors each defined by task blocks of a single task, and by the possibility of task-specific method variance
examples: The alternate uses task analysis in the discussion describes how working memory maintains goals such as generating creative uses while searching memory for remote applications
key_sources: Benedek Mathias, Jauk Emanuel, Sommer Markus, Arendasy Martin, Neubauer Aljoscha C. (2014). Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity. Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007

article_title: Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood
citation: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857
title: Executive attention network as the neural system underlying effortful control and self-regulation
description: Within Posner's neurocognitive model, executive attention is related to a neural network involving the anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal regions. The article states that "the executive attention network in Posner's model constitutes the neural system underlying EC" (Rueda, Posner, & Rothbart, 2005a). Executive attention is required in situations involving "overcoming well-learned or dominant responses, facing novel and/or dangerous situations, detecting and correcting errors and planning actions." The study uses this framework to interpret correlations between temperament, brain, and school measures.
requirements: The framework assumes measures of executive attention through conflict tasks correlate with parent and/or self-reported measures of effortful control.
constraints: The article notes the influence of effortful control on school competence is not the same at different ages.
target_learners: children and adolescents in school settings
examples: The study used a combined Flanker and Go/No-Go task with EEG to index the efficiency of the executive attention network in twelve-year-olds.
key_sources: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Extended 36-trial Red-Blue Test of inhibitory control with reported reliability
description: The Red-Blue Test is a Stroop/Day-Night-adapted computer task in which children name colors according to a reversed rule on an alien planet, scoring correct answers given within 2 s. The authors extended the original 16-trial preschool version to 36 trials for early primary school children, reasoning that children make more errors in later trials and that reliability increases with trial number. They report that "With the increase of trial number, the current test has gained sufficient reliability (split-half r = 0.82, Cronbach α = 0.71)."
requirements: One-to-one administration with two checking trials to ensure the child understands the rule
constraints: Scored by accuracy only, not reaction time; the authors note RT or speed may be more reliable in certain cognitive tests
target_learning_goals: assessment of inhibitory control as an executive function component
examples: Used as the inhibitory control measure in the 204-child study, with 36 trials total
key_sources: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000

article_title: Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School
citation: Daches Cohen L and Rubinsten O (2017) Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School. Front. Psychol. 8:1939. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01939
title: Dual-measure framework of math anxiety: accessible self-representations versus inaccessible cognitive structures
description: The article organizes math anxiety assessment around two kinds of representation: accessible self-representations measured by explicit self-report questionnaires such as the AMAS, and inaccessible cognitive structures activated automatically, measured implicitly through attentional bias in the numerical dot-probe task. Its central organizing finding is that "diﬀerent factors predict accessible self-representations as compared to inaccessible cognitive structures of children's math anxiety" — cognitive factors predicted the explicit measure while environmental factors predicted the implicit one. The framework motivates using both kinds of tools when assessing math anxiety in children.
requirements: Assessment must include both an explicit self-report questionnaire and an implicit task such as the numerical dot-probe task, since the two measure distinct facets
constraints: The article notes the explicit and implicit measures were non-significantly correlated in this sample and that the relatively small sample size warrants caution
examples: Sixth graders completed the AMAS self-report questionnaire and the numerical dot-probe task, whose congruency effect served as the implicit measure of attentional bias toward math-related stimuli
key_sources: Daches Cohen L and Rubinsten O (2017) Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School. Front. Psychol. 8:1939. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01939

article_title: When do socioeconomic resources matter most in early childhood?
citation: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001
title: Researchers studying the school transition should expand the concept to include the prekindergarten year.
description: The authors argue that because prekindergarten center-based education is now nearly universal and functions like school in shaping SES-related disparities, the "transition to school" concept should be broadened. They state: "we suggest that future research include the prekindergarten year when studying the transition to school." This reframing locates the peak SES–development relationship within the school transition period.
requirements: Longitudinal data covering the prekindergarten year is needed to study the expanded transition period.
constraints: The authors' evidence is indirect regarding mechanisms; they could not test explanations within the growth curve framework.
target_learning_goals: Understanding socioeconomic disparities in cognitive and behavioral school readiness
examples: The study's growth curve models showed the SES–development relationship peaking at the start of prekindergarten rather than at kindergarten entry.
key_sources: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001

article_title: Cognitive and behavioural predictors of adolescents' communicative perspective‐taking and social relationships
citation: Nilsen, E. S., & Bacso, S. A. (2017). Cognitive and Behavioural Predictors of Adolescents’ Communicative Perspective-taking and Social Relationships. Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2017.01.004
title: Communicative perspective-taking relies on domain-general executive function support
description: The article supports a model in which successful use of a conversational partner's perspective requires executive function resources in addition to mentalizing skills. Working memory allows an interlocutor to hold a partner's perspective in mind, while inhibitory control may allow suppression of one's own perspective. The authors state their results "supports the notion that reading the intentions of others relies on domain-general attentional and cognitive resources" and align with a model positing that "individuals also require the support of executive functions in order to make use of this information during conversational exchanges."
requirements: Individuals must possess mentalizing skills as well as executive function resources for perspective use in conversation
constraints: Weakness in executive functioning results in difficulty using a conversational partner's perspective
examples: Adolescents with elevated ADHD traits were less successful at detecting communicative intentions using facial expression, tone, and visual perspective cues
key_sources: Nilsen, E. S., & Bacso, S. A. (2017). Cognitive and Behavioural Predictors of Adolescents’ Communicative Perspective-taking and Social Relationships. Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2017.01.004

article_title: Instability versus quality: Residential mobility, neighborhood poverty, and children’s self-regulation.
citation: Roy, A. L., McCoy, D. C., & Raver, C. C. (2014). Instability Versus Quality: Residential Mobility, Neighborhood Poverty, and Children's Self-Regulation. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0036984
title: Experiential canalization framework: cumulative exposure to harsh, unpredictable environments disrupts stress physiology and executive function, with children's self-regulation trajectories environmentally modifiable in ways reflecting both insult and repair
description: The article draws on the theoretical framework of experiential canalization to explain how residential mobility and neighborhood poverty may affect children's cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Under this framework, "Cumulative exposure to harsh, unpredictable environments (especially where stressors are outside the individual's control) leads to disruptions in parasympathetic function" (e.g., altered diurnal cortisol patterns), which in turn affect prefrontal synaptic activity and executive function. The authors use this framework to interpret their findings as evidence that children's self-regulation trajectories are environmentally modifiable, reflecting both insult (moves to worse neighborhoods) and repair (moves to better neighborhoods).
requirements: The framework presupposes that stressors are outside the individual's control for the physiological disruption pathway to operate as described.
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical framework supported by prior studies it cites, not as a mechanism directly tested in the present study.
target_learners: low-income children from preschool through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: executive function and self-regulatory skills underlying behavioral adjustment and early learning
examples: The authors interpret moves to worse neighborhoods as illustrating insult and moves to better neighborhoods as offering points of protection and even remedy, citing Blair & Raver (2012).
key_sources: Roy, A. L., McCoy, D. C., & Raver, C. C. (2014). Instability Versus Quality: Residential Mobility, Neighborhood Poverty, and Children's Self-Regulation. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0036984

article_title: The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review
citation: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348
title: Explicitly teach background knowledge in a specific, sequenced way as foundational to reading comprehension instruction
description: The review recommends that explicitly teaching background knowledge should be considered foundational to increasing competency in reading, rather than an incidental aspect of instruction. Children would benefit from exposure to background knowledge in a specific, explicit and sequenced way — a knowledge-rich curriculum — in addition to teaching comprehension strategies such as summarizing. This contrasts with the prevalent approach of making generic reading comprehension strategies the prime focus of reading instruction.
requirements: Requires sustained, systematic and sequential building of background knowledge over time
constraints: Runs counter to the prevailing view that knowledge building is less relevant than building so-called soft-skills such as critical thinking and collaboration
examples: The review cites the Model of Reading Engagement (MORE) and Content-Area Literacy Instruction (CALI) as models that systematically build a knowledge base over a longer period of time and showed positive and significant effects on proximal reading measures.
key_sources: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348

article_title: Cognitive components of a mathematical processing network in 9‐year‐old children
citation: Szűcs Dénes, Devine Amy, Soltesz Fruzsina, Nobes Alison, Gabriel Florence. (2014). Cognitive components of a mathematical processing network in 9-year-old children. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12144
title: Executive memory function centric model of mathematical processing
description: The article proposes a preliminary network model in which working memory function, relying on executive functions (attentional shifting, updating, inhibition), is core to mathematical processing. Visuo-spatial STM/WM is more directly related to mathematics while verbal STM/WM supports both reading and math; phonological processing and verbal IQ rely on verbal STM/WM capacity. The network "serves mathematical symbol processing and symbol manipulation", with symbols initially grounded in magnitudes and count words, a grounding the study suggests has limited relevance after initial acquisition.
requirements: Requires considering the complex predictor space of mathematics rather than single explanatory factors
constraints: Preliminary model based on 9-year-old children with at least normal reading skill
examples: The best regression model (M3) operationalized the network with Dot Matrix, visual WM, Phonological Decoding, Spatial Orientation, Trail-making and WISC Vocabulary predictors
key_sources: Szűcs Dénes, Devine Amy, Soltesz Fruzsina, Nobes Alison, Gabriel Florence. (2014). Cognitive components of a mathematical processing network in 9-year-old children. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12144

article_title: Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence
citation: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/
title: Extended process model of emotion regulation: identification, selection and implementation stages
description: The review adopts the extended process model of emotion regulation (Gross, 2014; Sheppes et al., 2015), which organises regulation into three sequential stages beyond the original process model. As the review states, "This posits that emotion regulation occurs in three stages: (1) Identification, in which an emotional state is identified and the decision over whether or not to regulate this is made; (2) Selection, in which an appropriate regulatory strategy is selected and (3) Implementation". Each stage involves a perception-valuation-action cycle, and the review uses this framework to ask where adolescent development may differ from adults.
requirements: Requires the perception-valuation-action cycle to operate at each stage, as the model specifies
constraints: The review notes most adolescent research addresses only the Implementation stage, with Identification and Selection understudied
target_learning_goals: recognising when emotion regulation is needed
examples: The review applies the model to ask whether adolescents might fail at the Identification stage when peer presence makes a hedonic state not trigger the valuation of a need to regulate
key_sources: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/

article_title: Coordination of executive functions in monolingual and bilingual children
citation: Bialystok Ellen. (2011). Coordination of Executive Functions in Monolingual and Bilingual Children. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3139691/
title: Coordination of executive control components as a distinct aspect of executive function development shaped by bilingual experience
description: The article proposes that beyond the three core executive components (selective attention and inhibition, shifting, working memory), effective complex performance depends on a higher-order management function that coordinates them. Bilingual language use is framed as a constant "dual task" situation requiring speakers to "construct speech plans according to the current context", "selectively attend to linguistic structures in the target language while ignoring competition from the other language", and monitor progress. This experience is argued to enhance coordination of the components rather than any single component, and the article states that "an important outcome of bilingualism may be in managing executive control components to address complex goals".
requirements: A task that recruits multiple executive control components simultaneously, such as the dual-modality classification task used here
Groups differing in relevant experience, such as bilingual versus monolingual language use
constraints: The article states the components themselves may be at different levels in the two groups, but the assumption is that the need for coordination is above and beyond those individual levels
The bilingual advantage in this task was limited to the visual task, with verbal production possibly limiting auditory performance
target_learning_goals: coordination of executive control components in complex task performance
examples: 63 8-year-olds classified visual and auditory stimuli as animals or musical instruments in single and dual-modality blocks
Bilinguals outperformed monolinguals in the dual-task condition for the visual task but not the auditory task
key_sources: Bialystok Ellen. (2011). Coordination of Executive Functions in Monolingual and Bilingual Children. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3139691/

article_title: Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement
citation: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article
title: Executive functions as covert, goal-directed cognitive skills underlying learning
description: The article frames cognitive functions as the mental processes enabling attention, perception, memory, language and calculation, with executive functions as their goal-directed subset. It states that "EFs are covert, internally self-directed cognitive skills at the service of a goal", directing behavior and cognitive and emotional activity. In the study this framework motivates measuring five EF domains (inhibition/interference, working memory, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, social skills) and testing their links to fitness and academic achievement.
requirements: EF domains must be measured with validated instruments (here Stroop, Wechsler Memory Scale, Symbol Digit Modalities, Trail Making, MESSY)
constraints: The article treats EFs as measured by these specific neuropsychological tests in adolescents aged 12–16
target_learning_goals: executive function domains supporting academic achievement
examples: The study operationalized five EF domains with Stroop, Wechsler memory, Symbol Digit, Trail Making and MESSY tests in 713 adolescents
key_sources: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article

article_title: Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory
citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Developmental shift from unitary executive control toward increasing reliance on common goal-representation skills across the preschool period
description: The article proposes that the late-emerging relation of inhibition and working memory to mixing costs reflects age-related change in the processes children recruit, "with a shift from bottom-up or task-related processes to increasingly efficient top-down executive skills that are common to flexibility, inhibition and working memory." As children grow older, they "may increasingly draw upon developing goal representation skills to complete flexibility tasks as well as working memory and inhibition tasks." This account reconciles evidence for unitary executive function in preschoolers with the separable three-factor structure observed at later ages, positioning goal representation as possibly "a fundamental component of executive skills."
requirements: Longitudinal or cross-sectional designs spanning multiple preschool ages to detect the changing pattern of relations
constraints: The relation emerges only from age 4;6 onward; no association with inhibition or working memory is observed at age 3;9
target_learning_goals: understanding developmental changes in executive control and flexibility during early childhood
examples: The authors interpret the age-graded interaction pattern as evidence that older preschoolers recruit maturing goal-representation skills across flexibility, inhibition, and working-memory tasks
key_sources: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/

article_title: The role of metacognition in human social interactions
citation: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123
title: Explicit metacognition is a uniquely human ability evolved to enhance collaborative decision-making
description: The article argues that explicit metacognition's major function is social: it lets people communicate reflections on action and sensation, share experiences, justify behaviour, and thereby make joint decisions better than the best individual, build accurate world models without objective feedback, and improve individual perception. The author proposes this capacity emerged before language, with language arising as a communicative technology on top of it, distinguishing humans from honeybees whose sharing is automatic and limited to predetermined problems.
requirements: Capacity to discuss perceptual experiences and reasons for actions with others
Willingness to make metacognitive reports even when they do not reflect the true state of affairs
constraints: Absolute certainty about a partner's collaboration can never be achieved, though sufficient confidence suffices in practice
The human capacity for counterfactual representation differs from monkeys quantitatively rather than qualitatively
target_learning_goals: understanding the evolutionary and social function of explicit metacognition in human collaboration
examples: Pairs developing unique confidence vocabularies in the odd-ball task; collective intentionality in young children but not chimpanzees (Tomasello, as cited); honeybee waggle-dance sharing as a contrast case
key_sources: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123

article_title: A Randomized Control Study of Instructional Approaches for Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/
title: Explicit skills instruction versus implicit extensive reading as competing approaches to adult literacy instruction
description: The article frames adult literacy instruction as divided between two approaches. The explicit skills instruction approach "directly teaches adults how to decode and comprehend," operationalized through the SRA/McGraw-Hill Direct Instruction Corrective Reading program, which uses "a graduated sequence of steps," massed practice, immediate specific feedback, scripted lessons, and unison responding. The implicit approach "encourages students to read text that is of interest to them without directly teaching them decoding and comprehension skills," operationalized as Extensive Reading with self-selected high-interest/low-vocabulary books, sustained silent reading, teacher read-alouds, and book discussion, aligned with andragogy and self-directed learning. The study tested both approaches alone and in combination.
requirements: Teachers trained in the specific approach; the explicit program requires instructor scripts, placement tests, and decision rules for additional instruction
constraints: The article notes none of the Extensive Reading effectiveness studies employ systematic scientific measures and controls
target_learners: Adults reading single words between the 3.0 and 5.9 grade equivalency levels, including native speakers and ESL speakers
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to DF, DCF, ER, DCEF, or C/C conditions, each receiving 8 hours of instruction weekly for an opportunity of 100 hours
key_sources: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/

article_title: A Randomized Control Study of Instructional Approaches for Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/
title: Extensive Reading approach with high-interest/low-vocabulary library for adult learners
description: The Extensive Reading approach, administered to the ER and DCEF groups, provided "an extensive library of high interest/low vocabulary books" from publishers such as New Readers Press and Peppercorn Books. Students engaged in sustained silent reading, a read-aloud activity during which the teacher read while participants followed along, and book discussions. The teacher acts as a role model of a reader and does not present explicit instruction on how to read. ER students had two 40-minute silent reading blocks, 15 minutes of teacher read-aloud, and 10 minutes each of book discussion; in DCEF this was reduced to roughly 18 minutes of silent reading, 10 minutes of read-aloud, and 5 minutes of discussion.
requirements: A library of authentic materials at students' reading levels; student choice of reading materials based on interest
constraints: The article notes that although many studies show the approach's effectiveness, none employ systematic scientific measures and controls
target_learners: Adult literacy students, including university students and clerical workers per prior studies
target_learning_goals: Reading interest, reading vocabulary, reading skill through wide exposure to literature
examples: The ER group showed the lowest posttest word attack scores (M = 11.36) among the five conditions
key_sources: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/

article_title: Efficacy of Learning Strategies Instruction in Adult Education
citation: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291
title: Deliver learning strategies instruction explicitly, intensively, and systematically, with sufficient dosage for mastery
description: The article's design recommendation, drawn from the SIM validation literature and its own null trial, is that strategy instruction must be delivered in an explicit, intensive, and systematic fashion for learners to reach mastery and for large achievement effects to appear. The trial's four-phase method operationalizes this through describe, model, scaffolded practice with feedback, and mastery checks, but the authors conclude that "these principles proved to be elusive in the AE setting with AE learners" because attendance patterns limited delivered dosage to well under planned hours.
requirements: Sufficient instructional dosage for learners to acquire and automatize the strategy
Settings compatible with intensive delivery
Supports for persistence such as goal setting, progress monitoring, and mastery experiences
constraints: The authors call into question whether such instruction can be delivered in traditional adult education settings, given the conflict between the justified need for more dosage and the contextual and cognitive realities of adult literacy education
target_learners: Adults with low literacy or limited educational attainment
examples: The trial planned 8-week courses of 26 to 32 hours and added persistence supports (monetary incentives, phone calls to absent learners, readiness and goal-setting activities), yet completers still received only 68% to 86% of planned hours
key_sources: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291

article_title: Creativity and flexibility in young children's use of external cognitive strategies.
citation: Armitage, KL; Suddendorf, T; Bulley, A; Bastos, APM; Taylor, AH; Redshaw, J. (2023). Creativity and Flexibility in Young Children's Use of External Cognitive Strategies. Developmental Psychology, 59 (6), pp. 995-1005. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001562
title: External metacognitive offloading: awareness of one's own cognitive struggles used to offload internal demand into the environment
description: The article frames a cardinal feature of adult cognition as "the awareness of our own cognitive struggles and the capacity to draw upon this awareness to offload internal demand into the environment." External metacognitive strategies, such as setting physical reminders by marking a hidden prize's location, reduce internal memory demand. The study examines when children begin to self-initiate such strategies and how flexibly they adapt them across contexts, with development evident from age 4 and effective deployment from age 6.
requirements: Awareness of one's own cognitive struggle
An environment that affords external marking or reminder-setting actions
constraints: Developmental emergence is graded: 3-year-olds copy but do not modify strategies; flexible devising of novel strategies appears from age 4
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness and offloading of cognitive demand into the environment
examples: Children adopting demonstrated marking strategies and devising novel reminder-setting strategies across six transfer trials
key_sources: Armitage, KL; Suddendorf, T; Bulley, A; Bastos, APM; Taylor, AH; Redshaw, J. (2023). Creativity and Flexibility in Young Children's Use of External Cognitive Strategies. Developmental Psychology, 59 (6), pp. 995-1005. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001562

article_title: Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades
citation: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155
title: Design early reading intervention for struggling readers to be explicit, targeted, practice-rich, and actively engaging
description: Drawing on research reviews and meta-analyses, the article states that students with reading difficulties benefit from instruction that is purposeful, targeted at important objectives, and progresses from easier to more challenging skills, with mastery monitored so reteaching can occur. "Students with reading difficulties also benefit from (a) explicit instruction in which skills are clearly modeled and key concepts are directly taught," extended guided and independent practice with feedback including engaged reading of connected text, and formats promoting active student involvement and many opportunities to respond.
requirements: Careful monitoring of mastery of key skills and strategies so reteaching can be provided when needed
examples: The article cites Mathes et al. (2005), whose two first-grade small-group interventions, one scripted and one flexible, both embodied these characteristics and outperformed typical practice
key_sources: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155

article_title: A longitudinal assessment of the relation between executive function and theory of mind at 3, 4, and 5 years
citation: Marcovitch S., O'Brien M., Calkins S. D., Leerkes E. M., Weaver J. M., Levine D. W. (2014). A Longitudinal Assessment of the Relation between Executive Function and Theory of Mind at 3, 4, and 5 Years. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2014.07.001
title: Expression and emergence accounts of the EF–ToM relation
description: The article frames two competing accounts of why EF precedes ToM: expression accounts hold that ToM concepts exist but cannot be expressed without sufficient executive skills, while emergence accounts hold that ToM only develops after sufficient EF maturation. The authors note that "EF skills develop prior to and are involved in the expression and/or the emergence of ToM understanding," and propose distinguishing the accounts using ToM tasks with minimized executive demands. Their longitudinal asymmetry is consistent with both.
requirements: Longitudinal designs comparing EF and ToM tasks, ideally ToM tasks that minimize executive demands, to discriminate between the accounts
constraints: The present data support both accounts jointly and do not distinguish expression from emergence; the authors state their data do not directly address whether the asymmetry persists beyond early childhood
target_learning_goals: development of theory-of-mind reasoning and executive control
examples: The authors propose testing expression vs. emergence with deception tasks in which executive demands are reduced, citing Hala and Russell (2001)
key_sources: Marcovitch S., O'Brien M., Calkins S. D., Leerkes E. M., Weaver J. M., Levine D. W. (2014). A Longitudinal Assessment of the Relation between Executive Function and Theory of Mind at 3, 4, and 5 Years. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2014.07.001

article_title: Number and counting skills in kindergarten as predictors of grade 1 mathematical skills
citation: Martin Rebecca B., Cirino Paul T., Sharp Carla, Barnes Marcia. (2014). Number and counting skills in kindergarten as predictors of grade 1 mathematical skills. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.05.006
title: For struggling students, provide explicit and systematic focus on core skills most closely related to the desired outcome
description: The article recommends that for students who struggle in academic areas, instruction should explicitly and systematically target the core skills most proximal to the outcome, such as Arabic numerals in math. It states "an explicit and systematic focus on core skills that are most closely related to the desired outcome (i.e., words in reading, Arabic numerals in math) may be even more important" for struggling students. This principle follows from the finding that symbolic number skills strongly predict math outcomes.
requirements: Identification of the core skills most proximal to the target outcome for the domain
constraints: The article notes curricula vary in emphasis between conceptual relationships such as discovery learning versus number recognition, sequencing, and number combinations
target_learners: Students who struggle in academic areas, including kindergarten and grade 1 children
target_learning_goals: Early mathematics skills, including number recognition, sequencing, and number combinations
examples: The article cites studies emphasizing counting strategies for improving number combinations and generalizing to story problems in at-risk kindergarten students and students with math difficulties
key_sources: Martin Rebecca B., Cirino Paul T., Sharp Carla, Barnes Marcia. (2014). Number and counting skills in kindergarten as predictors of grade 1 mathematical skills. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.05.006

article_title: Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System
citation: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016
title: Spelling instruction should go beyond rote memorization and explicitly teach sound-to-spelling patterns, including context-conditioned choices
description: The review argues that because implicit statistical learning of spelling patterns is slow and incomplete, explicit teaching has an important role. It recommends that instruction cover the sound-to-spelling direction, not only spellings-to-sounds, and teach how context helps choose among alternative spellings: "more direct instruction about the sound-to-spelling direction could be helpful" and it "could be helpful to draw children's attention to the fact that context can help in making these choices". Generic statements can convey generalizations that would otherwise require many instances.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of phonology and spelling so they can interpret children's errors, e.g. recognizing that ‹CHRAP› for trap reflects careful listening plus a misclassification, not inattention.
constraints: The review notes current phonics approaches often rely on worksheets and drills that are boring for children, and that phoneme-level generic statements are harder for children to understand than everyday generics.
target_learners: children learning to spell in alphabetic writing systems, roughly ages 4 to 13
target_learning_goals: understanding of sound-to-spelling correspondences and their context conditioning
examples: The review describes whole-language classrooms where children receive no explicit spelling instruction, and contrasts these with phonics instruction, recommending engaging word-pattern teaching methods (Joshi et al., 2008–2009).
key_sources: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: Teach divergent thinking through explicit instruction of metacognitive strategy knowledge rather than relying on brainstorming exercises alone
description: The article argues that regular brainstorming exercises in visual arts lessons may limit learning because students need many experiences before building a rich knowledge base for divergent thinking. Instead, it recommends that "students may develop enhanced divergent thinking skills through explicit instruction of metacognition, because then students may learn to understand why, how and when to use which specific divergent thinking activities and strategies." A previous intervention focusing mainly on association improved fluency and flexibility but not originality, motivating a redesign that added generation through combination and abstraction.
requirements: Instruction must cover declarative, procedural, conditional and contextual knowledge about divergent thinking strategies
Teacher modeling and visual examples are needed to make abstract strategy knowledge concrete
constraints: A prior version of the instruction that focused mainly on generation through association did not improve originality of ideas
target_learners: Secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Enhance divergent thinking skills including fluency, flexibility and originality of generated ideas
examples: The redesigned intervention lesson explicitly taught twelve divergent thinking strategies across association, combination and abstraction, illustrated with visual examples from art and design, and had students practise and evaluate their strategy use
key_sources: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y

article_title: Does Everyone’s Motivational Beliefs about Physical Science Decline in Secondary School?: Heterogeneity of Adolescents’ Achievement Motivation Trajectories in Physics and Chemistry
citation: Wang, Ming-Te; Chow, Angela; Degol, Jessica Lauren; Eccles, Jacquelynne Sue. (2016). Does Everyone's Motivational Beliefs about Physical Science Decline in Secondary School?: Heterogeneity of Adolescents' Achievement Motivation Trajectories in Physics and Chemistry. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-016-0620-1
title: Expectancy-value theory as a framework for science motivation development
description: The article uses expectancy-value theory as its conceptual framework, defining ability self-concept as expectations for success and confidence in one's ability in a field, and subjective task values as the value placed on a field, including interest, utility value, and attainment value. The theory posits that "students' educational choices are greatly influenced by their cognitive competencies, their ability self-concepts, and the subjective task values they attach to each subject or field." The study applies it by modeling joint trajectories of both constructs and linking them to outcomes.
requirements: Measures of both ability self-concept and subjective task values in the target domain, as the framework treats the two as distinct but related indicators
constraints: The article operationalizes science motivation by combining physics and chemistry, noting the two domains may have unique motivational trajectories
target_learning_goals: Science motivation, science achievement, advanced science course taking, and STEM career aspirations
examples: The study modeled joint trajectories of ability self-concept and task values in physics and chemistry from seventh to twelfth grade and linked group membership to grades, AP enrollment, and aspirations
key_sources: Wang, Ming-Te; Chow, Angela; Degol, Jessica Lauren; Eccles, Jacquelynne Sue. (2016). Does Everyone's Motivational Beliefs about Physical Science Decline in Secondary School?: Heterogeneity of Adolescents' Achievement Motivation Trajectories in Physics and Chemistry. Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-016-0620-1

article_title: Academic Race Stereotypes, Academic Self-Concept, and Racial Centrality in African American Youth
citation: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615
title: Expectancy-value account: stereotype endorsement directly influences perceptions of one's own competence
description: Drawing on Eccles et al.'s expectancy-value model of achievement motivation, the article theorizes that "a child's perception of stereotypes directly influences perceptions of his or her own competence", so that endorsement of traditional academic race stereotypes would lead to lower self-perceptions of academic competence for African Americans. The two studies test this hypothesis and find support only among youth high in racial centrality, illustrating the interweaving of group and individual identity with motivational beliefs.
requirements: The individual must perceive the stereotype as personally applicable for it to influence self-perceptions
constraints: Support in this article is correlational and cross-sectional; causal direction was not established
target_learners: African American adolescents in middle school
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept, competence beliefs, achievement motivation
examples: The authors frame both studies as tests of the expectancy-value hypothesis that stereotype endorsement is negatively related to self-perceptions
key_sources: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615

article_title: Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools
citation: Frank Fischer, Heinz Mandl. (2005). Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 14(3), pp.405-441. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190855
title: External representation tools (content-specific vs. content-independent graphical representations) as collaboration supports
description: Graphical external representation tools provided to collaborating learners, distinguished by whether they are content-specific or content-independent. The article investigates "how two types of graphical representation tools influence the way in which learners use knowledge resources in two different collaboration conditions." Content-specific tools led learners to use more appropriate knowledge resources, while content-independent tools served as the comparison condition.
requirements: The tools are used within collaborative learning settings where learners draw on shared knowledge resources.
constraints: Content-specific representations increased appropriate resource use but did not increase knowledge sharing after collaboration.
examples: The study provided learners with content-specific or content-independent graphical representation tools while collaborating via videoconferencing or face-to-face.
key_sources: Frank Fischer, Heinz Mandl. (2005). Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 14(3), pp.405-441. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190855

article_title: Defensive and Expansive Cycles of Learning: A Study of Home Care Encounters
citation: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970
title: Expansive learning cycle as a framework for analyzing micro-cycles in recurring work encounters
description: The theory of expansive learning (Engeström, 2015) posits that learning is triggered by contradictions in activity systems and proceeds through seven expansive learning actions: questioning, analysis, modeling, examining, implementing, reflecting, and consolidating. The article applies this ideal-typical model to small-scale cycles within single home care encounters, noting that "a small expansive cycle may take place within a single intensive encounter that requires analysis and redesign of the practice." The authors map substance-specific actions of home care clients and workers onto these seven actions to construct working models for empirical analysis.
requirements: Contradictions in the existing activity must be present to trigger learning efforts
A new challenging set of actions and artifacts must be introduced into recurring cycles of scripted actions
constraints: The occurrence of a full-fledged expansive cycle in temporally compressed encounters is not common and typically requires deliberate efforts and interventions
Pure examples of fully expansive or fully defensive cycles were rarely found in the data
target_learning_goals: Constructing a qualitatively new pattern of activity oriented at sustainable mobility
Integrating physical mobility exercises into routine work scripts
examples: The authors mapped home care client and worker actions onto the seven expansive cycle actions (Table 1) and used this as a coding scheme for analyzing 30 videotaped visits
