key_sources: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970

article_title: Enhancing student learning and achievement through orchestration of group processes and group composition
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2023). Enhancing student learning and achievement through orchestration of group processes and group composition. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 18, 323–327. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09408-x
title: Explicit vs implicit scaffolding of collaboration: structured feedback interfaces vs orchestrating group composition
description: The editorial contrasts two scaffolding routes to productive collaborative learning. In the four issue articles, some interventions scaffold processes through "explicit scaffolding", such as a "structured peer feedback interface" or a script prompting deeper discussion, while others work indirectly: "interventions that group students in order to promote productive learning processes can be regarded as implicit scaffolding for collaboration". This framing organizes how the issue's studies─SRL email messages, meta-discourse enrichment, feedback design, and skill-based pairing─support learning. It also introduces the notion of orchestrating group composition and group processes to enhance learning.
requirements: Requires feedback or grouping mechanisms designed with knowledge of student skill levels or self-regulation profiles, as in stratified assignment by latent profiles
constraints: The editorial states past coarse-grained skill pairing failed to demonstrate an impact, so implicit scaffolding via composition depends on sufficiently fine-grained skill assessment
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge improvement via peer feedback

key_sources: L0b
examples.title: Stratified random assignment by latent self-regulation profiles is reported to enable analysis of learning and retention in a MOOC intervention

subclaims.text: Identifying four common latent student self-regulation profiles enabled stratified random assignment with equal representation of profiles across the three conditions.

evidence.source_quote: not only addressed the attrition issue but also enabled identifying four common latent student profiles and then performing a stratified random assignment of students to conditions, with equal representation of the latent student profiles across conditions.
evidence.description: The editorial reports, describing the Psathas et al. three-condition MOOC study, that waiting until students completed a questionnaire "enabled identifying four common latent student profiles and then performing a stratified random assignment". This careful setup afforded analysis of learning and retention as related to SRL measures and collaborative participation.

examples.discussion: The editorial calls the study the first ijCSCL article presenting an analysis of data from an intervention study embedded within a MOOC.

key_sources: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2023). Enhancing student learning and achievement through orchestration of group processes and group composition. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 18, 323–327. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09408-x

article_title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
citation: Sebastian Strauß, Isis Tunnigkeit, Julia Eberle, Arlind Avdullahu, Nikol Rummel. (2025). Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09430-7
title: External collaboration script with four timed phases and prompt scaffolding displayed during collaboration
description: A text scaffold presented in the margin of the shared video-conference screen during the learning phase, specifying phases and prompts for beneficial interaction. It provided "a sequence of actions (scene-level) and within each phase provided the group with prompts on beneficial actions". The four phases were "coordination (5 min), information pooling (7 min), discussion (10 min), and decision making (7 min)", each with one extra minute to read prompts, color highlighting, a progress bar, and audio signals at phase changes.
requirements: Script adherence was verified by coding video against the prescribed phases (maximum 20 points; weighted κ = 0.94 on a 30% subset)
constraints: Script groups received 34 minutes versus 30 minutes for other conditions due to prompt-reading time
The script directly targeted the interaction, unlike the reflection scaffold
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative interaction on information-pooling problems
examples: Groups in the script condition followed phase-structured prompts while solving a kindergarten floor-plan construction problem
key_sources: Sebastian Strauß, Isis Tunnigkeit, Julia Eberle, Arlind Avdullahu, Nikol Rummel. (2025). Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09430-7

article_title: Instructional approaches to foster third graders’ adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction
citation: Aiso Heinze, Julia Arend, Meike Gruessing, Frank Lipowsky. (2018). Instructional approaches to foster third graders' adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction. Instr Sci 46:869–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9457-1
title: Two idealized instructional approaches to fostering adaptive strategy use: explicit demonstration versus implicit generation
description: The article contrasts two idealized learning environments for fostering adaptive use of strategies. The explicit approach reduces cognitive load by demonstrating and practicing strategies with explicit efficiency criteria, building a strategy repertoire and routine execution. The implicit approach capitalizes on the generation effect: children analyze number characteristics, categorize problems as "easy problems", "smart problems" or "other problems", generate their own strategies, and compare their efficiency, with the teacher acting as a mentor who avoids presenting official strategies or preferences. Both environments used the same problems and strategy comparison from the beginning.
requirements: Students must be able to generate the target strategies correctly; the article states a necessary condition for the generation effect is that students are able to generate the target information correctly
The teacher must avoid setting socio-mathematical norms that implicitly privilege particular strategies
constraints: The generation effect does not hold for strategies too complex for students to generate, such as indirect subtraction and simplifying for third graders
target_learners: primary school students (third grade, 9–10 years old)
target_learning_goals: adaptive use of computation strategies in multi-digit addition and subtraction
examples: In the explicit condition the five strategy types were successively demonstrated and practiced over the first three days; in the implicit condition children categorized problems and generated and compared their own strategies
key_sources: Aiso Heinze, Julia Arend, Meike Gruessing, Frank Lipowsky. (2018). Instructional approaches to foster third graders' adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction. Instr Sci 46:869–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9457-1

article_title: Supports for preservice teachers’ metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons
citation: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0
title: Explanation completeness coding scheme with three key concepts per task
description: A paper-and-pencil coding scheme operationalizing explanation completeness as whether an explanation includes three key concepts per fraction comparison task, each with sub-components scored 0-2 and averaged into a completeness score out of 2. The article states: "We operationally defined explanation completeness as whether the explanation included three key concepts for the explanations for each task." Double-coded agreement was high, "with the average percent agreement of 98.13% on first draft and revision explanation coding," after an initial round with only 60% of codes matching.
requirements: Raters must be trained with practice rounds and discrepancy discussion; sub-components vary by task because some comparisons require more complex explanations
constraints: Only responses using the targeted strategy could be scored; strategies other than the targeted ones were not coded
target_learning_goals: complete and correct mathematical explanations of fraction magnitude comparisons
examples: For Task B (5/8 vs. 5/9), the three key concepts were recognizing the common numerator strategy, comparing unit fractions, and connecting that reasoning to the final answer
key_sources: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0

article_title: The influence of framing on transfer: initial evidence from a tutoring experiment
citation: Randi A. Engle, Phi D. Nguyen, Adam Mendelson. (2011). The influence of framing on transfer: initial evidence from a tutoring experiment. Instr Sci 39:603–628. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9145-2
title: Expansive versus bounded framing of learning contexts as an instructional mechanism for transfer
description: This theory holds that transfer is more likely when learning and transfer contexts are framed expansively, as opportunities for students to actively contribute to "larger conversations that extend across times, places, people, and activities". It contrasts expansive framings, whose boundaries are "wide-ranging and permeable", with bounded framings having constricted, impermeable, non-overlapping boundaries. The article operationalizes framing along five aspects of context: when, where, who, what, and how learners are positioned intellectually, and tested the theory in a randomized tutoring experiment.
requirements: Framing must be initiated through meta-communicative signals in social interaction, such as the tutor's language and actions across the five aspects
Student uptake of the proposed framing must be maintained, with the tutor encouraging the favored framing until uptake is achieved
constraints: In this experiment the framing had to be established within minutes rather than the weeks available in classroom settings
No statistically reliable effects were detected for transfer of the surface area principle, so the mechanism does not guarantee transfer of all content types
target_learning_goals: transfer of facts, conceptual principles, and learning strategies across body systems
examples: Tutors framed each day as one ongoing study versus separate completed studies, framed location as the university versus this room, revoiced students' self-explanations to credit authorship versus crediting the text, and framed the two days as one study about body systems versus two separate system topics
key_sources: Randi A. Engle, Phi D. Nguyen, Adam Mendelson. (2011). The influence of framing on transfer: initial evidence from a tutoring experiment. Instr Sci 39:603–628. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9145-2

article_title: Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice
citation: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z
title: Reserve explanations for the arbitrary aspects of the discipline while learners practice and discover
description: In explorative practice, verbal explanation is withheld for aspects learners can discover through practice, and reserved for what must simply be told. The article states that “Explanations are instead reserved for conveying what Hewitt (1999) might call the ‘arbitrary’ aspects of the discipline.” This positions direct instruction as serving discovery rather than replacing it.
requirements: Learners must engage in extended repetitive practice in which discoveries can be made; the author notes this “requires trust” or that students collude with the teacher.
constraints: The trust dimension of withholding information during practice was not explored and is named a potentially significant limitation of the present work.
target_learning_goals: Discovering structured aspects of a discipline while being told only its arbitrary conventions
examples: The martial arts case shows instruction in which explanations are reserved for arbitrary aspects while learners practice.
key_sources: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z

article_title: How do higher education students regulate their learning with video modeling examples, worked examples, and practice problems?
citation: Milou van Harsel, Vincent Hoogerheide, Eva Janssen, Peter Verkoeijen, Tamara van Gog. (2022). How do higher education students regulate their learning with video modeling examples, worked examples, and practice problems? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09589-2
title: Instructional design principles for self-regulated example-based learning at multiple complexity levels
description: The article organizes its analysis around five instructional design principles for novices acquiring problem-solving skills from examples and problems: the example-based-learning-principle (studying several examples, possibly alternated with problems, is more effective and efficient than problem solving only), the example-first-principle (start with an example), the lowest-level-first-principle and simple-to-complex-principle (start at the lowest complexity level and build up gradually), and the start-each-level-with-example-principle (start each new complexity level with example study). These principles, drawn from the 4C/ID model and example-based learning research, were used as a scoring rubric against which students' spontaneous task selections were evaluated.
requirements: Learners must be novices with little prior knowledge for whom the principles prescribe optimal support and complexity
A task database offering examples and problems at multiple complexity levels so that selection behavior can be scored against the principles
constraints: The expertise reversal effect limits the example-based-learning and example-first principles: learners do not need instructional support from examples anymore when their knowledge increases, and from that point onwards they learn more from solving problems than from example study
target_learners: Novice higher education students acquiring problem-solving skills
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of well-defined problem-solving procedures, such as mathematical integration methods
examples: In the study, each participant's six self-selected tasks were scored 0, 0.5, or 1 point per principle (maximum 5 points; ICC 0.96) to quantify adherence
key_sources: Milou van Harsel, Vincent Hoogerheide, Eva Janssen, Peter Verkoeijen, Tamara van Gog. (2022). How do higher education students regulate their learning with video modeling examples, worked examples, and practice problems? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09589-2

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: Give lesson study an explicit learning theory: variation theory adds explanatory and predictive power for designing and evaluating research lessons
description: The article argues that lesson study groups lacking "a common, explicit conceptual framework" struggle to develop tasks that reveal student thinking; adding variation theory supplies guiding principles for pedagogical design, lesson analysis and evaluation. The authors claim variation theory "has both explanatory and predictive power": analysis of the enacted pattern of variation predicted the comparison group's poor equal-shares understanding and explained class 4A's failure, while guiding the cycle 2 redesign that improved outcomes.
requirements: Teachers trained in the theory (a course of no less than 12 h)
Careful study of lesson enactment to check whether the intended pattern of variation was actually experienced by students
constraints: The authors do not argue research lessons from learning studies are perfect or that learning studies are generally superior to normal classroom teaching; other theories could be used
target_learning_goals: using learning theory to design, analyse and improve research lessons
examples: In the comparison group, the teacher's unguided pattern of variation led students to discern that the fraction depends on the numerator, something unintended
key_sources: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4

article_title: Process mining measures students’ help-seeking transitions when completing assignments in an online learning and assessment platform
citation: Hou, C., Kuhlmann, S. L., Greene, J. A., Bernacki, M. L., & Hogan, K. A. (2025). Process mining measures students' help-seeking transitions when completing assignments in an online learning and assessment platform. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09442-0
title: Executive versus instrumental help-seeking framework
description: The article organizes help-seeking into two kinds drawn from Nelson-Le Gall (1981), distinguished by their function for learning. As the article states, "Instrumental help-seeking refers to behaviors that promote learning and improve understanding, such as the use of scaffolding. Executive help-seeking refers to behaviors that look for shortcuts to achieve the learning goal, and avoid additional work, such as accessing solutions in online learning and assessment platforms." In the platform studied, hints map onto adaptive instrumental help-seeking and requesting solutions onto maladaptive executive help-seeking. The framework underpins the study's interpretation of why lower performers' solution access signals struggling.
requirements: Help-seeking must be observable as distinct digital events (e.g., hint requests versus solution requests) so the two kinds can be distinguished in trace data
constraints: The article notes students commonly use both kinds of help-seeking to achieve a learning goal, so the categories are not mutually exclusive in practice
Common help-seeking surveys such as the MSLQ do not differentiate between executive and instrumental help-seeking
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education, particularly STEM courses using online learning and assessment platforms
target_learning_goals: effective, adaptive help-seeking as part of self-regulated learning during online formative assessment
examples: In the studied platform, hints written to guide students toward the correct answer in an increasingly specific way were treated as instrumental help, while the request-answer button, which eliminates the opportunity to receive credit for the question, was treated as executive help-seeking
key_sources: Hou, C., Kuhlmann, S. L., Greene, J. A., Bernacki, M. L., & Hogan, K. A. (2025). Process mining measures students' help-seeking transitions when completing assignments in an online learning and assessment platform. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09442-0

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Exosystem policies and practices shaping belonging (Table 2)
description: Table 2 catalogs exosystem factors—financial aid rules, faculty hiring and promotion standards, accreditation mandates, student conduct policies, campus policing, institutional responses to harm, housing allocation rules, and budget allocations—with their mechanisms and potential impacts on belonging. The article states 'exosystem factors organize the conditions under which belonging is made possible or foreclosed.' It notes some levers (accreditation, budget allocations, conduct policies) have received little to no empirical attention in relation to belonging.
requirements: Research extending beyond micro- and meso-level interactions to structural policies
constraints: The article flags that empirical work linking accreditation mandates, conduct policies, and budget allocations directly to belonging is limited
target_learners: higher education students, especially disabled caregivers, working-class students of color, and other marginalized groups
target_learning_goals: understanding how distal institutional policies condition opportunities for belonging
examples: Financial aid policies tied to full-time enrollment assume a traditional student profile and exclude many disabled caregivers and working-class students of color
key_sources: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Explicit intention to learn: a proposed sixth principle of intelligent natural information processing systems
description: The paper proposes adding a sixth principle at the level of human cognition: the explicit intention to learn secondary knowledge, defined as "the explicit intention to acquire new secondary information into the information store to effectively act in the changing future environment". This principle addresses the emergence of controlled, conscious processing in working memory for biologically secondary information and the role of learner motivation, postulating the fundamental interconnectedness of cognition and motivation. It parallels Woolcott's preparedness for learning principle and implies that every learning task needs activities aimed at setting learners' explicit intention to learn.
requirements: Specific learner cognitive activities aimed at externally motivating and cognitively engaging learners prior to acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
constraints: The paper notes the principle could be suppressed in experts acting in their area of expertise, and this form of expertise reversal needs experimental investigation
target_learners: novice learners acquiring biologically secondary knowledge in formal instruction
target_learning_goals: motivated, cognitively engaged acquisition of secondary knowledge
examples: Activities may trigger curiosity, establish gaps in the knowledge base, or activate relevant available knowledge
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Expansive framing: a situative model of learning transfer built on authorship and intercontextuality
description: Expansive framing, advanced by Engle, is a situative model of learning transfer holding that transfer depends on how teachers and learners frame the boundaries of participation, not only on physical affordances and constraints. Engle argued that "when students were positioned as authors whose ideas were relevant beyond the immediate classroom, they perceived more affordances for applying their knowledge in future settings." The framework reframes transfer as social accountability and identity-building, with design principles concerning authorship, connections across time, place, and roles, accountability, and generalizing authorship across settings.
requirements: Teachers must invite students to author their own contributions rather than reproduce an authority's answers
constraints: Transfer depends on the relation between prior learning and the opportunities and constraints present in a new situation
target_learning_goals: Generative learning that transfers readily and widely across contexts
examples: Engle's 2006 reanalysis of the PDE study recordings, examining student performance on a challenging far-transfer performance task after significant delays and interruptions
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: The Reciprocal Effects Model is Robust to Alternative Modeling Specifications: A Response to Sorjonen et al., 2025
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Herbert W Marsh, Reinhard Pekrun, Oliver Lüdtke, Jiesi Guo. (2025). The Reciprocal Effects Model is Robust to Alternative Modeling Specifications: A Response to Sorjonen et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review, 37 (3), pp.79. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10059-7
title: Extended reciprocal effects model (REM): contemporaneous skill-development effects of achievement on self-concept and lagged self-enhancement effects of self-concept on achievement
description: The extended reciprocal effects model (REM) is a longitudinal model of reciprocal processes between academic self-concept (ASC) and achievement (ACH). The article describes it as positing "contemporaneous skill-development effects (of ACH on ASC) and lagged self-enhancement effects (of ASC on ACH)", so achievement and self-concept influence each other through two temporally distinct pathways. The article uses this model as the target structure its reanalyses test against alternative specifications proposed by Sorjonen et al. (2025).
requirements: Longitudinal data with a temporal structure that can distinguish contemporaneous (lag0) effects from lagged (lag1) effects between academic self-concept and achievement.
constraints: The article states that some alternative models proposed in the commentary "did not fully capture the temporal structure central to Marsh et al.'s (2024) extended reciprocal effects model (REM)".
target_learners: Students in longitudinal academic datasets (e.g., the PALMA dataset)
target_learning_goals: Understanding reciprocal relations between academic self-concept and achievement over time
examples: The article reanalyzed the original PALMA dataset used in Marsh et al. (2024) to test the extended REM against alternative models.
key_sources: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Herbert W Marsh, Reinhard Pekrun, Oliver Lüdtke, Jiesi Guo. (2025). The Reciprocal Effects Model is Robust to Alternative Modeling Specifications: A Response to Sorjonen et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review, 37 (3), pp.79. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10059-7

article_title: A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education
citation: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z
title: Extended heuristic framework of spatial ability uniting CHC factors with contemporary spatial factors
description: The article synthesises the spatial factors contained in the CHC theory with factors emerging from contemporary factor-analytic research into a single extended framework, presented as a conceptual diagram. It argues that "the remit of spatial ability could theoretically contain 25 factors", some known to be more powerful representations than others. The framework deliberately emphasises narrow factors (a splitter perspective) so that a greater variety of factors can be explored across STEM education contexts.
requirements: Empirical validation of the framework as a whole after its presentation; many factors within it may not exist as individual factors and may instead represent, in whole or part, currently well-established spatial factors
constraints: The framework is heuristic and not recognised as an absolute model; newly included factors are hypothetical or tentatively defined pending investigation
target_learners: STEM learners across disciplines and educational levels
target_learning_goals: Understanding and developing the spatial factors underlying STEM educational performance
examples: The article presents Table 2 listing factors not represented in the CHC theory (e.g. spatial orientation, spatial relations, imagery quality, dynamic factors, directional and speed judgement) and Figure 2 as a conceptual diagram of the extended framework.
key_sources: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z

article_title: Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges
citation: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review
title: Teoria ekspansywnego uczenia się jako trzecia metafora wykraczająca poza przyswajanie i uczestnictwo
description: Teoria ekspansywnego uczenia się (Engeström, 1987), zakorzeniona w kulturowo-historycznej teorii działalności Wygotskiego, Leontjewa, Iljenkowa i Dawidowa, wraz z ideami Batesona i Bachtina, utrzymuje, że uczenie się nie jest ani przyswajaniem, ani uczestnictwem, lecz rozszerzaniem: „teoria ekspansywnego uczenia się musi bazować na własnej metaforze, a mianowicie na poszerzeniu”. Uczący się wspólnie tworzą i wdrażają nowe obiekty i koncepcje dla ich kolektywnej działalności. Przegląd redefiniuje strefę najbliższego rozwoju Wygotskiego jako zbiorową odległość między codziennymi działaniami a historycznie nową formą działalności.
requirements: Analiza musi być wielowymiarowa, obejmująca to, czy uczenie się utrwala czy przekształca kulturę, ruch pionowy czy poziomy oraz przyswajanie/uczestnictwo czy formowanie pojęć teoretycznych
constraints: Artykuł argumentuje, że dychotomia przyswajanie–uczestnictwo Sfard prowadzi do nadmiernych uproszczeń i że teoria nie mieści się w żadnej z tych metafor
target_learners: społeczności i sieci praktyków w miejscach pracy i organizacjach
target_learning_goals: kolektywne przekształcanie obiektów i form wspólnej działalności
examples: Przykłady otwierające: pracownicy opieki społecznej w Helsinkach wspierający starszych klientów w domu oraz biblioteka uniwersytecka w Helsinkach redefiniująca swoje usługi dla naukowców
key_sources: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review

article_title: Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges
citation: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review
title: Cykl ekspansywnego uczenia się jako sekwencja działań uczenia się od kwestionowania do konsolidacji
description: Cykl ekspansywny modeluje kolektywne uczenie się jako sekwencję działań poznawczych: kwestionowanie, analiza (historyczno-genetyczna i faktyczno-empiryczna), modelowanie nowego związku, badanie modelu, wdrażanie go, a następnie refleksja i konsolidacja w nową stabilną formę praktyki. Artykuł podkreśla, że „cykl ekspansywnego uczenia się nie jest uniwersalną formułą poszczególnych faz i etapów”, lecz heurystycznym narzędziem opartym na przejściu od abstrakcji do konkretu, testowanym i wzbogacanym przy każdym użyciu.
requirements: Punkt początkowy cyklu to moment, w którym kwestionowany jest stabilny wzorzec działalności; punkt końcowy to moment, w którym nowy wzorzec jest konsolidowany
constraints: Artykuł stwierdza, że żaden rzeczywisty kolektywny proces prawdopodobnie nie podąża wyraźnie za wzorcowym modelem
target_learners: kolektywy, takie jak zespoły nauczycieli, grupy pracowników i sieci organizacyjne
target_learning_goals: generowanie i konsolidacja nowej, historycznie nowej formy działalności
examples: Model rozszerza sześć działań uczenia się Dawydowa, dodając krytyczne kwestionowanie oraz wdrażanie i konsolidację rzeczywistych, kulturowo nowych praktyk
key_sources: Engeström, Y., Sannino, A. (2010). Studies of expansive learning: Foundations, findings and future challenges. Educational Research Review, 5. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/educational-research-review

article_title: Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners
citation: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784
title: Explicit vs. implicit interventions as a two-branch taxonomy of school-based creativity support
description: The review organizes school-based creativity support into two branches. Explicit interventions are 'intentionally designed programs or instructional units aimed at developing creativity as a specific learning objective', typically structured, time-bound, and measurable. Implicit interventions are 'not framed as direct creativity training but are embedded in everyday classroom practices and broader school environments', operating through pedagogical strategies and contextual conditions. The taxonomy builds on Jeffrey and Craft's distinction between teaching for creativity and creative teaching, and structures the review's three research questions.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable by whether creativity is the explicit instructional objective or an indirect outcome of pedagogy and context
constraints: Distinction drawn for formal K-12 school settings; the review notes implicit interventions are more diffuse and context-dependent than explicit ones
target_learners: K-12 students in formal education (primary ages 6–12, secondary ages 13–18)
target_learning_goals: Creative thinking (divergent and convergent), creative self-efficacy, creative problem solving
examples: The review categorized 101 studies under RQ1 (explicit interventions) versus RQ2/RQ3 (implicit pedagogical and contextual approaches), e.g., brainstorming programs under ideation and inquiry-based STEM activities under student-centered inquiry learning
key_sources: Gu, X., Ritter, S. M., Frossard, F., van den Boom, L., Delfmann, L. R. & Barajas, M. (2026). Fostering creativity in formal schooling: A systematic review of explicit and implicit interventions for young learners. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100784

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Treat explicit and constructivist instruction as synergistic rather than mutually exclusive
description: The review argues that framing explicit and constructivist instruction as mutually exclusive sets in place "a false dichotomy"; there are synergies and neither approach has exclusive claims to particular instructional strategies. High-quality learning relies on students experiencing both explicit and independent approaches, and privileging one risks denying students learning opportunities the other affords. LRI operationalizes this synthesis so students benefit from the strengths each approach offers.
requirements: Educators must recognize points in learner development where each approach is appropriate, with effectiveness of one intertwined with the other
constraints: The divergence between the approaches lies mainly in the amount and type of instruction provided
target_learning_goals: comprehensive instructional support across novice-to-expert learning phases
examples: The review quotes Liem and Martin (2013): constructivist approaches are better assisted by direct and structured teacher input that builds knowledge needed for subsequent meaningful discovery and enquiry-based learning
key_sources: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w

article_title: Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024)
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4
title: Extended Skill Development Model (ESDM)
description: The ESDM is the authors' alternative to the reciprocal effects model of academic self-concept and achievement. It "posits a unidirectional effect of trait-like academic achievement on trait-like self-concept", and holds that time-specific scores on both constructs arise from those trait-like levels "in addition to common time-specific state factors, e.g., illness or mood", with autoregressive effects among the state factors and no direct prospective effects between occasion-specific scores. In this article it is fitted to simulated PALMA-like and TRAIN-like data, where its good fit suggests observed cross-lagged effects may be spurious.
requirements: Longitudinal multi-wave measures of both constructs; the model is estimated via SEM on covariances/correlations and sample size
constraints: The unidirectional trait effect is an assumption that cannot be distinguished statistically, at least not in observational data, from a confounder affecting both trait-like factors
examples: Fitted to simulated PALMA-like data (χ2 = 597, CFI = 0.977) and TRAIN-like data (χ2 = 821, CFI = 0.934) with good fit in both
key_sources: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Inconclusive Evidence for a Prospective Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Simulated Reanalysis and Comment on Marsh et al. (2024). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10008-4

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Allow extended instructional time with manipulatives and examine delay between learning and assessment
description: Drawing on embodied theories and discovery-learning arguments, the commentary recommends that future studies allow more instructional time spent interacting with manipulatives, because successful construction of internal representations likely requires extensive sensorimotor experience. It also recommends examining time between learning and assessment, since "it is likely that the effectiveness of approaches are overestimated when instruction and assessment occur in one session". This principle follows Pouw, van Gog, and Paas's argument that internalization of multimodality routines requires extensive interaction time.
requirements: Instructional designs must provide learners substantial opportunities to physically interact with manipulatives over extended periods
constraints: A review cited in the commentary found less than 5% of educational psychology studies accounted for time spent learning and time between learning and outcome measurement, with most research performed in periods of less than 1 day
target_learning_goals: Construction of robust internal representations and durable learning outcomes
examples: The commentary cites Hsieh et al. (2005) finding that the majority of educational psychology research is performed in abbreviated periods, usually less than 1 day
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda
citation: Vu, T., Magis-Weinberg, L., Jansen, B. R. J., van Atteveldt, N., Jansen, T. W. P. J., Lee, N. C., van der Maas, H. L. J., Raijmakers, M. E. J., Sachisthal, M. S. M., & Meeter, M. (2021). Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09616-7
title: Treat external factors (rewards, norms, requirements, feedback form, instruction quality) as entry points for interventions on the motivation-achievement cycle
description: The review argues that external influences — extrinsic rewards, autonomy support, cultural norms, verbal persuasion, outside requirements such as deadlines, quality of teaching, and the form of feedback — can start, sustain, or redirect a motivation-achievement cycle that might otherwise not start or falter. Such factors matter because "they offer entry points for interventions that enhance motivation, achievement, or both". For example, feedback framed as mastery rather than ranking changes perceived achievement, so true high achievement can still fail to support motivation.
requirements: Educational design elements (feedback form, requirements, instruction quality) must be adjustable to influence perceived performance, effort, or value
constraints: Extrinsic rewards may detract from intrinsic motivation as described in self-determination theory, though they may also jolt a cycle that would otherwise not start
target_learners: school students, including those whose motivation-achievement cycles have not started
examples: The review cites feedback form (De Kraker-Pauw et al., 2017) and attributional processes as design elements shaping perceived achievement independently of true achievement
key_sources: Vu, T., Magis-Weinberg, L., Jansen, B. R. J., van Atteveldt, N., Jansen, T. W. P. J., Lee, N. C., van der Maas, H. L. J., Raijmakers, M. E. J., Sachisthal, M. S. M., & Meeter, M. (2021). Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09616-7

article_title: Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning
citation: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w
title: Exemplar-based account of how variability shapes retrieval practice for transfer
description: The article proposes that retrieval practice is fundamentally memory-based, and that item variability determines the scope and organization of what is remembered. Drawing on exemplar-based models of category learning, it argues that "Repeated retrieval can be viewed as strengthening memory for specific exemplars, supporting accurate recall but offering limited transfer," whereas varied retrieval strengthens memory for multiple related exemplars whose overlapping representations support generalization. This account extends existing memory-strengthening theories of retrieval practice, which the article says were developed from repeated-item studies and do not explain how variability shapes transfer.
requirements: Learners must engage in retrieval attempts across multiple related exemplars for overlapping representations to form
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of their two experiments with artificial rule-learning tasks, not as a directly tested model
target_learners: adult learners in rule- and skill-learning contexts
target_learning_goals: generalization of learned rules to novel problems
examples: In Experiment 2, varied retrieval practice produced final-test performance comparable to varied worked examples, which the authors explain via overlapping exemplar representations
key_sources: Meng Cao & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Striking the Balance: How Variability Shapes Retrieval Practice and Worked Examples for Transfer Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10169-w

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Conceptual framework of script-based learning incorporating external and internal collaboration scripts
description: The article closes with a conceptual framework on script-based learning that incorporates both external and internal collaboration scripts. External scripts are instructional scaffolds provided by the environment, while internal collaboration scripts are the learners' own knowledge structures about collaboration. The framework holds that research on collaboration scripts needs to consider the learners' internal collaboration scripts as a further determinant of collaboration behavior, alongside the external scaffolds designers provide.
requirements: Design and research must consider both the provided external script and the learners' internal scripts
target_learners: Collaborative learners in schools and computer-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding and designing collaboration support that fits learners' internal scripts
key_sources: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2

article_title: Antecedents of student team formation in higher education
citation: Carlos A. de Matos Fernandes, Marion Hoffman, Jasperina Brouwer. (2024). Antecedents of student team formation in higher education. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101931
title: Exponential random partition model as an approach to modeling student team formation
description: The article applies an exponential random partition model to the formation of student teams in higher education. The model is listed among the article's own keywords alongside "Group composition", "Friendship", "Similarity", and "Project teams", indicating it is the article's core analytical framework for representing how students partition themselves into project teams. Within the article's scope, this framework treats team formation as a partitioning process whose antecedents can be modeled statistically.
requirements: Data on student team membership and on candidate antecedents such as friendship and similarity ties are needed to fit the model.
constraints: The framework is presented in the article for project teams in higher education settings.
target_learning_goals: understanding how student project teams form
key_sources: Carlos A. de Matos Fernandes, Marion Hoffman, Jasperina Brouwer. (2024). Antecedents of student team formation in higher education. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101931

article_title: The moderating role of the teacher-child relationship in the association between peer rejection and language competence in early childhood education
citation: Femke van der Wilt, Jantine Spilt, Sharisse van Driel, Hilde Colpin. (2025). The moderating role of the teacher-child relationship in the association between peer rejection and language competence in early childhood education. Learning and Instruction 100 (2025) 102217. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102217
title: Extended attachment perspective on teacher-child relationships: dyadic affective quality with closeness, conflict, and dependency dimensions
description: The article adopts the extended attachment perspective, which "emphasizes the dyadic, affective quality of teacher-child relationships, distinguishing three dimensions: closeness, conflict, and dependency". Closeness refers to warmth, support and positive affect, with the teacher as a secure base and safe haven; conflict describes struggles, tension and negative affect. The study focuses on closeness and conflict as moderators of the peer rejection-language competence link, framed by attachment theory and the academic risk hypothesis.
requirements: Measurement of the dyadic affective quality of the teacher-child relationship, e.g. via the Student-Teacher Relationship Scale
constraints: The study examined only the affective quality, without considering the cognitive dimension such as instructional support
examples: The study used the shortened Closeness and Conflict subscales of the Dutch Student-Teacher Relationship Scale (Cronbach's alpha .82 and .81)
key_sources: Femke van der Wilt, Jantine Spilt, Sharisse van Driel, Hilde Colpin. (2025). The moderating role of the teacher-child relationship in the association between peer rejection and language competence in early childhood education. Learning and Instruction 100 (2025) 102217. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102217

article_title: It's all a matter of expectancy: How expectancies about task execution perspective influence learning through video modeling examples
citation: de Jonge, T. H. S., de Koning, B. B., & van Wermeskerken, M. (2026). It's all a matter of expectancy: How expectancies about task execution perspective influence learning through video modeling examples. Learning and Instruction, 105, 102422. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102422
title: Expectation Alignment Hypothesis (EAH)
description: The Expectation Alignment Hypothesis is the article's proposed dynamic account of the perspective effect: "the benefit of a particular recording angle depends on how well it aligns with the viewer's expectations about the task angle". When recording angle and expected task angle mismatch, viewers must perform mental transformations (mental rotation or perspective taking) during observation, which "induce a significant degree of cognitive load" and reduce working memory available for encoding, impairing performance. The experiment supported the EAH: alignment effects on performance and load were larger than the recording-angle main effect.
requirements: The learner holds (or is induced to hold) an expectation about the angle from which the task will be performed, which can align or misalign with the recording angle
constraints: The article notes the ERH and EAH may both operate simultaneously and hold to varying degrees, with potentially additive effects
target_learners: undergraduate psychology students learning procedural tasks from video modeling examples
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge and task performance in circuit-board assembly from video modeling examples
examples: The experiment oriented a physical circuit next to the monitor and told participants they would perform the task from that orientation, manipulating expected angle independently of recording angle
key_sources: de Jonge, T. H. S., de Koning, B. B., & van Wermeskerken, M. (2026). It's all a matter of expectancy: How expectancies about task execution perspective influence learning through video modeling examples. Learning and Instruction, 105, 102422. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102422

article_title: The linguistic nature of Children's scientific reasoning
citation: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002
title: Exercise linguistic abilities — linguistic inferencing and academic vocabulary — in science education, not only visuospatial skills
description: Because linguistic inferencing predicted all three scientific reasoning components and academic vocabulary supported early-stage hypothesis validation, the authors argue that science education, which currently stresses visuospatial inferencing, underestimates the role of linguistic abilities. They conclude that "linguistic abilities – both linguistic inferencing and academic vocabulary – can and should be exercised as well". This extends the theoretical framework of individual differences in scientific reasoning to include verbal processing routes.
requirements: Attention to academic vocabulary (domain-general enquiry words and STEM words) and inferencing practice, e.g., in reading comprehension contexts
constraints: Based on cross-sectional correlational evidence; the authors call for longitudinal and intervention research
target_learners: primary school children in enquiry-based science education
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning: hypothesis validation, experimentation, generating conclusions
examples: The study measured academic vocabulary with a 54-item test covering physics, engineering, biology, mathematics, Earth and space, and general science
key_sources: Van de Sande, E., Kleemans, T., Verhoeven, L., & Segers, E. (2019). The linguistic nature of children's scientific reasoning. Learning and Instruction, 62, 20-26. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.02.002

article_title: Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study
citation: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209
title: Expose learners to the other side's narrative, authentically expressed by its representatives, to foster understanding of and empathy toward the other side
description: The principle holds that engaging with an alternative position, even through a text written by individuals who hold it, is a facilitative condition for understanding the other side and reflecting on one's own position. The article reports that "Being exposed to the narrative of the “other-side,” as authentically expressed by its representatives, appears to be a facilitative condition for understanding the “other-side” and showing empathy toward the “other-side.”" It extends prior work on hearing opposing arguments to engagement via authentic texts.
requirements: The alternative account should authentically represent the other side's position, written by members of that group.
constraints: Exposure evoked understanding and self-reflection but did not eliminate myside bias; evaluative comments remained in favor of students' own position.
target_learners: elementary school students in ethnically divided contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding of the other side's perspective, empathy, self-reflection on one's own position
examples: Students read a Turkish-Cypriot historian's account of the 1974 war; against-own-side comments doubled and own-side support halved at post-test when reading it.
key_sources: Iordanou, K., Fotiou, C., Manoli, A., & Zembylas, M. (2025). Examining myside bias on a controversial historical event after engagement in dialogic argumentation: Insights from a think aloud study. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102209

article_title: The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms.
citation: Gaspard, H., Parrisius, C., Piesch, H., Kleinhansl, M., Wille, E., Nagengast, B., Trautwein, U., & Hulleman, C. S. (2021). The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000663
title: Expectancy-value theory as the grounding framework for relevance interventions
description: The article grounds relevance interventions in Eccles et al.'s expectancy-value theory, in which students' academic behavior and choices are predicted by expectancies for success and the value they attach to tasks. "Eccles and colleagues (1983) distinguish four major components that contribute to subjective task value": intrinsic value, attainment value, and utility value contribute positively, while cost contributes negatively. Recent work decomposes these into subfacets (e.g., utility value by life domain and time horizon; cost into effort, emotional, and opportunity cost). Utility value is targeted by interventions because it is assumed more malleable than attainment and intrinsic value.
requirements: Interventions targeting value should account for the interplay of expectancies and values, since the highest outcomes are predicted when both are high
constraints: The article uses the term expectancies to cover self-concept and self-efficacy, which differ in malleability and frame-of-reference sensitivity
examples: The MoMa intervention logic model (Figure 1) details intervention components triggering expectancies, mindsets, and utility value, which should ultimately enhance achievement
key_sources: Gaspard, H., Parrisius, C., Piesch, H., Kleinhansl, M., Wille, E., Nagengast, B., Trautwein, U., & Hulleman, C. S. (2021). The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000663

article_title: College students’ reasons for leaving biomedical fields: Disenchantment with biomedicine or attraction to other fields?
citation: Rosenzweig, E. Q., Harackiewicz, J. M., Hecht, C. A., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., Asher, M. W., & Hyde, J. S. (2021). College Students’ Reasons for Leaving Biomedical Fields: Disenchantment with Biomedicine or Attraction to Other Fields? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000456
title: Expectancy-value theory as a framework for biomedical attrition
description: The article grounds its predictive models in Eccles and colleagues' expectancy-value theory of motivation, which "posits that there are two primary psychological variables that influence academic choices": expectations for success and the value of the field in terms of how "useful, interesting, and important it is". The theory assumes course experiences affect choices indirectly by shaping expectancies and task values, so students leave STEM because of low confidence and/or low value. The study operationalized the competence side through course grades and the value side through interest measures.
requirements: Requires measures of competence-related beliefs (here proxied by grades) and task value (here interest in biology) at relevant time points in students' trajectories
constraints: The study used grades rather than competence-related beliefs because grades are more frequently used in prior attrition research, limiting direct tests of the belief construct
target_learners: college students in introductory biomedical courses
target_learning_goals: persistence in biomedical majors and career paths
key_sources: Rosenzweig, E. Q., Harackiewicz, J. M., Hecht, C. A., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., Asher, M. W., & Hyde, J. S. (2021). College Students’ Reasons for Leaving Biomedical Fields: Disenchantment with Biomedicine or Attraction to Other Fields? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000456

article_title: The interplay of mastery and performance goals in social comparison: A multiple-goal perspective.
citation: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161
title: Design mastery-goal learning settings assuming performance-approach goals remain present and shape how mastery goals operate
description: Because "educational settings are rarely free from performance-approach goals, even when mastery goals are promoted", designers should anticipate that mastery goals will coexist with performance-approach goals and that the latter moderate the former's effects. The article shows that mastery goals lead to social comparison only when performance-approach goals are endorsed or induced, so designers should account for this interplay rather than treating goal conditions in isolation.
requirements: Awareness of learners' performance-approach goal endorsement when promoting mastery goals
constraints: Mastery goals predicted social comparison interest only in the performance-approach goal condition in Study 2
target_learning_goals: managing goal conditions when designing mastery-oriented learning environments
examples: Study 2 manipulated goal conditions and found mastery goals predicted interest in social comparison only in the performance-approach goal condition.
key_sources: Darnon, C., Dompnier, B., Gilliéron, O., & Butera, F. (2010). The Interplay of Mastery and Performance Goals in Social Comparison: A Multiple-Goal Perspective. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018161

article_title: Promoting persistence in the biological and medical sciences: An expectancy-value approach to intervention.
citation: Hecht, C. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2019). Promoting Persistence in the Biological and Medical Sciences: An Expectancy-Value Approach to Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000356
title: Expectancy-value theory: positive expectancy x value interaction in academic choices, extended to a two-process account of UVI effects
description: The article applies Eccles' expectancy-value theory, in which "students are most likely to pursue an education in a particular domain if they both value the domain and believe they can succeed in it." It extends this with a two-process account: UVIs initiate task engagement, which improves performance for struggling students, and personal relevance reflection, which amplifies confident students' persistence decisions. The UVI x confidence interaction on persistence is read as consistent with the theorized synergistic expectancy x value effect.
requirements: Effects on persistence are expected only when the intervention increases subjective task value in a domain students are considering pursuing, such as an introductory course for intended majors.
constraints: The authors note the personal-relevance process may be a double-edged sword: students with doubts may decide to pursue a field where they perceive both value and a high likelihood of success instead.
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biomedical science courses
target_learning_goals: course performance in gateway science courses
examples: The UVI x confidence interaction on two-year persistence was interpreted as consistent with the positive expectancy-value interaction, since only in the value-emphasizing UVI condition did confidence predict persistence.
key_sources: Hecht, C. A., Harackiewicz, J. M., Priniski, S. J., Canning, E. A., Tibbetts, Y., & Hyde, J. S. (2019). Promoting Persistence in the Biological and Medical Sciences: An Expectancy-Value Approach to Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000356

article_title: Mentality and school progress.
citation: Toops, H. A., and Pintker, R. (1918). Mentality and School Progress. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mentality+and+School+Progress+Toops+Pintner
title: Use extreme school-grade limits (four or more grades retarded; more than one grade advanced) as diagnostic indicators of mental status
description: The article proposes that when a middle 'normal' band is retained and extreme school-grade limits are applied, school position becomes a near-perfect indicator of mental diagnosis: "no individual who is four or more grades retarded in school is above normal in mentality", and none more than one grade advanced is below normal. This was demonstrated on group mental-test and grade data from three schools of differing social status (ages 6 to 16), yielding a perfect association under these limits. The principle allows screening questions about children to be answered without mental testing of large numbers.
requirements: Age-at-grade expectations must be defined per age (e.g., grades 3B/3A as normal for eight-year-olds), and children without the possibility of being retarded or advanced at least one year (ages 6, 14, 15 and above as applicable) must be excluded from the computation.
constraints: The coefficient of +.97 obtained without a middle mentality class was described by the authors as not such as to warrant using school grade as a prediction of mentality until the middle classes are eliminated; the perfect association holds only for the extreme classes defined by the stated limits.
target_learners: Elementary and junior-high school children, ages 6 to 16
target_learning_goals: Diagnosis of mental subnormality or advancement from school progress
examples: In the three-school survey, four grades or more of retardation perfectly indicated a mentality not higher than normal, and two grades or more of advancement at least a normal mentality.
key_sources: Toops, H. A., and Pintker, R. (1918). Mentality and School Progress. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mentality+and+School+Progress+Toops+Pintner

article_title: Supplemental Material for Learning With Animation and Illusions of Understanding
citation: Animation and Illusions of Understanding: Experiment Protocol Users Guide. http://get.adobe.com/flashplayer/
title: Experiment Protocol.swf: a Flash-based multimedia program that administered the animation experiment and recorded participant responses
description: The guide describes an interactive multimedia computer program, provided as the Adobe Flash file "Experiment Protocol.swf", that administered the experiment and "recorded all participant responses". The program "provides aural narration, which was a significant component of the protocol". Examiners can start the protocol at any point using drop-down list boxes for treatment condition and protocol location, controls that participants were not shown. Condition codes are entered on a code entry screen: "magenta" for the no animation condition, "purple" for directive animation only, "crimson" for representational animation only, or "violet" for both animations.
requirements: Requires an appropriate version of Adobe Flash Player, which at the time of publication was available freely at http://get.adobe.com/flashplayer/.
constraints: The "no connection" message signifies the program cannot connect to the server needed to capture user input; the guide states that not connecting to the server will not impact how the program behaves from the participant's point of view.
The drop-down list boxes for treatment condition and protocol location were not provided to participants; they exist so examiners can view different sections without starting from the beginning.
target_learners: participants in the animation-and-understanding experiment administered by this program
target_learning_goals: learning from a narrated multimedia protocol under four animation treatment conditions (none, directive only, representational only, both)
examples: Running the program and clicking Start without adjusting the list boxes reproduces the protocol exactly as participants saw it.
Entering the code "violet" on the code entry screen presents the condition with both directive and representational animations.
key_sources: Animation and Illusions of Understanding: Experiment Protocol Users Guide. http://get.adobe.com/flashplayer/

article_title: Uncovering subgroup heterogeneity in dyslexia intervention outcomes using explainable machine learning
citation: Tan, A.S.-C., & Ali, F. (2026). Uncovering subgroup heterogeneity in dyslexia intervention outcomes using explainable machine learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00429-3
title: Explanation-aware clustering: combining model explainers with unsupervised clustering to uncover heterogeneous subgroups within predicted classes
description: This framework pairs a model explainer with unsupervised learning to reveal heterogeneity hidden by binary classification. LIME "perturbs the input data locally around a single instance and fits a simple interpretable model" to identify predictors contributing to class membership; clustering of these LIME profiles (via K-Means, cluster number selected by lowest Davies-Bouldin Index) then identifies subgroups within each class, addressing explainer models' "tendency to overstate class homogeneity due to such local approximations". The article uses it to uncover 2 responder and 4 non-responder subgroups with distinct longitudinal outcomes.
requirements: A trained predictive model with explainer output (LIME coefficients), plus unsupervised clustering and a cluster-validity index to select subgroup count
constraints: Explainer models tend to overstate class homogeneity due to local approximations; clustered subgroups rest on predictor importance, not actual predictor values directly
target_learners: Students with dyslexia or learning difficulties in literacy intervention
target_learning_goals: Prediction of intervention responsiveness and long-term literacy development to inform personalized intervention
examples: K-Means applied to LIME coefficients from a Gaussian Naive Bayes model identified responder and non-responder subgroups whose membership predicted trajectories 68.2 months post-intervention
key_sources: Tan, A.S.-C., & Ali, F. (2026). Uncovering subgroup heterogeneity in dyslexia intervention outcomes using explainable machine learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00429-3

article_title: No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study
citation: Hehl, M., Toyonaga, T., Carson, R. E., Dupont, P., Van Laere, K., Swinnen, S. P. & Cuypers, K. (2026). No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00451-5
title: Expansion-renormalization model of learning-related gray matter change
description: The article invokes the expansion-renormalization model to frame expectations about when learning-related gray matter changes should be detectable. As the article states, "This has given rise to the expansion-renormalization model which predicts an initial increase in GM volume, followed by a selection process and a partial or complete return to baseline GM volume". The model implies an inverted U-shape time course, with reported motor-related GM changes occurring within 5 days to 6 weeks and partially reverting after 2–4 months of retention or continued training beyond 4 weeks. The study's measurement schedule (MRI at baseline, 2 and 4 weeks; PET at 4 weeks) was designed around this anticipated window of maximal structural plasticity.
requirements: Measurement timing must be aligned with the expected expansion window while participants are still actively improving the skill
constraints: The article notes neuroplastic changes could have been transient and not sufficiently captured with measurements at 2 and 4 weeks, and a closer meshed measurement paradigm with a longer follow-up might help
target_learners: young healthy adults learning a new motor skill
target_learning_goals: motor skill acquisition and its neural substrates
examples: The study scheduled MRI assessments at baseline, 2 weeks and 4 weeks, and PET at 4 weeks, intended to coincide with the anticipated window of maximal structural plasticity
key_sources: Hehl, M., Toyonaga, T., Carson, R. E., Dupont, P., Van Laere, K., Swinnen, S. P. & Cuypers, K. (2026). No significant changes in synaptic density and gray matter volume following motor learning—a pilot study. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00451-5

article_title: Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education
citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Explicate the theoretical lens through which educational inequality is studied
description: Because disciplines frame inequality differently—some problematizing unequal outcomes, others unequal treatment or unequal provision—researchers should make their framing explicit. The article states "the need to explicate the lens through which the problem of inequality in education is studied," since answering "what needs to be equal to speak of equality" makes clear whether unequal treatment and/or outcomes are problematized or strived for.
requirements: Researchers must answer what needs to be equal to speak of equality, clarifying whether unequal treatment and/or unequal outcomes are problematized or strived for
constraints: The authors note these lenses "may be very different, and therefore not self-evident"
target_learning_goals: Fruitful combining of insights and ideas from across disciplines on educational inequality
examples: The article points to review articles such as the works of Jencks and Espinoza as aids for researchers placing their work vis-à-vis the broad range of perspectives
key_sources: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z

article_title: The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom
citation: Ayame Tamura, Kou Murayama, Ryo Ishii, Michiko Sakaki and Ayumi Tanaka. (2022). The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom. npj Science of Learning 7:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00125-y
title: Monoamine/locus coeruleus arousal account of exercise effects on classroom mood and cognition
description: The article frames its intervention with a physiological mechanism account in which "engaging in physical exercise triggers changes in neurotransmitter levels, especially monoamines", improving mood, and in which exercise-activated locus coeruleus norepinephrine release supports alertness, arousal, and attention to task-relevant stimuli. It uses this account to predict improved mood and reduced mind-wandering and sleepiness in class, though no physiological measures were collected in the study.
requirements: Future research incorporating physiological measures (plasma measures, pupil diameters, saliva alpha-amylase) to test the proposed pathway
constraints: The study itself assessed no arousal or physiological measures, so the mechanism remains untested in this data
examples: The authors hypothesised that exercise during a university lecture would positively influence emotional and cognitive engagement on the basis of this account
key_sources: Ayame Tamura, Kou Murayama, Ryo Ishii, Michiko Sakaki and Ayumi Tanaka. (2022). The effect of low-intensity exercise on emotional and cognitive engagement in the classroom. npj Science of Learning 7:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00125-y

article_title: Home numeracy experiences are associated with number-related brain activity and connectivity in early childhood
citation: Girard, C., Longo, L., Chesnokova, H., Epinat-Duclos, J., & Prado, J. (2026). Home numeracy experiences are associated with number-related brain activity and connectivity in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00419-5
title: Experience-dependent tuning account: richer home numeracy experience reduces local activity while increasing inter-regional connectivity
description: The authors propose that richer early home numeracy experiences tune the developing number-processing network, so that regions communicate more and each works less locally. They note that "a pattern of reduced local activity coupled with increased inter-regional connectivity has been described as a hallmark of experience-induced optimization in cortical networks." On this account, greater communication between regions may decrease local processing demands, explaining why higher home numeracy predicts lower digit-specific activity but stronger left-IPS connectivity. They caution the account "remains speculative given the lack of observed relation between brain activity and numerical performance."
requirements: A measure of the home numeracy environment (practice frequency, games at home) and task-based fMRI in children around school entry
