constraints: Cross-sectional design cannot establish whether connectivity precedes activity or draw causal conclusions
Efficiency interpretation remains speculative without brain-behavior correlations; reduced activation may partly reflect shallower attention during passive viewing
Interpretations cannot be disentangled within the current passive paradigm
target_learners: Five-year-old children at the start of formal schooling
target_learning_goals: Symbolic number processing and foundational numeracy
examples: PPI analyses showed positive associations between home numeracy practices and left-IPS connectivity, while whole-brain regressions showed negative associations with digit-specific activity in the same sample
key_sources: Girard, C., Longo, L., Chesnokova, H., Epinat-Duclos, J., & Prado, J. (2026). Home numeracy experiences are associated with number-related brain activity and connectivity in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00419-5

article_title: High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype
citation: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8
title: Exercise-induced physiological cascade account: HIIT primes motor learning by creating an environment conducive to neuroplasticity
description: The article explains the HIIT benefit via a mechanistic account in which "Exercise, particularly performed at higher intensities, causes a cascade of physiological effects" — increased cerebral blood flow, oxygen, metabolites, neurotransmitters and neurotrophins such as BDNF — "which ultimately creates an environment conducive for neuroplasticity, and therefore learning and memory". Increased arousal from noradrenaline and cortisol may improve focus, and exercise modulates cortical excitability to facilitate LTP-like plasticity. Within-session gains are attributed to a generalised influence rather than specific online or offline processes.
requirements: Higher-intensity exercise appears central: the account ties facilitation to intensity-dependent upregulation of neurotrophins and plasticity responses.
constraints: The authors state the exercise influence on consolidation may be relatively specific to retention hours-days after training rather than brief rest periods within a session; the mechanism account is interpretive, not directly tested in this study.
target_learners: Healthy young adults learning novel motor skills
target_learning_goals: Motor skill acquisition (visuomotor accuracy and speed)
examples: Participants cycled 20 minutes of HIIT (alternating two-minute high-intensity up to 90% HRR and three-minute moderate intervals) 10 minutes before SVIPT practice.
key_sources: Brooks, E., Hawi, Z., Hosler, J. et al. (2026). High-intensity cardiovascular exercise facilitates online motor skill learning, with no effect of BDNF genotype. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00432-8

article_title: Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children
citation: Romanovska, L., Janssen, R. & Bonte, M. (2022). Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children. npj Science of Learning 7:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00118-3
title: Expansion-renormalisation / inverted-U account of reading-skill automatisation in the developing speech-language network
description: The article proposes that non-linear, inverted-U developmental trajectories in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli reflect a gradual switch from effortful to automatised processing. It states that "skill learning in general is thought to re ﬂect an expansion-renormalisation pattern, with an initial increase in cortical activation/volume in the key areas involved in the acquisition of a speci ﬁc skill, followed by a decrease once pro ﬁciency is reached". Applying this to reading, the observed left STG and pre-CG changes "may re ﬂect changes during the proposed prolonged time-course of letter-speech sound automatisation", paralleling reported inverted-U trajectories in VWFA/ventral occipito-temporal cortex. The account integrates active explicit mapping strategies early in learning with passive associative mechanisms as proficiency increases.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement spanning the developmental period in which letter-speech sound mappings become automatised
Tasks that engage the letter-speech sound mapping regions being tracked
constraints: The authors state the pattern must be verified in larger samples and that it "may re ﬂect" rather than demonstrates the mechanism
No significant ventral occipito-temporal session differences were found, possibly because the simple "aba"/"ada" text stimuli "do not provide optimal engagement of the VWFA"
target_learners: Typically reading children aged 8–11 in the first years of reading instruction
target_learning_goals: Automatisation of letter-speech sound mappings supporting word decoding
key_sources: Romanovska, L., Janssen, R. & Bonte, M. (2022). Longitudinal changes in cortical responses to letter-speech sound stimuli in 8–11 year-old children. npj Science of Learning 7:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00118-3

article_title: Real-world effectiveness of a social-psychological intervention translated from controlled trials to classrooms
citation: Chen, P., Teo, D. W. H., Foo, D. X. Y., Derry, H. A., Hayward, B. T., Schulz, K. W., Hayward, C., McKay, T. A., & Ong, D. C. (2022). Real-world effectiveness of a social-psychological intervention translated from controlled trials to classrooms. npj Science of Learning 7:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00135-w
title: Exam Playbook: a scalable, self-administered online version of the Strategic Resource Use intervention
description: The Exam Playbook is an online app adaptation of the previously validated Strategic Resource Use intervention, delivered through ECoach to 14 large introductory STEM and Economics classes. It prompts pre-exam self-reflection: "It prompted students to anticipate the format and demands of their upcoming exam, provided a comprehensive checklist of learning resources available in the class, and asked students to select which would be useful". Students then explain each choice and plan when, where, and how to use the resources, and receive a printable summary of their responses.
requirements: Delivery through ECoach with class-specific customization of the resource checklist and exam reminders by psychologists, designers, and instructors
Access made available 10 days prior to each exam via personalized ECoach reminders
constraints: Designed for exam preparation in courses with scheduled exams; use was voluntary and tracked only when students clicked through the complete intervention
target_learners: College students in large introductory STEM and Economics courses
target_learning_goals: Strategic, self-regulated use of learning resources to improve exam performance
examples: Made freely available before all exams in 14 classes over 2 semesters; on average 43.6% of students in each class engaged with it at least once
key_sources: Chen, P., Teo, D. W. H., Foo, D. X. Y., Derry, H. A., Hayward, B. T., Schulz, K. W., Hayward, C., McKay, T. A., & Ong, D. C. (2022). Real-world effectiveness of a social-psychological intervention translated from controlled trials to classrooms. npj Science of Learning 7:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00135-w

article_title: Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1
title: Executable production-rule model of help seeking with a taxonomy of maladaptive help-seeking behaviors
description: The article's central theoretical artifact is a knowledge-engineered, rule-based, executable model of help seeking during tutored problem solving, built through cognitive task analysis guided by tutor log and pre/post-test data. Unlike prior descriptive models, it is detailed and executable and can drive tutoring via model tracing. "In its final incarnation, the model comprised approximately 80 production rules. It included a taxonomy of maladaptive help-seeking behaviors with broad categories such as Help Abuse, Help Avoidance, Try-step Abuse, and more detailed subcategories." Recent findings suggest revisions: the model should prescribe help use in a narrower range of circumstances and account for bottom-out hints aiding learning when self-explained.
requirements: Requires knowledge engineering guided by theories of help seeking and supported by classroom observations and mined log and pre/post-test data
constraints: Narrower in scope than prior models, focusing only on help seeking in the context of tutored problem solving
Does not capture that bottom-out hints may aid learning when self-explained, and needs narrower prescriptions about when help use is appropriate
target_learners: Students learning with step-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Effective (adaptive) help seeking as a self-regulated learning skill
examples: The Help Tutor applied the model with the standard model-tracing algorithm, saying, e.g., 'Try to take more time to read the hint' when a student clicked through hint levels quickly
key_sources: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1

article_title: Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers
citation: Aleven, V., McLaren, B. M., Sewall, J., van Velsen, M., Popescu, O., Demi, S., Ringenberg, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers. International Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0088-2
title: Example-tracing tutors as intelligent tutoring systems
description: The article argues that example-tracing tutors should be viewed as ITS based on VanLehn's criterion that ITSs have an inner loop providing step-level guidance. The authors update this argument, offering an alternative definition of adaptivity with three factors: empirical grounding in learner understanding, individualization across psychological dimensions, and appropriate interactivity. They argue "example-tracing tutor technology supports the building of tutors that exhibit all three factors that make up this definition".
requirements: The tutor must exhibit adaptive behavior grounded in empirical understanding of learners, individualization, and interactivity.
constraints: Example-tracing tutors currently do not have features for responding adaptively to student self-regulation, metacognition, or affect.
key_sources: Aleven, V., McLaren, B. M., Sewall, J., van Velsen, M., Popescu, O., Demi, S., Ringenberg, M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Example-Tracing Tutors: Intelligent Tutor Development for Non-programmers. International Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0088-2

article_title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
citation: Nye, B. D., Graesser, A. C., & Hu, X. (2014). AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0029-5
title: Expectation-misconception tailored discourse framework with the 5-step tutoring frame
description: AutoTutor's core explanatory framework stores anticipated correct answers (expectations) and frequent invalid answers (misconceptions), and uses semantic matching to evaluate student input against them. Dialogs follow a 5-step frame in which the tutor poses a question, the student answers, the tutor gives brief feedback, collaboration improves the answer, and the tutor checks understanding. Discourse moves such as pumps, hints, prompts, assertions, and summaries guide students to cover each expectation, with assertions as a bottom-out response. The review presents this framework as the shared design inherited across the AutoTutor family.
requirements: Authoring of expectations, misconceptions, and discourse moves per main question via curriculum scripts or authoring tools
Semantic analysis techniques (e.g., LSA, regular expressions, word-overlap, logical entailment) to match student input to expectations and misconceptions
constraints: Finding good misconception coverage often requires multiple design iterations because even experts have trouble anticipating misconceptions
Dialogs for a full physics problem can last 30 to 100 turns before all expectations are covered
target_learners: learners across domains including computer literacy, physics, biology, and critical thinking
target_learning_goals: constructing explanations and answers to deep reasoning questions
examples: A sample physics dialog in Table 1 shows the tutor using a main question, pump, hint, answer, prompt, and short feedback to help a learner explain that two objects in free fall have the same acceleration
key_sources: Nye, B. D., Graesser, A. C., & Hu, X. (2014). AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0029-5

article_title: Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches
citation: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1
title: Taxonomy of item difficulty prediction approaches: expert-driven versus machine-driven
description: The review introduces a classification (its Fig. 1) that distinguishes two families of item difficulty prediction approaches. Expert-driven approaches are qualitative, resting on "an expert consensus that exploits their domain knowledge and experience" and on pre-defined features from educational taxonomies or experts' difficulty perceptions. Machine-driven approaches quantify difficulty using statistical or data-driven prediction models to enhance scalability and minimise human intervention. The review uses this taxonomy to organise the field and to motivate its focus on automatic, text-based, a priori prediction.
requirements: Applies to a priori prediction of textual assessment items; the review excludes post-administration estimation and non-textual items
constraints: The review restricts scope to difficulty sources intrinsic to the question text, excluding learner knowledge and performance factors
target_learners: test-takers in traditional classrooms, eLearning platforms, CAT systems and ITSs
target_learning_goals: accurate a priori estimation of assessment item difficulty for item calibration and sequencing
examples: The review's Fig. 1 presents the taxonomic decomposition of item difficulty prediction approaches into expert-driven and machine-driven branches
key_sources: Samah AlKhuzaey, Floriana Grasso, Terry R. Payne, Valentina Tamma. (2023). Text-based Question Difficulty Prediction: A Systematic Review of Automatic Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00362-1

article_title: Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring
citation: Funayama, H., Matsubayashi, Y., Asazuma, Y., Mizumoto, T., & Inui, K. (2025). Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00474-w
title: Expanded RIKEN SAS dataset with 10,000 new annotations
description: The RIKEN SAS dataset is a publicly available Japanese collection of annotated high school students' answers to reading comprehension questions, with rubrics, prompts, and analytic-criterion scores. The authors "added 10,000 new data annotations (20 prompts with 500 answers each)" to it, yielding 34 prompts treated as 109 independent analytic-criterion prompts. It served as the testbed for all cross-prompt pre-finetuning experiments, with six prompts (21 analytic criteria) as targets and 28 prompts (88 criteria) as cross-prompt pre-finetuning data.
requirements: Rubrics with key phrases and human-annotated gold scores for each prompt
constraints: Limited to Japanese reading-comprehension questions from high school students
examples: Six target prompts were split into 200 train, 50 development, and 250 test answers per prompt
key_sources: Funayama, H., Matsubayashi, Y., Asazuma, Y., Mizumoto, T., & Inui, K. (2025). Cross-prompt Pre-finetuning of Language Models for Short Answer Scoring. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00474-w

article_title: Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age
citation: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5
title: Build AI models designed for explainability and interpretation from the start, around theoretical constructs, rather than probing black boxes after the fact
description: This principle directs AIED developers to design models for explainability and ease of interpretation from the beginning, built around a theoretical understanding of the relevant constructs — the psychological domain, content and motivational constructs, the social need, and the interaction constructs. The article argues that "We need to build models that are designed for explainability and ease of interpretation from the start, not as an after-the-fact attempt to poke into a complex black-box model after it has been built." It is used in the commentary to respond to datafication criticisms, stressing that interpretation of data, a human collaborative thing, should drive decisions.
requirements: Relevant theoretical constructs built in from the start of model design
Human collaborative interpretation of data to drive decisions
constraints: The author states much current explainable AI effort consists of great big Band-Aids not addressing the fundamental issues; post-hoc labeling moves construct development from beginning to end and does not save time
target_learners: All learners served by AIED systems, since model decisions affect them
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of learner data to support instructional decisions
examples: The author warns that otherwise researchers must figure out by labeling example clusters what drives a deep learning model's predictions, opening the door to right predictions for wrong reasons via indicator variables spuriously correlated with true causal variables
key_sources: Ken Koedinger. (2024). Navigating Ethical Benefits and Risks as AIED Comes of Age. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00350-5

article_title: Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience
citation: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x
title: Exaggerated-mirror tutee modeling: giving the teachable agent the user's own errors amplified to prompt noticing and correction
description: BELLA's core instructional pattern is to give Elle the same types of deficiencies as the user but more exaggerated, so the user notices, corrects, and in doing so refreshes their own understanding. The article explains that if the user evaluates operations left to right, "Elle will be given that same tendency with an even higher likelihood to the same sort of operator-precedence error, so Elle will make even more egregious and obvious such errors which the user will have a good chance of noticing, correcting." When the user corrects Elle, BELLA both learns about the user and gives them a small esteem-building experience.
requirements: Requires an accurate user model to identify which errors to exaggerate
constraints: If the user does not notice Elle's mistake, BELLA may keep or worsen Elle's model to make the error more obvious, or have Elle self-reflect
target_learning_goals: Noticing and repairing one's own misconceptions by correcting a tutee's errors
examples: Elle's model is kept slightly behind the user's; as the student learns, BELLA improves Elle's model so it makes fewer mistakes
key_sources: Lenat, D. B., & Durlach, P. J. (2014). Reinforcing Math Knowledge by Immersing Students in a Simulated Learning-By-Teaching Experience. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0016-x

article_title: A comparative study of students’ adoption and usage of mobile learning in developing countries: Tunisia, Morocco, and Libya
citation: Elaish, M. M., Al-Azawei, A., Yadegaridehkordi, E., Hussein, M. H., Hwang, G.-J., Majoul, B., Ouchaouka, L., & Alaaraj, S. (2026). A comparative study of students' adoption and usage of mobile learning in developing countries: Tunisia, Morocco, and Libya. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10613-2
title: Extended UTAUT model integrating Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Trust, and Compatibility for m-learning acceptance
description: The study proposes an acceptance model grounded in UTAUT — whose constructs are Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Social Influence, Facilitating Condition, Behavioural Intention, and Use Behaviour — extended "by also drawing on Hofstede's Cultural Dimension theory (Hofstede, 1980), Trust (TR), and Compatibility (COMP)". The model posits thirteen hypotheses linking these constructs to behavioural intention and use behaviour, and was tested with SEM on student samples from three developing countries. It provides a context-sensitive framework for studying technology acceptance where cultural and economic factors matter.
requirements: Measurement of UTAUT, Hofstede, Trust, and Compatibility constructs via validated questionnaire items adapted from prior studies
Sample size following the rule of at least 10 times the number of indicators or structural paths
constraints: Developed and tested for m-learning acceptance among university students in developing countries (Tunisia, Morocco, Libya)
Data collected only from selected regions within each country
target_learning_goals: Acceptance and adoption of mobile learning technologies
examples: The model was tested on 588 respondents (147 Tunisia, 243 Morocco, 198 Libya) using SmartPLS, with country and academic year as control variables
key_sources: Elaish, M. M., Al-Azawei, A., Yadegaridehkordi, E., Hussein, M. H., Hwang, G.-J., Majoul, B., Ouchaouka, L., & Alaaraj, S. (2026). A comparative study of students' adoption and usage of mobile learning in developing countries: Tunisia, Morocco, and Libya. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10613-2

article_title: Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research
citation: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
title: Make causal assumptions explicit before data analysis to expose and prevent bias
description: The paper argues that researchers should articulate their causal assumptions graphically before collecting or analyzing data, because "there are no causal conclusions without causal assumptions". Explicit assumptions make it possible to trace whether a proposed causal effect is identified given the assumed structure, and to detect confounding, overcontrol, and collider bias before they distort estimates.
requirements: Researchers must commit to a causal structure (which arrows are present and which are absent) prior to estimation.
constraints: The value of the exercise depends on the plausibility and completeness of the assumed graph; a misspecified DAG can itself mislead.
examples: The paper's running example of an intervention X and outcome Y shows how adding a confounder Z as a fork immediately reveals a non-causal back-door path that would otherwise contaminate the estimate.
key_sources: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Design machine learning systems used in education with explainability built in from the outset
description: The article argues that because "learning and assessment of learning are problems that can never be completely formalised", some level of interpretability and explainability is necessary for machine learning systems used in education, unless incorrect results have no significant consequences. The capability to explain decisions should be programmed in during design, using explanation types from rationale to impact, each comprehensible to the decision's recipient without exposing commercially protected algorithms. This serves fairness, bias minimization, user trust and legal compliance such as GDPR.
requirements: Explainability mechanisms must be incorporated during system design, not added post hoc
Explanation methods must be matched to domain, use case and type of user
constraints: Where systems are used only informally or as adjuncts with no severe consequences for incorrect results, explainability requirements are lower
target_learners: all learners affected by educational machine learning systems
target_learning_goals: fair and interpretable decisions about learning and assessment
examples: Industry guidance distinguishing six explanation types from rationale to impact explanation
The CRASE automated writing-scoring engine rejected in Australia despite equivalent reliability because of a conflict between commercial confidentiality and explainability
key_sources: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2

article_title: Supporting learners’ experiment design
citation: Siswa van Riesen, Hannie Gijlers, Anjo Anjewierden, Ton de Jong. (2018). Supporting learners' experiment design. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:475–491. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9568-4
title: Experiment Design Tool (EDT): a step-by-step scaffold for designing experiments with built-in CVS heuristics
description: The EDT is a scaffold integrated into an online inquiry learning environment that "provides learners with structure by breaking down the process of designing and conducting an experiment into several steps": choosing and role-assigning variables, assigning values, conducting the experiment, and analyzing results. It builds in heuristics such as 'vary one thing at a time' by restricting varied variables to one, offers simple values via sliders, gives pop-up feedback on actions, and automatically assigns control-variable values across trials. It was designed following the Scaffolding Design Framework (Quintana et al. 2004).
requirements: Learners work within an online learning environment containing a virtual laboratory so that EDT-designed trials can be automatically transferred and run
constraints: The EDT restricts learners to a maximum of six experimental trials at once and to a predefined list of variables
target_learners: secondary school pre-university track students (14–15 years old)
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of Archimedes' principle and buoyancy
examples: In the study, EDT learners planned experiments for thirteen specific research questions grouped under five broader questions in the Splash laboratory on buoyancy and Archimedes' principle.
key_sources: Siswa van Riesen, Hannie Gijlers, Anjo Anjewierden, Ton de Jong. (2018). Supporting learners' experiment design. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:475–491. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9568-4

article_title: Educational quality and technological complexity on recognition of enhanced learning platform in developing countries using PLS-SEM in a post COVID era
citation: Patience E. Idoga, Dokun Iwalewa Oluwajana, Ibrahim Adeshola. (2022). Educational quality and technological complexity on recognition of enhanced learning platform in developing countries using PLS-SEM in a post COVID era. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10150-8
title: Extended TAM conceptual model combining self-efficacy, educational quality, and technological complexity with TAM constructs
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework that extends Davis's Technology Acceptance Model by adding three external constructs — self-efficacy, educational quality, and technological complexity — as antecedents of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, which in turn drive behavioral intention. The model "adopts constructs drawn from the TAM and the motivational factors of e-learning adoption" and was tested with PLS-SEM on 299 Nigerian instructors. It addresses the gap that no prior Nigerian study had examined "the motivational factor of the instructor’s efficacy, technological complexity, and educational quality" together.
requirements: Measurement via validated multi-item Likert-scale indicators for each construct, as in the article's questionnaire
constraints: The authors state the dimensions of the external variables are insufficient to adequately capture the TAM's influence on e-learning
target_learners: University instructors in Nigerian higher education
target_learning_goals: Instructors' acceptance and adoption of e-learning platforms for teaching
examples: The model was estimated with ADANCO 2.0.1; model fit satisfied SRMR < 0.08 and discrepancy criteria in Table 4.
key_sources: Patience E. Idoga, Dokun Iwalewa Oluwajana, Ibrahim Adeshola. (2022). Educational quality and technological complexity on recognition of enhanced learning platform in developing countries using PLS-SEM in a post COVID era. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10150-8

article_title: Impact of learning analytics-based personalized feedback: an experimental study on student behavior in a large introductory STEM course
citation: Jae-Eun Russell, Anna-Marie Smith, Salim George, Adam Brummett. (2026). Impact of learning analytics-based personalized feedback: an experimental study on student behavior in a large introductory STEM course. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10728-6
title: Excel-based if/then template system for generating personalized feedback emails from learning analytics data
description: The intervention used a scalable personalization pipeline: "Feedback messages were generated from structured templates using predefined if/then decision rules implemented in Excel." Analytics variables such as practice problems completed and homework start times were evaluated against thresholds (e.g., ≤ 20 practice problems, exam score < 60%) that flagged behaviors and populated standardized text blocks, rather than assigning students to pre-defined groups. Generated emails were reviewed by the course instructor before distribution via mail merge.
requirements: Instructor review of generated messages prior to distribution to ensure the combination of feedback elements was appropriate and coherent
constraints: The article notes the degree or specificity of personalization implemented may not have been sufficient to generate performance gains beyond generic messages
target_learners: undergraduate students in a large introductory chemistry course
examples: Four personalized emails were sent to the experimental group at key points (after Exams 1 and 2, before Exam 3, and before the final), while the control group received two generic emails emphasizing the same behaviors
key_sources: Jae-Eun Russell, Anna-Marie Smith, Salim George, Adam Brummett. (2026). Impact of learning analytics-based personalized feedback: an experimental study on student behavior in a large introductory STEM course. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10728-6

article_title: Is too much help an obstacle? Effects of interactivity and cognitive style on learning with dynamic versus non-dynamic visualizations with narrative explanations
citation: Marta M. Koć-Januchta, Tim N. Höffler, Helmut Prechtl, Detlev Leutner. (2020). Is too much help an obstacle? Effects of interactivity and cognitive style on learning with dynamic versus non-dynamic visualizations with narrative explanations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09822-0
title: Expertise reversal account of the self-paced static pictures disadvantage for highly developed visualizers
description: The article offers two hypothetical explanations for why highly developed visualizers learned poorer with self-paced static pictures and narration. The first invokes the expertise reversal effect: "Highly developed visualizers experience self-paced static pictures with narration as providing too much external support, which hinders them from constructing their own mental representations of processed information." The second proposes that generating mental images of spoken words while processing pictures overloaded the visual channel. Both are stated as speculation requiring further research.
requirements: Further research is required, including measuring interactive intensity of learner-control button usage and eye-tracking of attention processes
constraints: The article labels both explanations hypothetical and speculative; neither was tested in the study
target_learning_goals: understanding primary reactions of photosynthesis from multimedia environments
examples: The study found the positive correlation between visual cognitive style and experienced cognitive load (r = .20) in the self-paced static pictures condition, which the authors say may support the expertise reversal assumption
key_sources: Marta M. Koć-Januchta, Tim N. Höffler, Helmut Prechtl, Detlev Leutner. (2020). Is too much help an obstacle? Effects of interactivity and cognitive style on learning with dynamic versus non-dynamic visualizations with narrative explanations. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09822-0

article_title: Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos
citation: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5
title: Expanded instructional video treatment
description: The Expanded video was the most complete of five instructional video treatments, lasting 4′58″. It demonstrated the base-unit strategy, explained why it works, contrasted it with the ineffective default piling-on strategy, and — uniquely — alerted students to the feelings that draw them to the default strategy and to internal cues for switching. As the article describes it, "The Expanded treatment includes the Contrast + Explain content and further alerts students to the feelings that draw them to the default strategy (i.e., cognitive ease)." It was compared against ablated variants and a no-video control across five experiments.
requirements: Delivered after students explored the Balancelet simulation, which set up the video's relevance
constraints: The key instructional message occurred in a mere few sentences embedded in the video, which the authors note as a possible reason for small between-video differences
target_learners: eighth- and ninth-grade students in Colombian public and private schools
examples: Experiment 1 compared Show and Expanded; Experiment 5 included all five video treatments plus Control with a larger, more diverse sample
key_sources: Ana Saavedra · Daniel L. Schwartz. (2026). Improving the transfer of inquiry strategies by using short instructional videos. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10648-5

article_title: To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education
citation: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032
title: Explicitly tell students about the benefits and drawbacks of lecture capture so they use it as a supplement rather than an alternative
description: The review recommends that instructors and educators raise awareness among students that lecture capture needs to be utilised as a supplementary resource rather than an alternative to face-to-face lectures. "Students should be explicitly told about the benefits and the drawbacks of lecture capture." This ensures students make the most of the technology while obviating its drawbacks.
requirements: Instructors and educators take responsibility for raising student awareness of best practice
constraints: One cannot assume students to be aware of the best practice by default
target_learning_goals: effective use of lecture capture as a learning resource
examples: The review urges instructors to reflect on why students should attend face-to-face sessions and thereafter also watch the recorded lectures.
key_sources: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032

article_title: Investigating the Acceptance of Mobile Library Applications with an Extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)
citation: Rafique, H., Almagrabi, A. O., Shamim, A., Anwar, F., & Bashir, A. K. (2020). Investigating the acceptance of mobile library applications with an extended technology acceptance model (TAM). Heliyon, 6(6), e03733. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e03733
title: Extended Technology Acceptance Model for mobile library applications
description: The article proposes an extended TAM model incorporating two external variables, habit and system quality, alongside the core TAM constructs of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, to predict behavioural intention to use mobile library applications. The model was tested using SEM on survey data from 340 MLA users at COMSATS University Islamabad. The authors state that "the current research extended TAM by incorporating two external factors (habit (H) and system quality (SQ)) with the core constructs of TAM".
requirements: Survey data from users of the mobile library application
SEM analysis software (AMOS)
constraints: The results cannot be generalized to other contexts or countries not advanced in technology
The study targeted a specific MLA (INSIGNIA ILS) in a developing country context
target_learners: University students using mobile library applications
target_learning_goals: Understanding factors affecting technology acceptance in library contexts
key_sources: Rafique, H., Almagrabi, A. O., Shamim, A., Anwar, F., & Bashir, A. K. (2020). Investigating the acceptance of mobile library applications with an extended technology acceptance model (TAM). Heliyon, 6(6), e03733. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103732

article_title: Educators' open educational collaboration online: The dilemma of emotional ownership
citation: Educators' Open Educational Collaboration Online: The Dilemma of Emotional Ownership. (2016). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115784
title: Model of exposure to collaborative OER development at the moment of engagement
description: Figure 3 presents a synthesis model positioned at the moment of exposure when the educator discovers the opportunity to engage in collaborative OER development. The context and setting revealed during exposure set the conditions against which the educator weighs whether to engage; the critical issue is the expected level of openness and transparency, and for contribution behaviors, trust, comfort and familiarity with the practice are strong predictors.
requirements: Exposure to an opportunity to engage in collaborative development of OER in a virtual community
constraints: Engagement-related behavior is not constant or linear; motivating factors may change over time, and the analysis does not indicate that moving from closed to open is a process or sequence of events
target_learners: educators participating in virtual communities for OER development
target_learning_goals: deciding whether to contribute to or dismiss opportunities for collaborative OER development

title: Experiential learning pattern for climate resilience education with disaster experts and GIS mapping
description: The article prescribes an experiential learning pattern for climate resilience education in which students actively discuss their understanding, practice actions with concepts, and engage with relevant local examples of climate change impacts. The appropriate learning model is applied to students especially in areas affected by climate change using experiential learning by presenting hydro meteorological disaster experts and utilizing GIS for mapping disaster-prone areas. Learning media are real media that can be seen and touched or audio-visual media.
requirements: Presentation of hydro meteorological disaster experts
GIS applications for mapping disaster-prone areas
real or audio-visual learning media
constraints: intended for students especially in areas affected by climate change such as floods, landslides, droughts, tornadoes
target_learning_goals: 21st-century skills such as critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and creativity

article_title: Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel.
citation: Mecías‐Calvo M., Sobrido‐Prieto M., Navarro‐Patón R. (2026). Instruments for Assessing Basic Life Support Knowledge in Secondary School Students: A Scoping Review and Expert Panel. The Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.70223
title: Expert-panel framework of four key content domains for BLS knowledge assessment in secondary schools
description: A five-member interdisciplinary expert panel (evidence synthesis, Applied Didactics, school-based interventions, BLS and first aid education, and nursing education) convened in a structured 90-min virtual meeting defined the core domains for assessing secondary students' BLS knowledge. The panel agreed that "questionnaires should include at least four key domains: recognition of cardiac arrest, activation of emergency services, BLS sequence, and CPR maneuvers." Although these form a continuous chain of survival, the panel recommended assessing them separately "to better identify specific knowledge gaps." The panel also emphasized that unconsciousness alone is insufficient to identify cardiac arrest and that breathing assessment should be essential.
requirements: Assessment instruments should cover at least the four agreed key domains, assessed separately rather than as a single composite.
constraints: The panel recommends incorporating knowledge retention assessment only when study conditions allow, given logistical difficulties such as loss of follow-up in school settings.
target_learning_goals: basic life support knowledge including CPR and AED use
examples: The panel reviewed the scoping review findings and reached unanimous agreement through open discussion in a structured 90-min virtual meeting.

article_title: The impact of experiential learning on healthcare students' attitudes towards dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Wong Ion Hong, Gao Xiaoyu, Tan Zhengyi, Fang Yiping, Wang Qun, Lei Wai In, Van Iat Kio, Tan Meijing, Liu Ning, Wu Jianwei. (2026). The impact of experiential learning on healthcare students’ attitudes towards dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-026-07573-w
title: Theoretical accounts of why experiential learning shifts dementia attitudes: Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, Construal Level Theory, and the Affect Heuristic
description: The review interprets its pooled findings through three frameworks. Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory "posits that learning is most effective when learners actively engage with experiences, reflect, abstract conceptual knowledge, and apply it in practice", supporting hands-on interaction. Construal Level Theory holds that closer psychological distance promotes more concrete, personalized representations, so experiential learning "reduces this distance, replacing abstract stereotypes with tangible, empathetic impressions". The Affect Heuristic explains why brief, emotionally charged experiences such as simulations can rapidly shift attitudes by bypassing rational deliberation.
requirements: Interventions must involve active engagement with experiences and reflection, per Kolb's cycle as the review describes it
constraints: The review presents these as interpretive frameworks for its findings, not as mechanisms tested within the included studies
target_learners: healthcare undergraduate students (medical, nursing, gerontology, social work, physiotherapy, dentistry, occupational therapy, pharmacy)
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes towards individuals with dementia
examples: The review uses the Affect Heuristic to explain why single-session formats such as dementia simulations or firsthand narratives yielded significant DAS improvements
key_sources: Wong Ion Hong, Gao Xiaoyu, Tan Zhengyi, Fang Yiping, Wang Qun, Lei Wai In, Van Iat Kio, Tan Meijing, Liu Ning, Wu Jianwei. (2026). The impact of experiential learning on healthcare students’ attitudes towards dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-026-07573-w

article_title: Validity evidence for communication skills assessment in health professions education: a scoping review.
citation: Dorrestein L, Ritter C, De Mol Z, Wichtel M, Cary J, Vengrin C, Artemiou E, Adams CL, Ganshorn H, Coe JB, Barkema H, Hecker KG. (2025). Validity evidence for communication skills assessment in health professions education: a scoping review. BMJ Open 15(9):e096799. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-096799
title: Communication skills assessment studies should explicitly define the communication construct, clarify validity sources, and define the intended purpose and use of scores
description: The review recommends that gaps in validity evidence be addressed by studies that "explicitly defin[e] the communication skill construct(s) assessed, clarifying the validity source(s) reported and defining the intended purpose and use of the scores (ie, for learning and feedback, for decision making purposes)". This principle guides assessment design toward evidence-centred practice, linking construct definition, validation process and score interpretation. It stems directly from the review's finding that only 18% of studies defined the construct and only 10% used a validity framework.
requirements: A clear statement of the communication construct(s) to be measured before designing the assessment
Specification of the situation in which the assessment will be employed and the level of validity evidence needed
Employment of a validation process and continuous quality assurance of the assessment
constraints: Score interpretation is constrained by the heterogeneity of the definition of communication skills across the health professions and the reporting quality of the studies
target_learning_goals: Communication skills assessment for learning and feedback
Communication skills assessment for summative decision making
examples: The review's four-step evidence-centred design approach: stating the construct, listing validity evidence sought, specifying assessment methods, and interpreting the resulting data
key_sources: Dorrestein L, Ritter C, De Mol Z, Wichtel M, Cary J, Vengrin C, Artemiou E, Adams CL, Ganshorn H, Coe JB, Barkema H, Hecker KG. (2025). Validity evidence for communication skills assessment in health professions education: a scoping review. BMJ Open 15(9):e096799. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-096799

article_title: Competencies and pedagogical foundations for faculty development in interprofessional health education: a scoping review.
citation: Leite Daniella Rosaly; Carneiro Patrícia Silva; Mininel Vivian Aline; Rossit Rosana Aparecida Salvador; Leonello Valéria Marli; Gonçalves Geisa Colebrusco de Souza; da Silva Jaqueline Alcântara Marcelino. (2025). Competencies and pedagogical foundations for faculty development in interprofessional health education: a scoping review. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2024-0421en
title: Make pedagogical foundations and learning theories explicit and aligned with IPE characteristics in faculty development initiatives
description: Based on the finding that many pedagogical interventions in IPE lack precise details on the learning theory chosen to guide them, this review recommends that health course managers, faculty development program coordinators, and educational policy makers recognize the importance of learning theories in strengthening IPE and faculty development. The review recommends that "these pedagogical foundations/theories be made explicit and aligned and consistent with the characteristics of IPE." The absence of theories or pedagogical approaches can hinder the construction and implementation of successful faculty development initiatives in IPE.
requirements: Faculty development initiatives should explicitly state the learning theories underpinning them
constraints: The review notes that learning theories are partial and restricted approaches to specific aspects of learning, so pedagogical planning may need to be based on more than one theory or approach
target_learning_goals: Alignment of pedagogical foundations with IPE characteristics
examples: The review found that three studies used more than one learning theory but did not describe how they were linked to other pedagogical components and their impacts

article_title: Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review.
citation: Kouranloo K, Myall N, Christie J. (2025). Current level of rheumatology teaching amongst undergraduate medical students: a systematic literature review. Clinical Rheumatology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10067-024-07297-5
title: Exposure pathway from undergraduate rheumatology teaching to specialty career choice
description: The review proposes an explanatory account in which undergraduate and Foundation Programme exposure to a specialty shapes students' awareness of what the specialty entails, which in turn influences career choice and ultimately workforce recruitment. The authors state that "the overall lack of exposure to rheumatology in undergraduate programmes has been associated with a lack of uptake of rheumatology as a career amongst medical students globally". Placement experience is described as "crucial in determining their future career choice".
requirements: Adequate exposure to the specialty throughout training
constraints: The pathway is an association drawn from cross-sectional surveys, not a tested causal model
examples: The review cites only 154 of 4970 Foundation Programme jobs having dedicated rheumatology placement, mostly in London

article_title: Self-directed learning assessment practices in undergraduate health professions education: a systematic review.
citation: Taylor, T.A.H., Kemp, K., Mi, M., & Lerchenfeldt, S. (2023). Self-directed learning assessment practices in undergraduate health professions education: a systematic review. Medical Education Online, 28(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2189553
title: Expanded seven-step self-directed learning (SDL) framework for identifying SDL activities and assessment methods
description: The authors developed an SDL framework from a literature review of accreditation standards and guidelines across health professions education programs. It "comprises seven steps, each step of which involves various components or activities", and was used to develop research objectives, identify SDL components in included studies, and count the number of steps in reported SDL interventions. The authors state these steps "may serve as a framework for identifying SDL activities and/or SDL interventions discussed in research articles and assessment methods employed for studying outcomes of SDL interventions". It was built because there is no agreed-upon standard defining SDL, how it should be taught, or how it should be assessed.
requirements: Studies are included as SDL if the article authors state that SDL was incorporated in a teaching or learning method; the framework did not itself define SDL criteria
constraints: The criteria to define SDL were not developed in this review; the framework draws on accreditation standards and guidelines from different health profession programs
target_learners: undergraduate health professions students (medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dental, and allied fields)
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills and lifelong learning
examples: The framework was applied to code the number of SDL components (1–7) present in each of the 141 included studies, reported in Table 2

article_title: Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data.
citation: Martin A, Booth JN, McGeown S, Niven A, Sproule J, Saunders DH, Reilly JJ. (2017). Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data. Current Obesity Reports, 6(3), 297–313. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-017-0272-9
title: Executive function development as an explanation for age- and subject-specific obesity–achievement associations
description: The review proposes that obesity-related deficits in academic achievement may manifest only during adolescence because cognitive abilities related to academic achievement, social functioning and emotional control (executive functions such as reasoning, working memory, cognitive flexibility and inhibition) "develop steeply from the age of 6 years, develop throughout adolescence and reach adult levels at about age 20". Puberty-related neural reorganisation in the prefrontal cortex may explain why younger children show no association. The theory also proposes that non-verbal maths tasks invoke brain regions (prefrontal cortex, hippocampus) associated with obesity and energy-balance behaviours, potentially explaining why obesity is negatively associated with maths but not reading/language achievement.
requirements: Longitudinal data spanning the developmental period from childhood through adolescence
constraints: Proposed as a plausible explanation; the review calls for further research to understand these mechanisms
examples: The review cites evidence that working memory, reasoning, inhibition and cognitive flexibility are strongly associated with maths achievement and have been shown to be impaired in children and adolescents with obesity
key_sources: Martin A, Booth JN, McGeown S, Niven A, Sproule J, Saunders DH, Reilly JJ. (2017). Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data. Current Obesity Reports, 6(3), 297–313. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-017-0272-9

article_title: From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education
citation: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006
title: Exploration-first adoption framework for GenAI personalization in CS education
description: The review proposes an exploration-first deployment stance in which instructors and institutions "pilot small instrument interactions" and "scale in response to evidence, with learning-preserving defaults built into tools and policies." Concretely it specifies help-design defaults that preserve productive struggle (explanation-first hints, solution withholding, graduated hint ladders with reflection prompts), artifact grounding in student code, failing tests, and assignment specifications, human-in-the-loop audits of generated tests, items, and grades with logs retained for pedagogy and moderation, a pilot-measure-scale cycle, and enablement governance with vetted instances, data minimization, and allow-lists plus process evidence instead of AI detectors. The framework is the review's organizing proposal for moving from pilots to institutionalized practice.
requirements: Instructors and institutions pilot small instrumented interactions before scaling
Learning-preserving defaults built into tools and policies
Human-in-the-loop audits of generated tests, items, and grades with logs retained
Enablement governance: vetted or enterprise instances, data minimization, and prompt and version change logs
constraints: The review presents this as a proposal based on patterns in successful deployments, not a tested intervention; it states the aim is not to enforce hard thresholds but to encourage routine monitoring and structured decision-making
target_learners: Higher-education computer science learners and instructors
target_learning_goals: Preserving productive struggle while scaling personalized support
Durable learning and fairness in GenAI-enabled personalization
examples: The review's phased roadmap (Table 5) operationalizes the framework: foundation (working group, vendor vetting, policy template), pilot (1–2 sections with instrumented metrics), evaluation (process and outcome metrics, equity stratification), scale, and sustain phases with illustrative success indicators
key_sources: Reihanian, I.; Hou, Y.; Sun, Q. (2026). From Pilots to Practices: A Scoping Review of GenAI-Enabled Personalization in Computer Science Education. AI. https://doi.org/10.3390/ai7010006

article_title: Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention: Findings of Year 1
citation: Christian Doabler, Ben Clarke, Keith Smolkowski, Hank Fien, Scott Baker. (2014). Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention: Findings of Year 1. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: Explicit and systematic small-group math instruction design
description: ROOTS lessons follow an explicit and systematic instructional approach: "modeling and demonstrating what students will learn, providing guided practice opportunities, using visual representations of mathematics, and delivering academic feedback." Students receive frequent structured practice to build procedural fluency, visual representations deepen conceptual understanding, and instructional scaffolds are systematically withdrawn once students demonstrate initial proficiency, promoting learner independence and math verbalizations.
requirements: Interventionist guidelines for demonstrating concepts and providing timely academic feedback
Structured practice opportunities embedded in each lesson
constraints: Designed for small-group Tier 2 delivery rather than whole-class Tier 1 instruction
target_learners: kindergarten students at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: mathematical discourse and verbalization of thinking
examples: Each ROOTS lesson consists of 4 to 5 brief math activities delivered in 20-minute sessions over 50 lessons

article_title: Learning Algebra by Example in Real-World Classrooms
citation: Booth, J., Oyer, M., Paré-Blagoev, E. J., Elliot, A. J., Barbieri, C., Augustine, A., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Learning Algebra by Example in Real-World Classrooms. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1055636
title: Example-study mixed with problem solving within classroom assignments
description: The pattern replaces part of a standard practice set with worked examples to study and explain, interleaved with problems to solve. Each worked-example assignment kept base problems isomorphic to the control assignments but substituted "2-3 correct examples to explain, 2-3 incorrect examples to explain, and 5-6 problems to solve" for some of the practice items. Incorrect examples are marked as such and the error is highlighted, drawing on evidence that marked incorrect examples deepen conceptual understanding.
requirements: Assignments must fit into teachers' regular instruction without altering their teaching methods; examples target key misconceptions of the content
constraints: Effects were demonstrated over one content unit (approximately 3-4 weeks) in Algebra I classrooms; the overall benefit in the larger multi-topic experiment was not significant
target_learners: Middle and high school Algebra I students, including low prior knowledge students
target_learning_goals: Algebraic concepts and procedures, targeting common misconceptions such as the meaning of the equals sign and negative signs
examples: Experiment 1 and 2 students received four treatment or four control assignments during their content unit, completing them as in-class independent practice
key_sources: Booth, J., Oyer, M., Paré-Blagoev, E. J., Elliot, A. J., Barbieri, C., Augustine, A., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Learning Algebra by Example in Real-World Classrooms. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1055636

article_title: Interactive Multimedia Package in Ameliorating Communicative Skill in English
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2011). Interactive Multimedia Package in Ameliorating Communicative Skill in English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 1(4), October-December. https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Extend interactive multimedia packages across standards, subjects and learner types where communicative or subject learning is weak under conventional methods
description: From the study's findings the author draws educational implications recommending broader use: "The study can be extended to other schools", packages "may be prepared for other subjects also", the package "can be introduced in teaching grammar", and it "may be used to encourage and activate the gifted learners". The rationale is that conventional methods displeased learners and produced very low scores, while the package increased enthusiasm and scoring ability.
requirements: A validated, reliable package prepared for the target content, as the researcher did with jury validity and split-half reliability
constraints: Evidence base is a single quasi-experiment at standard VI in one school; extension to other standards, subjects and schools is the author's recommendation, not a tested result
examples: The author suggests preparing Interactive-Multimedia Packages for other subjects and introducing them in grammar teaching

article_title: Using Excel in Teacher Education for Sustainability
citation: Serhat Aydın. (2016). Using Excel in Teacher Education for Sustainability. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, 18(2). https://doi.org/10.1515/jtes-2016-0017
title: Excel-application-based Basic Statistics course with individualized datasets from the Turkish National Statistics Institute
description: An instructional design in which a whole one-term Basic Statistics course for pre-service science teachers is taught through Excel applications: after the instructor introduces a concept, students examine Excel applications on their own notebooks, then complete application tasks using unique datasets downloaded from the Turkish National Statistics Institute, which they elaborate at home and present to peers. The article states that "the pre-service science teachers in the treatment group were assigned application tasks in which they should find the dataset assigned for them from the website of Turkish National Statistics Institute". Task files and presentations were scored and constituted the course grades.
requirements: Each student needs a computer with Excel installed and datasets ready for each topic
Unique datasets must be assigned to each student for each application task
constraints: Tasks were initially designed to be 12 times but in practice could only be performed 6 times
The author reports a huge amount of time needed occasionally to solve tiny technical problems, suggesting an assistant technician for each 3-4 students
target_learning_goals: descriptive and inferential statistics concepts and operations
examples: In the treatment group all concepts, tests, graphs, tables and interpretations were given using Excel applications in class, while the control group was taught the same content theoretically

article_title: Benefits of Structured After-School Literacy Tutoring by University Students for Struggling Elementary Readers
citation: Lindo, E. J., Weiser, B., Cheatham, J. P., & Allor, J. H. (2018). Benefits of structured after-school literacy tutoring by university students for struggling elementary readers. Reading & Writing Quarterly, 34(2), 117–131. https://doi.org/10.1080/10573569.2017.1357156
title: Provide minimally trained volunteer tutors with ongoing supervision by reading professionals, including placement, pacing, and text-level monitoring
description: The article argues that structure alone is insufficient: a course professor and graduate research assistants with reading expertise modeled procedures during training, answered questions mid-semester, set initial placement, and monitored progress. The authors write, "It is likely that this ongoing support was a key component of the effective use of these minimally trained tutors; however, at any given time we had only one or two supervisors to approximately 20 tutors." Supervision included brief reminders to follow scripts, model correct pronunciation, and give corrective feedback.
requirements: Supervisors must have expertise in reading instruction
Supervisors handle initial curriculum placement and regularly monitor student advancement and text level
constraints: The study did not compare levels of supervision required, so the necessary supervision intensity is unknown
target_learners: Struggling elementary readers in Grades K–6
target_learning_goals: Reading outcomes delivered through volunteer tutoring programs
examples: Each semester had a ratio of two supervisors to approximately 20 tutors, and tutors kept daily field notes and reflective journals that supervisors read and annotated

citation: Kousar Perveen. (2010). Effect Of The Problem-Solving Approach On Academic Achievement Of Students In Mathematics At The Secondary Level. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, 3(3).
title: Combining expository explanation of facts and procedures with heuristic problem-solving work
description: The article states that the experimental teaching approach "was, as a matter of fact, a combination of the expository strategy and problem -solving approach", because facts, rules, and action sequences such as terms, formulas and procedures had to be explained through exposition before the heuristics could be used. This lesson-level pattern pairs direct explanation of foundational content with student problem-solving practice built on heuristic steps.
requirements: Foundational facts, rules, formulas and procedures must be explained expositionally before heuristic problem-solving work begins
constraints: The article reports this combination as what was actually implemented, not as a separately tested condition
examples: Six weeks of lesson plans in which exposition of terms, formulas and procedures preceded heuristic problem-solving activities

article_title: Examining the Effect of Teacher Guidance on Collaborative Argumentation in Middle Level Classrooms
citation: Hsu, P.-S., Van Dyke, M., & Chen, Y. (2015). Examining the effect of teacher guidance on collaborative argumentation in middle level classrooms. RMLE Online, 38(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Examining+the+Effect+of+Teacher+Guidance+on+Collaborative+Argumentation+in+Middle+Level+Classrooms

description: Based on their finding that script-based guidance deepened collaborative argumentation, the authors recommend that "middle level teachers should use extended teacher guidance rather than minimal teacher guidance to lead students in high level cognitive tasks in a large-class setting." A high-level cognitive task suited to scripted scaffolding
constraints: Evidence covers only the depth feature of argumentation quality; the authors call for future research on other aspects of quality
target_learners: middle level students across cognitive development stages
examples: Six seventh-grade classes argued a familiar social issue (cell phones in school) before transferring to science topics

article_title: Efficacy of Aggression Replacement Training among Children from North-West Russia
citation: Koposov, R., Gundersen, K. K. & Svartdal, F. (2014). Efficacy of Aggression Replacement Training among Children from North-West Russia. International Journal of Emotional Education, 6(1), 14-24. https://www.um.edu.mt/cres/ijee
title: Extended Aggression Replacement Training (ART) programme for children
description: ART is a multi-focused intervention consisting of "three equal components: social skills t raining, anger control training and moral reasoning training", each taught weekly over a 10-week period. It makes considerable use of role-playing and exercises and includes transfer and maintenance strategies.
requirements: Trainers received 72 hours of educational training over three meetings plus 18 practice sessions with colleagues before training youth groups
Sessions led by two qualified ART trainers, with groups of 4 to 6 children
constraints: The article notes efficacy depends on systematic, well-focused implementation and cultural adaptation, and that implementation can be disrupted by trainer illness, workload and children's refusal to continue
target_learners: children aged 6-15 with behavioural problems in schools and social institutions
examples: In the Russian evaluation, children in the intervention group received the extended ART course including 30 sessions in each of the three components spread over ten weeks, with sessions lasting 45 to 90 minutes

citation: Sabriye Seven, Asiye Pinar Koksal, Gulsen Kocak. (2017). The Effect of Carrying out Writing to Learn Activities on Academic Success of Fifth Grade Students in Secondary School on the Subject of "Force and Motion". Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(5): 744-749. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050506
title: Expressive versus product-oriented writing-to-learn categories
description: The article categorizes writing-to-learn into two types, citing Chatel and Lord (1998). "Expressive writing allows for students to investigate their personal thoughts without concern for compromise, while product -oriented writing is more formal and requires attention for literacy image". Table 1 lists examples: expressive writing includes free writing, brainstorming, concept maps, keeping journal and taking notes; product-oriented writing includes essays, research and laboratory reports, editorials and news reports. The study's journal activity falls in the expressive column of this adapted table.
requirements: Activities must be matched to the category's purpose: personal exploration for expressive writing, formal literacy image for product-oriented writing
examples: Keeping journal is listed under expressive writing (writing to express claims), while essays, laboratory reports and editorials appear under product-oriented writing
