article_title: Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class
citation: Saovapa Wichadee and Fasawang Pattanapichet. (2017). Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 77-92. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: When using game-based quizzes, instructors should explain correct answers and tell students the real learning purpose beyond competition
description: The article's concluding recommendation for gamified language activities is that competition and enjoyment should not be the endpoint. Because "the game concerns winning and losing, instruc tors need to inform them of the real purpose of gamifying language activities", namely learning new content such as grammar and vocabulary. Further, "when a correct answer is shown, instructors s hould explain and give details about it", so that game feedback becomes instructional feedback. The article aligns this with Marklund and Alklind's recommendation that tasks for teachers should be clear from the start when using games in class.
requirements: Instructors must make the learning purpose of game activities explicit to students
Correct answers shown in the game must be followed by instructor explanation and detail
constraints: The recommendation is offered in the context of game-based language activities where winning and losing are salient
target_learners: university EFL students in gamified courses
target_learning_goals: understanding that gamification serves learning, not just competition
examples: In the study's Kahoot quizzes, scores did not count toward grades, and the authors state instructors should explain answers when the correct answer is displayed
key_sources: Saovapa Wichadee and Fasawang Pattanapichet. (2017). Enhancement of Performance and Motivation through Application of Digital Games in an English Language Class. Teaching English with Technology, 18(1), 77-92. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1170635

article_title: Fraction Intervention for Students with Mathematics Difficulties: Lessons Learned from Five Randomized Controlled Trials
citation: Lynn S. Fuchs, Amelia S. Malone, Robin F. Schumacher, Jessica Namkung, and Amber Wang. (2017). Fraction Intervention for Students With Mathematics Difficulties: Lessons Learned From Five Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416677249
title: Provide at-risk students with well-designed small-group intervention built on systematic, explicit instructional principles and deep content focus
description: The article's central design recommendation is that students at risk for mathematics difficulty "can succeed with challenging mathematics content, if they are provided with a well-designed intervention". The intervention occurred outside class in groups of two to four, three times weekly for 30 to 35 minutes over 12 weeks, and relied on systematic, explicit principles to maximize clarity, address cognitive and linguistic limitations, optimize attention and perseverance, and ensure responsive tutor feedback. A moderator analysis the authors cite found differentially strong outcomes regardless of incoming achievement level.
requirements: Small-group format with systematic, explicit instructional principles and state-of-the-art thinking about the content area
Intervention delivered outside the classroom, three times per week for 30 to 35 min per session over 12 weeks
constraints: Not all intervention students responded sufficiently to preclude the need for continuing intervention; students below the 13th percentile on the screening measure failed to reach normalized NAEP performance
The intervention addresses only fourth-grade fraction standards; multiplying and dividing fractions remain unaddressed
target_learners: Fourth-grade students at risk for difficulty learning fractions due to poor whole-number computational skill
examples: Across five RCTs, intervention students significantly outperformed business-as-usual control students on number line estimation, calculations, and NAEP items each year
key_sources: Lynn S. Fuchs, Amelia S. Malone, Robin F. Schumacher, Jessica Namkung, and Amber Wang. (2017). Fraction Intervention for Students With Mathematics Difficulties: Lessons Learned From Five Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416677249

article_title: Improving 7th Grade Students' Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model
citation: Kızkapan, O., & Bektaş, O. (2021). Improving 7th Grade Students’ Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model. Pedagogical Research, 6(3), em0095. https://doi.org/10.29333/pr/10949
title: Give priority to explicit teaching of epistemological beliefs over implicit approaches
description: The article concludes that epistemological beliefs develop when instruction explicitly raises them for discussion, rather than assuming they grow implicitly through inquiry or subject teaching. Its first recommendation states that "explicit teaching of epistemological beliefs is more effective compared to implicit teaching. Therefore, explicit teaching of epistemological beliefs should be given priority." The EETAM results, where only the group with explicit epistemological discussions outperformed the comparison group, ground this principle.
requirements: Structured discussion sessions in which students justify claims about epistemological dimensions using subject content they have learned
constraints: Evidence comes from a six-week intervention with 7th graders in one school; TAM-EETAM difference itself was not statistically significant
target_learning_goals: Epistemological beliefs about the nature of scientific knowledge and learning
examples: EETAM students discussed whether knowledge in books can change and whether success depends on intelligence or hard work, using the matter unit content as evidence
key_sources: Kızkapan, O., & Bektaş, O. (2021). Improving 7th Grade Students’ Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model. Pedagogical Research, 6(3), em0095. https://doi.org/10.29333/pr/10949

article_title: Examining the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention
citation: Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Smolkowski, K., Baker, S. K., Fien, H., & Strand Cary, M. (2016). Examining the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 49(2), 152–165. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219414538514
title: Design Tier 2 mathematics interventions around explicit and systematic instruction with validated delivery principles
description: The article argues that mathematics interventions for at-risk students should teach "essential skills in the most effective and efficient manner possible" through explicit and systematic instruction, which in small groups can deeply engage students in critical content and increase intensity through differentiated instruction. ROOTS operationalizes this with modeling and demonstrating, guided practice, visual representations, academic feedback, and elicited math verbalizations, plus systematic design features such as sequencing simpler teaching examples first and systematically withdrawing scaffolds.
requirements: Small-group instructional formats; interventionists follow specific guidelines for demonstrating concepts and providing timely academic feedback
constraints: The article presents this approach as supported by an emerging body of evidence for students at risk for math difficulties, not as proven by this study alone
target_learners: kindergartners at risk for mathematics learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: whole number concepts and skills, including counting, operations, and place value
examples: ROOTS lessons provide interventionists with guidelines for demonstrating whole-number concepts, use visual representations to deepen conceptual understanding, and elicit individual and group math verbalizations, including easier response opportunities for students struggling with base 10 ideas
key_sources: Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Smolkowski, K., Baker, S. K., Fien, H., & Strand Cary, M. (2016). Examining the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 49(2), 152–165. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219414538514

article_title: Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Bogale, Y. N. (2018). Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(2), 93–117. http://ijci.wcci-international.org
title: Explicit reading strategy instruction cycle: describe, model, guided practice, independent use
description: The intervention followed a four-step instructional sequence: the researcher first "provided a detailed description on h ow each strategy use can be applied in reading a text using the thinking aloud technique", then "modeled ea ch strategy briefly using various examples", then had students use each strategy with scaffolding, and finally had students employ the strategies independently. The model was adapted from Vogt & Echevarria (2008) and was chosen because it requires no sophisticated materials and can be utilized with limited teacher training time.
requirements: Teacher modeling and feedback
adequate time for guided and independent practice
a training manual prepared before each lesson
constraints: Applied in a 12-week intervention with four reading passages, taught by the researcher who was also the students' ordinary teacher
examples: Students practiced prediction with predictions written on the whiteboard and checked against the text, then summarized main ideas of texts
key_sources: Bogale, Y. N. (2018). Conceptualizing Reading to Learn: Strategy Instruction and EFL Students' Reading Comprehension. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction 10(2), 93–117. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1207221

article_title: Investigating the Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Shima Rajabi, Akbar Azizifar, & Habib Gowhary. (2015). Investigating the of Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.53
title: Teach pragmatic speech acts explicitly alongside grammatical knowledge in EFL classrooms
description: The article concludes that pragmatic knowledge is teachable and should be taught explicitly rather than left to implicit acquisition, especially in EFL contexts where classrooms are the only medium of exposure. It states that "pragmatic knowledge is teachable and it should be taught along with grammatical knowledge", and recommends "incorporating consciousness-raising activities in theclassroom". The experimental evidence showed explicit instruction produced significant gains while control instruction did not.
requirements: Teachers need awareness of social and cultural norms of the target language; instruction should cover how and when to use speech acts in appropriate situations
constraints: Classroom time is limited and mostly restricted to grammar and major skills, making implicit acquisition of pragmatics difficult in EFL contexts
target_learners: Iranian EFL learners at intermediate and advanced levels
target_learning_goals: Socio-pragmatic competence, specifically appropriate performance of speech acts
examples: Experimental groups received extra instruction about how and when to use speech acts in appropriate situations, while control groups received only the institute's normal program
key_sources: Shima Rajabi, Akbar Azizifar, & Habib Gowhary. (2015). Investigating the of Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.53

article_title: Investigating the Effect of the Activities Based on Explanation Assisted REACT Strategy on Learning Impulse, Momentum and Collisions Topics
citation: Eser Ültay & Nedim Alev. (2017). Investigating the Effect of the Activities Based on Explanation Assisted REACT Strategy on Learning Impulse, Momentum and Collisions Topics. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.7. https://www.iiste.org
title: Explanation assisted REACT strategy: the REACT strategy extended with an explanation principle for context-based learning
description: The REACT strategy teaches a topic related to daily-life contexts through five principles: "Relating", "Experiencing", "Applying", "Cooperating" and "Transferring". Prior studies found discussion and explanation parts were missing, so this study extends REACT by adding an explanation principle, used cyclically across all principles in lesson plans. Making explanation is said to help students replace unfruitful pre-existing ideas because students often cannot find new thinking ways without teachers' guidance.
requirements: A daily-life context related to the topic (e.g. the "Ice Rink" text)
Teacher explanations after activities and guided discussion environments
Lesson materials developed with physics education experts
constraints: Some alternative conceptions were not eliminated even when stressed by the activities and experiments
Teachers' knowledge and skills in applying context-based learning in real classrooms were reported insufficient in prior studies
target_learners: prospective science teachers (freshmen in Science Education)
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of impulse, momentum and collisions
examples: Two lesson plans used all principles cyclically: PSTs read an "Ice Rink" text, performed a POE-based experiment, solved problems, and presented homework on momentum conservation in daily life
key_sources: Eser Ültay & Nedim Alev. (2017). Investigating the Effect of the Activities Based on Explanation Assisted REACT Strategy on Learning Impulse, Momentum and Collisions Topics. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.7. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1137601

article_title: The Effectiveness of Using Group Story-Mapping Strategy to Improve Reading Comprehension of Students with Learning Disabilities
citation: Nada Alturki. (2017). The effectiveness of using group story-mapping strategy to improve reading comprehension of students with learning disabilities. Educational Research and Reviews. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR
title: Teach graphic organizer use explicitly and have students practice it repeatedly across different texts
description: The article's literature review concludes that the benefit of graphic organizers depends on how the educator provides them, and that instruction should teach the organizer explicitly and give students repeated practice with different texts. The article states the review "emphasized the importance of teaching how to use graphic organizers explicitly" and practice "over and over, using different texts". In this study the researcher modeled each story-map component before students completed maps independently.
requirements: Explicit instruction on how to use the graphic organizer
Repeated practice opportunities across different texts
target_learners: Students with learning disabilities in reading comprehension
examples: In the study, the researcher displayed the story-map elements, explained each component individually, discussed instances of each component, and then asked participants to complete their story maps independently
key_sources: Nada Alturki. (2017). The effectiveness of using group story-mapping strategy to improve reading comprehension of students with learning disabilities. Educational Research and Reviews. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR

article_title: Effectiveness of Experiential Learning-Based Teaching Material in Mathematics
citation: Mutmainah, Rukayah, Mintasih Indriayu. (2019). Effectiveness of experiential learning-based teaching material in Mathematics. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol. 8, No. 1, March 2019, pp. 57-63. http://iaescore.com/journals/index.php/IJERE
title: Experiential learning-based Mathematics teaching material for fifth-grade volume of cube and beam
description: A student-centered Mathematics teaching material developed on Kolb's four-stage experiential cycle, evaluated in this study against conventional material consisting only of content and questions. The conventional material the schools used was "still abstract, not accompanied by the visualization of the material". The experiential material instead starts from concrete experience with picture illustrations that "can clarify the material content, increase the attractiveness, and reduce the students' boredom", then moves through reflection, conceptualization, and application. It was tested with a 30-question multiple-choice instrument (reliability 0.730 via ITEMAN).
requirements: A test instrument with validity above 0.2787 and reliability of 0.730 was used to measure cognitive ability before and after use
constraints: Evaluated only on fifth-grade volume of cube and beam content in Gunungpati Sub-district elementary schools
examples: Compared against conventional teaching material that led directly to example questions without comprehensive concept explanation
key_sources: Mutmainah, Rukayah, Mintasih Indriayu. (2019). Effectiveness of experiential learning-based teaching material in Mathematics. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol. 8, No. 1, March 2019, pp. 57-63. http://iaescore.com/journals/index.php/IJERE

article_title: An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes
citation: Hank Fien, Christian T. Doabler, Nancy J. Nelson, Derek B. Kosty, Ben Clarke & Scott K. Baker (2016). An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1119229
title: NS1 explicit instructional framework built on three interrelated design principles
description: NS1's instructional framework applies explicit instruction principles drawn from meta-analyses of interventions for low achievers and students with mathematics difficulties. The article states that "The explicit instructional framework of NS1 centers on the following three interrelated design principles": instructional scaffolding with progressive fading of supports, opportunities for guided practice with immediate specific academic feedback and review, and differentiated support to learners. The framework aims to present new information in a manner that is unambiguous and easy to understand.
requirements: Instruction begins with simpler examples and progresses to more complex ones as students demonstrate conceptual understanding
Practice opportunities with immediate, highly specific academic feedback to attain procedural fluency and conceptual understanding
target_learners: first-grade students with or at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: whole-number concepts and skills, including counting strategies, place value, and problem solving
examples: NS1 instruction on new content begins with virtual representations such as place-value models and transitions to more abstract representations as students demonstrate proficiency
key_sources: Hank Fien, Christian T. Doabler, Nancy J. Nelson, Derek B. Kosty, Ben Clarke & Scott K. Baker (2016). An Examination of the Promise of the NumberShire Level 1 Gaming Intervention for Improving Student Mathematics Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1119229

article_title: The Effectiveness of Web-Based Multimedia Applications Simulation in Teaching and Learning
citation: Azidah Abu Ziden, Muhammad Faizal Abdul Rahman. (2013). The Effectiveness of Web-Based Multimedia Applications Simulation in Teaching and Learning. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Experiential design method for virtual reality environments
description: The article cites Fazidin Mohd Jabar et al. (2007) describing a virtual reality or game-theory design approach called the "experiential design method" with "4 major areas which are 'Focus', 'Emotion', 'Space/Form' and 'Orientation'". Focus concerns experiencing sense of place, skill or role play; in Virtual Haj it makes users feel as if they are in Mecca performing the pilgrimage; Emotion concentrates on inner feelings and, for Virtual Haj, can elevate faith and devotion. The study applies this framing to justify its pilgrimage simulation.
requirements: The virtual environment must engage users through the four areas of Focus, Emotion, Space/Form and Orientation as described by the cited framework
constraints: The framework is attributed to Fazidin Mohd Jabar et al. (2007) and applied here specifically to a Hajj pilgrimage simulation
target_learners: Form Four Malaysian secondary school students studying Islamic Education
target_learning_goals: Understanding and performing the rituals of the Hajj pilgrimage
examples: The Virtual Haj simulation was designed so that Focus makes users feel as if they are in Mecca doing the Haj pilgrimage
key_sources: Azidah Abu Ziden, Muhammad Faizal Abdul Rahman. (2013). The Effectiveness of Web-Based Multimedia Applications Simulation in Teaching and Learning. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085400

article_title: From Research to Practice: The Effect of Multi-Component Vocabulary Instruction on Increasing Vocabulary and Comprehension Performance in Social Studies
citation: Graham, L., Graham, A., & West, C. (2015). From Research to Practice: The Effect of Multi-Component Vocabulary Instruction on Increasing Vocabulary and Comprehension Performance in Social Studies. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(1), 147-160. https://www.iejee.com
title: Teach content-area vocabulary explicitly and multi-componentally because comprehension of content depends on understanding its vocabulary
description: The article argues that conveying content requires that students first understand its vocabulary, and that multi-component strategies providing repeated exposure in different contexts keep students engaged. It concludes that "multi -component vocabulary instruction in 4th grade social studies improved performance in both vocabulary and comprehension areas" and that retention of the improvement was demonstrated. The principle directs teachers to embed direct, explicit vocabulary strategy instruction within content-area lessons rather than treating vocabulary as separate from content.
requirements: Structured weekly instructional time devoted to vocabulary within the content area
Teacher training in explicit instruction and the multi-component strategies
constraints: The authors note that addressing vocabulary "can be a time-consuming process," and participating teachers reported time pressure and concern about content coverage
examples: Treatment teachers spent 90 minutes per week on social studies vocabulary using explicit instruction, vocabulary maps, connections webs, semantic feature analysis, and engagement games
key_sources: Graham, L., Graham, A., & West, C. (2015). From Research to Practice: The Effect of Multi-Component Vocabulary Instruction on Increasing Vocabulary and Comprehension Performance in Social Studies. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(1), 147-160. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078850

article_title: Effectiveness of Animated Instructional Resource for Learning Facilitation among Secondary School Student in Bauchi Nigeria
citation: Isaac Ali Kwasu; Ema Ema. (2015). Effectiveness of Animated Instructional Resource for Learning Facilitation among Secondary School Student in Bauchi Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. https://www.iiste.org
title: Extrinsic and intrinsic barriers to using animation concepts and practices in teaching
description: Citing Ema (2010), the article organises barriers to the use of animation in teaching and learning into two main categories. "Extrinsic has to do with the following: Access, time, support services, resources and training", while intrinsic barriers concern attitudes, beliefs, practices and resistance. The article states these concepts and practices impact the level and frequency of use of instructional materials in the classroom, and that inadequate understanding of animation may lead to rejection and discontinuance of its use.
requirements: Teachers need adequate knowledge of the instructional method and materials, the learners and the learning environment for successful use of animation.
constraints: Every technology or material used in class is subject to the teacher's control; the teacher's creativity and performance skills determine success or failure of the activities.
target_learning_goals: Effective integration of animated instructional media into classroom teaching
examples: The article recommends flyers or booklets accompanying animated materials to explain the functioning principles underlying how the material works.
key_sources: Isaac Ali Kwasu; Ema Ema. (2015). Effectiveness of Animated Instructional Resource for Learning Facilitation among Secondary School Student in Bauchi Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.21. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079103

article_title: Methodological Complications of Matching Designs under Real World Constraints: Lessons from a Study of Deeper Learning
citation: Zeiser, K., Rickles, J., & Garet, M. S. (2014). Methodological Complications of Matching Designs under Real World Constraints: Lessons from a Study of Deeper Learning. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566014
title: Devote study resources to explaining methods in friendly language so practitioners can judge trustworthiness and generalizability
description: A communication principle for complex quasi-experimental studies: because complex sampling and analysis strategies require appropriate caveats, studies should "Devote study resources to explication of methods in friendly language". The article warns that studies using jargon make practitioners question whether they can trust findings and to which schools results apply.
requirements: Study resources allocated to communicating methods in accessible language
constraints: Jargon-heavy reporting threatens perceived internal and external validity
target_learners: decision-makers and practitioners using research evidence
target_learning_goals: appropriate interpretation and contextualization of research findings
examples: The authors stressed results were limited to the set of schools in the proof-of-concept study and recommended presenting pair-specific results alongside average effects.
key_sources: Zeiser, K., Rickles, J., & Garet, M. S. (2014). Methodological Complications of Matching Designs under Real World Constraints: Lessons from a Study of Deeper Learning. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562805

article_title: Using Worked Examples Assignments in Classroom Instruction
citation: Paré-Blagoev, J., Booth, J., Elliot, A., & Koedinger, K. (2013). Using Worked Examples Assignments in Classroom Instruction. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED584939
title: Example–your-turn item pairing with self-explanation prompts
description: The instructional pattern pairs each worked example with an immediately following problem for the student to solve. Each example shows a fictional student's work, marked correct or incorrect, and is followed by questions that "highlight key mathematical concepts students often misunderstand even after significant instructional time." Responding gives students practice analyzing, critiquing, and articulating mathematical arguments, operationalizing the laboratory finding that interleaving examples with problems benefits novices.
requirements: Students must actively engage with the examples by answering self-explanation questions
target_learners: middle school and early high school algebra students
target_learning_goals: algebra conceptual understanding and procedural skill
examples: Example items state whether a fictional student such as Natasha solved a problem correctly or did not complete a graph correctly
key_sources: Paré-Blagoev, J., Booth, J., Elliot, A., & Koedinger, K. (2013). Using Worked Examples Assignments in Classroom Instruction. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED564068

article_title: Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana
citation: John T. Agor. (2014). Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p175
title: Teach language-learner strategies explicitly by name with modelling, practice and self-evaluation opportunities
description: The article endorses Chamot's (2005) view that explicit strategy instruction is far more effective than implicit or integrated approaches. Explicit instruction, as defined in the article, "includes the development of students’ awareness of their strategies, teacher modelling of strategic thinking, identifying the strategies by name, providing opportunities for practise and self-evaluation". In the study, the teacher helped students recognise and name strategies they already used, modelled new strategies, created practice opportunities, and showed video clips of strategy use for learners to pinpoint.
requirements: A teacher who models strategic thinking and identifies strategies by name
Opportunities for learners to practise strategies and self-evaluate
constraints: The article notes the functional categorisation of strategies by modality is adopted only for the sake of convenience
target_learners: Junior high school students learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Listening, speaking, reading and writing proficiency in English
examples: The experimental class was taught 17 strategies across listening, speaking, reading and writing, and by the end of the first term could identify strategies deployed by colleagues and distinguish productive from less productive ones
key_sources: John T. Agor. (2014). Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p175

article_title: Racing against the Vocabulary Gap: Matthew Effects in Early Vocabulary Instruction and Intervention
citation: Coyne, M. D., McCoach, D. B., Ware, S., Austin, C. R., Loftus-Rattan, S. M., & Baker, D. L. (2019). Racing Against the Vocabulary Gap: Matthew Effects in Early Vocabulary Instruction and Intervention. Exceptional Children, 85(2), 163–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402918789162
title: Extended vocabulary instruction: high-utility words, student-friendly definitions, multiple exposures, and deep processing
description: The article's instructional approach, informed by Beck and McKeown, incorporated four principles: "(a) a focus on high-utility academic vocabulary that occurs across content areas, (b) student-friendly definitions, (c) multiple exposures to words across different meaningful contexts, and (d) extended opportunities to interact with vocabulary to promote deep processing." This approach was refined over a series of studies and called extended vocabulary instruction. It produced greater breadth and depth of word learning than less intensive, more incidental instruction.
requirements: Multiple exposures across meaningful contexts
Extended opportunities for interaction with vocabulary
target_learning_goals: breadth and depth of target word learning
examples: Tier-1 lessons were delivered in a 5-day sequence for about 20 min each day with oral, listening, and workbook-based activities
key_sources: Coyne, M. D., McCoach, D. B., Ware, S., Austin, C. R., Loftus-Rattan, S. M., & Baker, D. L. (2019). Racing Against the Vocabulary Gap: Matthew Effects in Early Vocabulary Instruction and Intervention. Exceptional Children, 85(2), 163–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402918789162

article_title: The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on Mastering the Speech Act of Thanking among Iranian Male and Female EFL Learners
citation: Ghaedrahmat, M., Alavi Nia, P. & Biria, R. (2016). The Effect of Explicit Vs. Implicit Instruction on Mastering the Speech Act of Thanking among Iranian Male and Female EFL Learners. Latin American Journal of Content and Language Integrated Learning, 9(2), 401-425. https://doi.org/10.5294/laclil.2016.9.2.7
title: Curricula should include materials that explicitly teach the structure of speech acts such as thanking
description: The article's discussion recommends that curriculum developers build explicit treatment of speech acts into EFL materials, because the study found explicit instruction of thanking significantly improved learners' DCT performance while implicit teaching did not produce comparable gains. As the authors put it, "it is suggested that the curriculum developers should include materials that cover the explicit nature of different speech acts like the speech act of thanking." English practitioners are likewise told that explicit teaching enhances pragmatic awareness.
requirements: Instruction must make the structures used in the speech act explicit, unlike the implicit condition which taught the act "without any reference to the structures used".
constraints: Evidence comes from one small quasi-experiment (30 learners, one institute, one speech act, DCT measure) in the Iranian EFL context.
target_learners: Intermediate EFL learners in foreign-language settings without contact with the target community
target_learning_goals: Pragmatic competence in performing the speech act of thanking
examples: The experimental group was taught the speech act of thanking used by native English speakers explicitly over 3 sessions, while the control group was taught it implicitly.
key_sources: Ghaedrahmat, M., Alavi Nia, P. & Biria, R. (2016). The Effect of Explicit Vs. Implicit Instruction on Mastering the Speech Act of Thanking among Iranian Male and Female EFL Learners. Latin American Journal of Content and Language Integrated Learning, 9(2), 401-425. https://doi.org/10.5294/laclil.2016.9.2.7

article_title: Explicit versus Implicit Modes of EFL Reading Literacy Instruction: Using Phonological Awareness with Adult Arab Learners
citation: Mahmoud Ibrahim. (2018). Explicit Versus Implicit Modes of EFL Reading Literacy Instruction: Using Phonological Awareness With Adult Arab Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p144
title: Explicit versus implicit modes of language instruction
description: The article organizes literacy and language teaching around a schism between implicit instruction, meaning "intensive exposure to language- without explicit instruction", and explicit instruction, in which the structure is explained, exemplified, and the rule presented ready for use. It situates phonological awareness instruction as the explicit mode for literacy, contrasting it with the implicit exposure of ordinary EFL classes, and cites the Norris and Ortega (2000) meta-analysis concluding explicit teaching is far more effective for language skills.
requirements: For the explicit mode: structured materials that present sound-letter associations, blending, and segmentation in a sequenced, non-alphabetical order
constraints: The article notes PA instruction proven effective with one background of learners does not guarantee success with other backgrounds, due to phonological differences between English and the learners' L1
target_learners: Adult Arab EFL learners in university foundation programs
examples: The study operationalized the explicit mode as 24 hours of Jolly Phonics PA instruction and the implicit mode as normal intensive EFL classes using New Headway
key_sources: Mahmoud Ibrahim. (2018). Explicit Versus Implicit Modes of EFL Reading Literacy Instruction: Using Phonological Awareness With Adult Arab Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p144

article_title: The Development and Implementation of Learning Material on Exposition Text to Improve Students' Achievement on Bahasa Indonesia
citation: Wenny Silaban, Biner Ambarita & Usman Hadi. (2018). The Development and Implementation of Learning Material on Exposition Text to Improve Students' Achievement on Bahasa Indonesia. International Education Studies, 11(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n11p53
title: Printed learning material on exposition text with a process for senior high school Bahasa Indonesia
description: A printed learning package for first-year senior high school Bahasa Indonesia consisting of five sub-chapters covering exposition-text theory, contextual examples, supporting figures, tables and illustrations, and four integrated guided projects leading to a formal academic report. The article states the material "has been arranged in good order contained simple to complex examples of exposition text with a process" and was standardized against Indonesian National Education Standards Board criteria before classroom use.
requirements: Validated by Bahasa Indonesia lecturers and teachers and standardized against BSNP criteria on content, depth, legibility, extension, design and language before classroom use
constraints: Developed and evaluated for first-year senior high school students majoring in science at one Indonesian state senior high school
target_learners: First-year senior high school (SMA) students majoring in science
target_learning_goals: Writing exposition text with a process in formal academic reports in Bahasa Indonesia
examples: Used as the main resource in two experimental classes while two control classes used the ordinary school book with supplemented writing projects; students completed four integrated projects
key_sources: Wenny Silaban, Biner Ambarita & Usman Hadi. (2018). The Development and Implementation of Learning Material on Exposition Text to Improve Students' Achievement on Bahasa Indonesia. International Education Studies, 11(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n11p53

article_title: Extended Discourse in First and Second Language Acquisition: A Challenge and an Opportunity
citation: Catherine E. Snow. (2014). Extended discourse in first and second language acquisition: A challenge and an opportunity! Journal of Japanese Linguistics 30. https://www.wordgen.serpmedia.org
title: Extended-discourse model of vocabulary instruction: words and word meanings learned through participation in debate and discussion
description: An explanatory account grounded in first language acquisition research: young children first learn words as turns in conversations to accomplish communicative intentions, and rich discourse — more input, wider topics, narratives, explanations — is the context for rapid vocabulary growth. The article extends this to older learners, proposing instruction in words and word meanings embedded in extended discourse, the contexts in which it is normal to learn words, operationalized through classroom debate and discussion in Word Generation.
requirements: Opportunities for students to participate in classroom discussion
Target words presented initially in semantically rich contexts with recurrent exposure in varied contexts
constraints: Students still in early stages of English learning did not benefit without careful adaptation
The mechanism explaining the value of classroom discussion is not entirely clear
target_learners: adolescent second and foreign language learners
first language speakers with limited literacy experiences
examples: The article describes "a m o d e l  f o r  i n s t r u c t i o n  i n  w o r d s  a n d  w o r d  m e a n i n g s embedded in extended discourse, the contexts in which it is normal to learn words."
key_sources: Catherine E. Snow. (2014). Extended discourse in first and second language acquisition: A challenge and an opportunity! Journal of Japanese Linguistics 30. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED571513

article_title: Reading Comprehension and Strategy Awareness of Grade 11 English Second Language Learners
citation: Cekiso, M. (2012). Effects of strategy instruction on the reading comprehension and strategy awareness of Grade 11 English Second Language learners in the Eastern Cape. Reading & Writing 3(1), Art. #23. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v3i1.23
title: Teach reading strategies through explicit instruction rather than leaving learners to acquire them implicitly
description: The article states that explicit instruction in reading strategies can improve learners' reading comprehension and that teachers should design reading strategy instruction that focuses on explicit instruction. It draws on Van Keer's view that even when children do not use effective comprehension strategies on their own, explicit reading strategies instruction is a feasible tool for teaching learners to apply them successfully. The study's own quasi-experimental results are offered as support for this recommendation.
requirements: Instruction must explain the main features of a strategy and why it should be learned, linking benefits to learners' reading profiles
constraints: Evidence base is a single quasi-experimental study in one school using convenience sampling
examples: The experimental group received three months of explicit instruction while the control group's lessons were presented in the normal way with no strategy development or practice.
key_sources: Cekiso, M. (2012). Effects of strategy instruction on the reading comprehension and strategy awareness of Grade 11 English Second Language learners in the Eastern Cape. Reading & Writing 3(1), Art. #23. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v3i1.23

article_title: Enhancing Reading Comprehension among Students with High-Functioning Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Pilot Study
citation: Catherine Roux, Eric Dion, Anne Barrette. (2015). Enhancing Reading Comprehension Among Students With High-Functioning Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Pilot Study. Canadian Journal of Education 38:1. https://www.cje-rce.ca
title: Explicit, structured small-group intervention combining vocabulary, story reading, main idea identification, and text structure
description: The article pilots a theory-based intervention in which, over 10 weeks, a research assistant offered three 30-minute sessions per week to small groups of three to four students, totalling 15 hours. Instruction was "structured (it followed a detailed protocol) and explicit (a clear and coherent terminology was used)", with students' participation continuously required. Most sessions combined tier-2 vocabulary teaching, story reading, main idea identification, and text structure review, with three separate sessions on anaphoric relations.
requirements: A detailed protocol and clear, coherent terminology; the same research assistant delivered sessions to reduce adaptation difficulties for students with ASD
constraints: Conclusions on efficacy cannot be drawn because of the small sample size; the anaphoric-relations component showed no effect, possibly due to only three sessions
target_learners: students with high-functioning autism spectrum disorder, age approximately 9 years, in regular or special classrooms
examples: Each vocabulary and text reading session consisted of four activities: teaching eight tier-2 words with boards showing syllables and illustrations, story reading of a roughly 350-word narrative, main idea identification, and text structure review with drawings
key_sources: Catherine Roux, Eric Dion, Anne Barrette. (2015). Enhancing Reading Comprehension Among Students With High-Functioning Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Pilot Study. Canadian Journal of Education 38:1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057963

article_title: Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory
citation: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85
title: Integrate extracurricular activities with classroom foreign-language study to strengthen environmental education
description: The sixth pedagogical condition holds that integrating appointed and extracurricular activities creates the possibility of effective environmental education through the foreign language. The article reasons that "Extracurricular work is the continuation of academic studies and allows improving the knowledge and skills in a foreign language that pupils acquire in the classroom". In the experiment this was realized in a fan club of English and ecology, debates, and participation in regional environment-oriented school activities.
requirements: Extracurricular work must continue and consolidate the knowledge and skills acquired in classroom study
constraints: Evidence comes from the two Kazan experimental schools
examples: The authors report that pupils increasingly participated in regional natural history and environment-oriented life of the school after the extracurricular work
key_sources: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85

article_title: The Role of Refusal Instruction in Pragmatic Development
citation: Farahman Farrokhi, Soheil Atashian. (2012). The Role of Refusal Instruction in Pragmatic Development. World Journal of Education, Vol. 2, No. 4. http://dx.doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n4p85
title: Teach speech acts explicitly because explicit instruction proves more efficient for learners' pragmatic development
description: The article recommends that language teachers make learners' pragmatic needs explicit in instruction, stating that "explicit approach of teaching speech acts turns out to be more efficient in learners' pragmatic development". It rests this recommendation on its quasi-experimental finding that the explicit group's pragmatic performance improved more than the implicit and control groups' over a 42-hour treatment term.
requirements: Instruction must target specific speech acts (here, refusals) with explicit awareness-raising tasks on refusal forms
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study of upper-intermediate Iranian EFL learners at a single language institute
target_learning_goals: pragmatic performance of refusals in English
examples: In the study, the explicit group received focus-on-forms instruction with explicit awareness-raising tasks on refusals, with sentence structures elaborated so learners could deduce refusal forms
key_sources: Farahman Farrokhi, Soheil Atashian. (2012). The Role of Refusal Instruction in Pragmatic Development. World Journal of Education, Vol. 2, No. 4. http://dx.doi.org/10.5430/wje.v2n4p85

article_title: Improving 4th Grade Primary School Students' Reading Comprehension Skills
citation: Aydın Bulut. (2017). Improving 4th Grade Primary School Students' Reading Comprehension Skills. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(1): 23-30. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050103
title: When teaching SQ3R to struggling primary readers, give extra attention and time to the Recite stage and to oral skills development from first grade
description: Because students in this study struggled most when giving oral and written reports about what they had understood from the text, the authors recommend that teachers and researchers planning to use SQ3R pay particular attention to the Recite stage. They advise that "teachers should spend more time on various ac tivities/exercises for i mproving students' o ral skills from the first year of primary school," building the oral reporting skills the Recite stage depends on before strategy instruction begins.
requirements: Additional activities and exercises targeting oral reporting and summarizing skills, introduced early in primary school
constraints: The recommendation arises from difficulties observed in one small action research study with seven students
target_learners: primary school students who struggle with reading and comprehension
examples: In the study, only about half of the written answers in Recite-stage writing exercises were successful, and students were bored during those exercises
key_sources: Aydın Bulut. (2017). Improving 4th Grade Primary School Students' Reading Comprehension Skills. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(1): 23-30. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050103

article_title: Improving Academic Success for Undecided Students: A First-Year Seminar/Learning Community Approach
citation: Tampke, D. R., & Durodoye, R. (2013). Improving Academic Success for Undecided Students: A First-Year Seminar/Learning Community Approach. Learning Communities Research and Practice, 1(2), Article 3. http://washingtoncenter.evergreen.edu/lcrpjournal/vol1/iss2/3
title: Extending the first-year seminar to all undecided students to improve first-term GPA and good standing
description: The article recommends extending the FYS intervention to all undecided students on the subject campus, given that the seminar's content focused on career and major exploration along with academic skill-building activities and produced significant first-term GPA and good-standing gains. The authors state that "the FYS intervention could be extended to all undecided students on the subject campus with the intention of positively effecting GPA and good standing in the first term."
requirements: Instructors must meet the education level required by regional accreditors and receive orientation to course outcomes, texts, and assessments, including review of a 100+ page instruction manual.
Instructors agree to serve as their students' academic advisors for their first semester and participate in advisor training.
constraints: The study is a single-campus study, so generalizing the results to other institutions should be done with great care.
The control group could be subject to self-selection bias despite statistical similarity on several at-risk categories.
target_learning_goals: Improved first-term GPA and good academic standing
examples: The FYS was a three-credit core-curriculum course focused on critical analysis of potential career and major choices, with common career-related assessments and an undergraduate peer mentor attending one class session per week.
key_sources: Tampke, D. R., & Durodoye, R. (2013). Improving Academic Success for Undecided Students: A First-Year Seminar/Learning Community Approach. Learning Communities Research and Practice, 1(2), Article 3. http://washingtoncenter.evergreen.edu/lcrpjournal/vol1/iss2/3

article_title: Investigating the Longitudinal Effects of a Core Mathematics Program on Evidence-Based Teaching Practices in Mathematics
citation: Doabler, C. T., Nelson, N. J., Kennedy, P. C., Stoolmiller, M., Fien, H., Clarke, B., Gearin, B., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2018). Investigating the Longitudinal Effects of a Core Mathematics Program on Evidence-Based Teaching Practices in Mathematics. Learning Disability Quarterly, 41(3), 144–158. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948718756040
title: Explicit mathematics instruction as a structured pedagogical approach built on three critical teaching practices
description: The article defines explicit mathematics instruction as "a structured pedagogical approach that incorporates empirically validated principles of instruction to effectively and efficiently teach critical mathematics concepts and skills to mastery." At its core it comprises three evidence-based teaching practices: teachers present new concepts through overt demonstrations and explanations, students practice the objective through guided support that is systematically withdrawn, and teachers complement practice with timely informational academic feedback. The ELM program operationalizes this framework in kindergarten core instruction.
requirements: Teachers must deliver overt demonstrations and explanations, frequent student practice opportunities, and timely informational academic feedback during core mathematics instruction.
constraints: The article notes some particulars about practice are debated, though well-designed practice is generally agreed to build conceptual understanding and promote fluency.
target_learners: Kindergarten students with or at risk for mathematics learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Critical mathematics concepts and skills taught to mastery, including counting, operations, base ten, measurement, and geometry
examples: The ELM efficacy trial observed whether classrooms using the explicitly designed ELM program delivered higher rates of models, practice opportunities, and feedback than control classrooms.
key_sources: Doabler, C. T., Nelson, N. J., Kennedy, P. C., Stoolmiller, M., Fien, H., Clarke, B., Gearin, B., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2018). Investigating the Longitudinal Effects of a Core Mathematics Program on Evidence-Based Teaching Practices in Mathematics. Learning Disability Quarterly, 41(3), 144–158. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948718756040

article_title: Utility-Value Intervention with Parents Increases Students' STEM Preparation and Career Pursuit
citation: Rozek, Svoboda, Harackiewicz, Hulleman, & Hyde. (2016). Utility-value intervention with parents increases students' STEM preparation and career pursuit. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1607386114
title: Expectancy-value theory: achievement-related choices depend on expectations for success and subjective task value, with utility value malleable to intervention
description: Expectancy-value theory posits that individuals make achievement-related choices, such as how hard to study or which courses to enroll in, based on (i) their expectations for success and (ii) their subjective task value. The theory distinguishes intrinsic value (a task is enjoyable), attainment value (a task relates to identity), and utility value (a task is relevant or useful for a current or future goal). The article applies it because utility value is viewed as malleable, predicting that increasing the personal relevance of topics increases motivation and achievement.
requirements: Interventions must increase perceived utility value, e.g., by communicating relevance directly, having students generate connections, or engaging parents to do so
examples: The parent intervention is framed as increasing students' perceived utility value of math and science through parent communication
key_sources: Rozek, Svoboda, Harackiewicz, Hulleman, & Hyde. (2016). Utility-value intervention with parents increases students' STEM preparation and career pursuit. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1607386114

article_title: Preschoolers' Alphabet Learning: Letter Name and Sound Instruction, Cognitive Processes, and English Proficiency
citation: Theresa A. Roberts, Patricia F. Vadasy, Elizabeth A. Sanders. (2018). Preschoolers' Alphabet Learning: Letter Name and Sound Instruction, Cognitive Processes, and English Proficiency. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2018.04.011
title: Explicit alphabet instruction should be designed to enlist the cognitive learning processes required for alphabet learning
description: The article's guiding conceptualization is that "highly effective instruction explicitly engages the primary learning processes involved in learning alphabet content, activates these processes in multiple ways and across multiple occasions during learning, and creates conditions for learning that promote engagement." Instruction operationalized paired-associate learning plus articulation-referencing (verbal component) and orthographic learning via letter writing (visual component). The experimental conditions built on this design outgrew typical instruction on taught content.
requirements: Instruction must explicitly activate paired-associate learning and its verbal and visual subcomponents across multiple occasions
constraints: The article notes prior alphabet instruction has not fully and consistently capitalized on these cognitive learning processes
target_learners: preschool children with limited alphabet knowledge
examples: Nine weeks of 10-minute sessions four days/week in small groups of 3-5, with letters introduced by name, sound, or both depending on condition, plus weeks 7-9 cumulative review with letter writing from memory
key_sources: Theresa A. Roberts, Patricia F. Vadasy, Elizabeth A. Sanders. (2018). Preschoolers' Alphabet Learning: Letter Name and Sound Instruction, Cognitive Processes, and English Proficiency. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2018.04.011

article_title: Experiential Learning: Improving the Efficacy of an Undergraduate Business Degree
citation: Frank DeSimone and John Buzza. (2013). Experiential Learning: Improving The Efficacy Of An Undergraduate Business Degree. American Journal Of Business Education, 6(1). http://www.cluteinstitute.com/
title: The type of experiential intervention and the depth of professor participation shape program success
description: Drawing on Abrami et al.'s (2008) proposition that experiential components "are not all equal," the authors argue that the choice of experiential intervention and how deeply the professor participates can be major success factors. Their two programs differ on both dimensions: a marketing incubator with the professor as account executive versus a full venture start-up with the professor as CEO. They also state the research needs refining to assess the optimal choice of incubator client or start-up company.
requirements: Deliberate selection of the experiential intervention type and an active, engaged professorial role
constraints: The article presents this as a proposition drawn from prior meta-analytic work and the authors' own observations, not as a directly tested manipulation
examples: The authors plan to compare three program variants involving approximately 100 students in spring 2012, including a compressed three-company incubator format
key_sources: Frank DeSimone and John Buzza. (2013). Experiential Learning: Improving The Efficacy Of An Undergraduate Business Degree. American Journal Of Business Education, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1054187

article_title: Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching through Problem Solving
citation: Jonathan D. Bostic, Stephen J. Pape, Tim Jacobbe. (2016). Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching Through Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, Volume 8, Number 3. https://rcml.org
title: Make procedures and practice with them an explicit part of problem-solving instruction
description: Because the TTPS intervention group underperformed on unit-specific content, the authors conclude that problem-solving instruction must attend to procedural fluency. "We conclude that teachers must make procedures (and practice with them) an explicit part of problem-solving instruction." They argue students need instructional time to develop procedural fluency through exercises just as they need problem-solving experiences, and that intervention students might have needed help abstracting procedures from problem-solving experiences.
requirements: Time for students to practice employing procedures after using them within problem-solving contexts
constraints: The article states this conclusion arises from a study with limited statistical power and a single unit
examples: The comparison teacher's explicit, procedure-focused instruction was associated with higher unit-test scores
key_sources: Jonathan D. Bostic, Stephen J. Pape, Tim Jacobbe. (2016). Encouraging Sixth-Grade Students' Problem-Solving Performance by Teaching Through Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, Volume 8, Number 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094896

article_title: Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446
title: Use explicit instruction with clear explanations, modeling, guided and independent practice, feedback, and cumulative review for at-risk learners
description: The most successful prior fraction intervention studies adopted an explicit instructional approach characterized by clear explanations, modeling, guided and independent practice, feedback, and cumulative review. This approach is in line with national panel conclusions synthesizing the instructional literature for at-risk students. The article's own intervention incorporated these elements within a 36-lesson manualized program.
requirements: Clear explanations, modeling, guided and independent practice, feedback, and cumulative review
examples: Each lesson comprised four activities: introduction of concepts or skills, group work, the speed game, and individual work.
key_sources: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446

article_title: Effects of Motivational Prompts on Motivation, Effort, and Performance on a Low-Stakes Standardized Test
citation: Hawthorne, K. A., Bol, L., Pribesh, S., & Suh, Y. (2015). Effects of Motivational Prompts on Motivation, Effort, and Performance on a Low-Stakes Standardized Test. Journal of General Education, 64(2). https://doi.org/10.1353/jge.2015.0016
title: Expectancy-value theory of achievement motivation as a framework for test-taking motivation on low-stakes assessments
description: The study is framed by the expectancy-value theory of achievement developed by Eccles and refined by Wigfield and Eccles, in which "expectancy is defined as a student's belief that he or she can complete a task successfully, and value is defined as a student's perceptions about why he or she should complete a task." In low-stakes assessment contexts the model is expanded to include perceived effort and intrinsic value. The authors used this framework to hypothesize that personalized prompts would elicit different motivation than generic prompts.
requirements: Motivation is treated as situated, contextual, and domain-specific, so the framework must be applied to a specific testing task
constraints: The authors report a paradox: students reported above-average importance scores yet performed well below the national mean, which requires additional investigation
target_learning_goals: test-taking motivation and effort on low-stakes assessments
examples: The varying instructions were designed to manipulate student motivation by appeals to their "academic citizenship."
key_sources: Hawthorne, K. A., Bol, L., Pribesh, S., & Suh, Y. (2015). Effects of Motivational Prompts on Motivation, Effort, and Performance on a Low-Stakes Standardized Test. Journal of General Education, 64(2). https://doi.org/10.1353/jge.2015.0016

article_title: Self-Explanation and Explanatory Feedback in Games: Individual Differences, Gameplay, and Learning
citation: Killingsworth, S. S., Clark, D. B., & Adams, D. M. (2015). Self-Explanation and Explanatory Feedback in Games: Individual Differences, Gameplay, and Learning. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology, 3(3), 162-186. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075243
title: Place explanation activities after students correctly complete the level they will explain
description: Based on lessons from an earlier prototype study (Adams and Clark, 2014), the authors adopted the prescription that "explanation activities should occur after students correctly complete the level that they will be explaining." Postponing self-explanation until after a correct solution decreases perceiving the functionality as unhelpful, avoids disrupting the solution process, and focuses students on the correct solution, which may be necessary for effective self-explanation.
requirements: Students must first identify a working solution before explanation prompts are posed
constraints: Prescriptions were adopted in reprogramming explanation functionality in The Fuzzy Chronicles specifically
target_learning_goals: physics relationships such as the relation between applied force and change in velocity
key_sources: Killingsworth, S. S., Clark, D. B., & Adams, D. M. (2015). Self-Explanation and Explanatory Feedback in Games: Individual Differences, Gameplay, and Learning. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology, 3(3), 162-186. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1066360

article_title: Integrated Reading and Writing: A Case of Korean English Language Learners
citation: Cho, H., & Brutt-Griffler, J. (2015). Integrated reading and writing: A case of Korean English language learners. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 242-261. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Explicit paraphrasing instruction with authentic reading materials helps ELL students develop sophisticated paraphrasing skills and plagiarism awareness
description: The article recommends that "for more improved and sophisticated paraphrasing, explicit instruction and authentic reading materials can be helpful." Teaching the paraphrasing skill can enhance students' understanding of plagiarism, and "practice of paraphrasing, not punishment of plagiarism, should be emphasized." Authentic texts expose students to varied and complex sentence structures and vocabulary that may seldom occur in simplified L2 reading texts.
requirements: Students need to expand their lexical and syntactical knowledge to improve their summarizing ability.
constraints: Even students at the advanced proficiency level did not paraphrase the original sentences sufficiently or correctly after the intervention.
examples: A student in the advanced level paraphrased "The Yankees offered Lou a $1500 bonus to sign plus a good salary" as "The Yankees gave Lou a $1500 bonus to sign plus a good pay," replacing only one word.
key_sources: Cho, H., & Brutt-Griffler, J. (2015). Integrated reading and writing: A case of Korean English language learners. Reading in a Foreign Language, 27(2), 242-261. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: The Impact of Training Metacognitive Strategies on Reading Comprehension among ESL Learner's
citation: Habibian, M. (2015). The Impact of Training Metacognitive Strategies on Reading Comprehension among ESL Learner’s. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(28). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1082693
title: Teach metacognitive reading strategies explicitly to help ESL learners control their comprehension process
description: The article recommends that ESL reading instruction should include explicit teaching of metacognitive strategies rather than relying on routine reading practice alone. The author states that "by using metacognition, instructors can assist individuals to analyze and organize their thinking, reading, and learning process" and that explicit instruction contributed to students' reading comprehension ability in the study.
requirements: Instruction must cover declarative knowledge (what strategies are), situational knowledge (when to apply them), and procedural knowledge (how to employ them)
constraints: The author notes internal validity is under question because the experimental and control group instructors were different
examples: The experimental group received twelve weeks of instruction three days a week, one hour per day, covering strategies such as highlighting main points, paraphrasing, identifying keywords, monitoring reading, re-reading, self-testing, and adjusting reading rate
key_sources: Habibian, M. (2015). The Impact of Training Metacognitive Strategies on Reading Comprehension among ESL Learner’s. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(28). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1081318

article_title: The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on the Learnability of English Consonant Clusters by Iranian Learners of English
citation: Ruhollah Khanbeiki; Seyed Jalal Abdolmanafi-Rokni. (2015). The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on the Learnability of English Consonant Clusters by Iranian Learners of English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, Vol. 6 No. 2. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.103
title: Direct learners' attention explicitly to pronunciation features through rule explanation, examples, and cross-language comparison
description: The article recommends that pronunciation instruction be explicit: presenting phonetic symbols, pronunciation rules, and stress patterns, and providing extra examples. The explicit group received "a detailed explanation of what he meant by English consonant cluster rules" including comparison of English and Persian syllable structures, which produced the largest gains.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of the phonetic system of the target language to explain rules and compare syllable structures.
constraints: The finding is specific to Iranian intermediate EFL learners learning English consonant clusters over ten sessions.
target_learning_goals: Correct pronunciation of English consonant clusters
examples: The explicit group received rule explanation, extra examples, comparison of English and Persian syllable structures, and error correction over ten sessions.
key_sources: Ruhollah Khanbeiki; Seyed Jalal Abdolmanafi-Rokni. (2015). The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on the Learnability of English Consonant Clusters by Iranian Learners of English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, Vol. 6 No. 2. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.103

article_title: The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on the Learnability of English Consonant Clusters by Iranian Learners of English
citation: Ruhollah Khanbeiki; Seyed Jalal Abdolmanafi-Rokni. (2015). The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on the Learnability of English Consonant Clusters by Iranian Learners of English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, Vol. 6 No. 2. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.103
title: Explicit vs. implicit learning distinction based on awareness of the structure being learned
description: The article draws on DeKeyser's (2003) distinction between explicit and implicit learning, where implicit learning is "learning without awareness of what is being learned" and explicit learning involves rule explanation or directed attention to forms. These are treated as orthogonal to the inductive/deductive distinction, allowing combinations such as explicit-inductive and implicit-deductive learning.
requirements: Distinguishing explicit from implicit instruction requires identifying whether rule explanation or directed attention to forms is part of the treatment.
constraints: The article notes that the combination of deductive and implicit learning is less obvious but possible, citing parameter setting in Universal Grammar as an example.
target_learners: Second language learners, especially adult learners
target_learning_goals: Second language pronunciation and linguistic competence
examples: The explicit group received rule explanation and directed attention; the implicit group received only exposure without awareness of the rule.
key_sources: Ruhollah Khanbeiki; Seyed Jalal Abdolmanafi-Rokni. (2015). The Effect of Explicit vs. Implicit Instruction on the Learnability of English Consonant Clusters by Iranian Learners of English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, Vol. 6 No. 2. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.2p.103

article_title: Preschoolers' Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22
citation: Ackerman, D. J., & Friedman-Krauss, A. H. (2017). Preschoolers’ Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22. https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12148
title: Executive function is a set of high-level cognitive and behavioral processes that support goal-directed behavior
description: The report defines executive function as an interrelated and complex set of high-level cognitive and behavioral processes that all people should possess, beginning to develop early in life. These include the ability to anticipate and initiate actions, appropriately direct and sustain short-term attention, inhibit inappropriate behaviors, problem solve, incorporate relevant feedback, selectively revise plans, and retrieve rules and ideas from long-term memory to develop and implement appropriate strategies. EF also involves the capacity to use working memory and inhibit and control thoughts and actions. In children, EF skills help them control behavior and attention, delay gratification, resist impulses, and engage in goal-directed behaviors.
requirements: The report notes that EF is highly dependent on human brain development, particularly rapid development of the prefrontal cortex during ages 3–6 years.
constraints: The report acknowledges many overlapping theories of EF stemming from different perspectives, with no single consensus definition.
key_sources: Ackerman, D. J., & Friedman-Krauss, A. H. (2017). Preschoolers’ Executive Function: Importance, Contributors, Research Needs and Assessment Options. Policy Information Report and ETS Research Report Series No. RR-17-22. https://doi.org/10.1002/ets2.12148

article_title: Enhancing Online Distance Education in Small Rural US Schools: A Hybrid, Learner-Centred Model
citation: de la Varre, C., Keane, J., & Irvin, M. J. (2010). Enhancing online distance education in small rural US schools: A hybrid, learner-centered model. Journal of Asynchronous Learning Networks, 15(4).
title: Expanded teacher-facilitator model distributing instructional components between online instructor and on-site facilitator
description: The article proposes an expanded teacher-facilitator model in which the four components of the online instructor role identified by Berge — pedagogical, social, organizational, and technical — are distributed between the online instructor and the on-site facilitator. The instructor teaches the course and follows the curriculum, while the social, organizational, and technical components are jointly managed through regular communication. This creates "a truly hybrid learning environment" linking the local classroom more closely with the online environment.
requirements: Each school must appoint an on-site facilitator to be present when students take the class each day
Facilitators need basic web-based training before the course starts
constraints: The extent to which facilitators took responsibility for social, organizational, and technical areas depended on their own personal characteristics
target_learners: Rural high school students in small schools
target_learning_goals: Access to advanced courses such as AP English through online distance education
examples: Schools were randomly assigned to intervention or control; intervention facilitators received scenario-based learner-centered training while control facilitators received standard technical training

article_title: Exploring 3D anatomy: A free online course supporting novice learner inquiry and spatial conceptualization.
citation: Zhang J, Sachdeva M, McCaig C, Gordon E, Shapiro L, Keenan ID. (2026). Exploring 3D anatomy: A free online course supporting novice learner inquiry and spatial conceptualization. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70288
title: Exploring 3D Anatomy: a free open online course for three-dimensional spatial awareness
description: Exploring 3D Anatomy is an open online course, collaboratively produced at universities in the United Kingdom and South Africa, and available free of charge via Canvas. It is designed to develop three-dimensional spatial awareness remotely, using accessible household objects and art-based learning, and can be described as a small-scale, open, free, formative, instructor-guided, vocational open online course. The external Instructure course achieved 460 users (2023-2026), while 4447 users joined the internal Canvas version since launch (2021-2026).
requirements: Delivered via the Instructure Canvas learning management system, with a general Course Information module introducing educators, course aims, required materials, and navigation guidance
constraints: Available free of charge to institutional and non-institutional users; serves as a supplement to, rather than a replacement for, conventional teaching in areas under-represented in formal curricula
target_learning_goals: Understanding of three-dimensional and cross-sectional anatomical concepts
examples: Launched internally at Newcastle University and University of Cape Town in academic year 2021/22, with an international launch via the external Instructure platform coinciding with World Anatomy Day, October 15, 2023
key_sources: Zhang J, Sachdeva M, McCaig C, Gordon E, Shapiro L, Keenan ID. (2026). Exploring 3D anatomy: A free online course supporting novice learner inquiry and spatial conceptualization. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70288

citation: Zhang J, Sachdeva M, McCaig C, Gordon E, Shapiro L, Keenan ID. (2026). Exploring 3D anatomy: A free online course supporting novice learner inquiry and spatial conceptualization. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70288
title: Pedagogical framework of Exploring 3D Anatomy: multimodal, experiential, and social learning with art-based cycles
description: The course is underpinned by pedagogical principles including multimodal, experiential, and social learning; critical observation and visualization; and evidence-informed art-based learning approaches including Haptico-visual observation and drawing and Observe-reflect-draw-edit-repeat. The modular course structure is deliberately underpinned by Observe-reflect-draw-edit-repeat experiential learning cycles, with elements of building upon prior knowledge, experiential cycles, and social learning underpinned by theories of cognitive constructivism, experiential learning, and social learning respectively.
requirements: Each exercise requires learners to engage in haptic and visual observation during practical art-based activities using easily available and accessible household objects
constraints: Anatomical resources/models are not required nor recommended; exercises use household objects such as forks, jars, citrus fruit, and boxes
examples: The course includes an Astronaut Exercise for cognitive visualization, a Fork Exercise introducing haptic and visual observation of a physical object, a Jar Exercise drawing anatomical planes onto a jar, and a Fruit Exercise cutting a citrus fruit along drawn body planes
key_sources: Zhang J, Sachdeva M, McCaig C, Gordon E, Shapiro L, Keenan ID. (2026). Exploring 3D anatomy: A free online course supporting novice learner inquiry and spatial conceptualization. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70288
