title: Modular exercise sequence progressing from cognitive visualization to combined haptic-visual drawing
description: The course is structured in distinct modular exercises that learners move through in sequence, beginning with the Astronaut Exercise, with each module unlocked as learners progress and revisitable at any time. Distinct exercises support learner progression from a simple starting point of cognitive visualization activities through visual and haptic activities involving household objects, with drawing activities included at deliberate points in the course, serving as visual representations of cognitive understanding.
requirements: Each webpage provides clear instructions, guidance through a sequence of tasks, gathering of appropriate materials, and setting of expectations such as time required to complete tasks
constraints: Modules are unlocked in the recommended sequence (left to right; top to bottom), though they can be revisited at any time
target_learning_goals: Progressive development of cognitive and physical spatial awareness
Visualization of two-dimensional cross-sections of anatomical planes
examples: The sequence runs Astronaut (<10 min), 3D Body (<10 min), Fork (<20 min), Jar (<55 min), Fruit (>60 min), Visual and Haptic Observation (<10 min), Haptico-visual observation and drawing (>120 min), and Box (<25 min) exercises

article_title: How to Conduct Usability Testing of Medical Education Simulations: Methods Tutorial Using a Telemedicine Simulation for Maternal Care.
citation: Lesselroth BJ, Douglas A, Monkman H, Marcilly R, Bellavia K, Anderson M, Van Buren J, Parsons C, Mohanty S, Homco J, Richards M, Gold KP. (2026). How to Conduct Usability Testing of Medical Education Simulations: Methods Tutorial Using a Telemedicine Simulation for Maternal Care. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/102697
title: External validity framework for usability evaluation of educational simulations
description: The article applies a two-dimensional external validity model, created by the authors for usability evaluations of health information technology, to educational simulation testing. It holds that "External validity comprises (1) population validity (ie, the extent to which the sample represents the population) and (2) ecological validity (ie, the extent to which the setting matches the real world)." Fidelity on each dimension is set by evaluation objectives, and usability is treated as an emergent property of the whole work system rather than of the interface alone. The team mapped constructs such as learner attributes, clinical environment, technology, and scenario onto their telemedicine use case.
requirements: Evaluation must replicate realistic conditions regarding participants, task complexity, environmental constraints, and instructor support
Testers should match a defined user persona for population validity
constraints: The appropriate fidelity level for each validity dimension depends on the evaluation objectives
target_learning_goals: designing and conducting usability testing of educational simulations
examples: The team chose to test with faculty rather than learners to assess case accuracy and whether tasks were appropriately calibrated for residents

article_title: Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study.
citation: Zhu Xiaocheng, Tang Anliu, Chin Munle, Chang Huan. (2026). Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10042-y
title: Provide explicit objectives and observation frameworks to prevent early clinical exposure from becoming passive watching
description: The article argues that early clinical exposure without clear objectives and structured guidance "may become passive watching rather than purposeful learning". Clarifying learning objectives and providing a workflow-oriented observation checklist gives novice learners a practical framework for organizing attention around specific perioperative tasks and professional roles, which the authors propose explains the higher primary outcome score in the structured group.
requirements: Learning objectives explicitly presented before clinical exposure
An observation checklist translating complex clinical processes into observable and reflectable learning tasks
Instructor prompts during observation to highlight priorities and connect events to clinical context
constraints: Developed and evaluated in an anesthesiology early-exposure context at a single institution; generalizability to other settings requires further study
target_learners: Novice undergraduate medical students in early clinical exposure
target_learning_goals: Connecting observations with patient safety, workflow, and professional roles
examples: The structured group used a perioperative workflow-oriented observation checklist during Participatory learning, with instructors supplementing checklist items not covered in a single operating room during group discussion

article_title: Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study.
citation: Shin Sujin, Choi Jaehwa, Hong Eunmin, Lee Miji, Go Jinseon, Yu Subin, Lee Minjae. (2026). Development of vignette-based evaluation with generative artificial intelligence (VEGA) for nursing students: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09685-8
title: Ground AI-generated assessment items in a recognized competency framework with expert content validation before learner use
description: The article validates AI-generated educational content through expert review before implementation: six experts rated vignettes, items, and feedback on a 4-point scale, with CVI thresholds of ≥ 0.78 item-level and S-CVI/Ave ≥ 0.90 considered acceptable. The authors warn that "AI-generated content may be clinically inaccurate or inconsistent due to prompt instability or model variability," so ongoing expert review is needed. This principle directs developers to pair generative tools with structured human validation.
requirements: A panel of qualified experts rating content validity on a structured scale before and during deployment
constraints: The article notes learners who uncritically accept incorrect AI feedback may develop misconceptions with potential patient safety implications
target_learners: nursing students using AI-based learning tools
target_learning_goals: accurate clinical judgment development from AI-generated content
examples: Expert suggestions led to revising the prompt structure to exclude diagnostic labels and standardizing the feedback format

article_title: Can ChatGPT pass the polish national medical specialization examination in orthopedics and traumatology?
citation: Maciąg Bartosz, Bujak Krzysztof, Jegierski Dawid, Stolarczyk Artur. (2026). Can ChatGPT pass the polish national medical specialization examination in orthopedics and traumatology? Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-026-06435-9
title: Examination success should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical competence or readiness for independent surgical practice
description: The article argues that success in multiple-choice testing should not be equated with genuine clinical competence. The authors state that "LLMs generate probabilistic text outputs on the basis of patterns in training data and do not possess embodied clinical judgment, situational awareness, or professional accountability." Specialist practice in orthopedics extends far beyond declarative knowledge to include manual skills, intraoperative adaptability, tactile feedback, team communication, and time-sensitive decision-making under uncertainty.
requirements: AI tools used in medical education should be positioned as adjunctive rather than as substitutes for clinical training
constraints: Even highly capable language models cannot perform physical examination maneuvers, assess tissue quality, manipulate instruments, control bleeding, or modify surgical strategy in response to intraoperative findings
target_learners: AI tool developers in medical education
target_learning_goals: accurate calibration of AI capabilities in medical contexts
responsible integration of AI into medical education and assessment

citation: Tomobi Oluwakemi, DeFazio Sarah, Lin Dena, Brashear Alyssa, Smart Klint, Epps Gregory, Woodberry Kerri. (2026). Advancing health equity through simulation-based education for pre-health students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354377
title: Experiential learning theory as the basis for simulation-based education.
description: The article frames simulation within experiential learning, citing Kolb's definition that "Learning is the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience." Simulation is described as a form of experiential learning in a controlled environment using role-playing actors, manikins, and equipment to replicate clinical contexts with no risk to real patients, thereby translating academic knowledge into practical application and reducing the gap between classroom learning and clinical performance.
requirements: A controlled, realistic environment replicating clinical contexts
Active learner participation and experience transformation
constraints: The article cites this framework from Kolb (1984) rather than testing it directly; it serves as the conceptual rationale for the intervention
target_learning_goals: connecting basic science knowledge to clinical practice
examples: The one-day simulation program operationalized experiential learning by having students manage realistic emergency cases immediately after receiving relevant lecture content

It states that "Clinical workshops, simulation-based learning, case-based discussions, and supervised MDT practice sessions may provide valuable experiential learning opportunities that bridge the gap between theory and practice." Nurses who performed or observed MDT gained firsthand exposure to wound assessment, patient selection, application techniques, monitoring, and complication management, which the authors argue deepens understanding beyond theoretical instruction.

title: Structure supervised adoption of THD-Anolift with mentorship extended to at least 20–25 cases rather than the conventionally proposed 10 mentored cases
description: The article proposes that training benchmarks for THD-Anolift be revised upward based on empirically derived CUSUM learning-curve data. At case 10 the cumulative failure rate was 60% and mean operative time exceeded 28 min with no plateau, while proficiency emerged near case 23. The authors "argue for a substantial revision of empirically set training benchmarks for THD-Anolift, with structured mentorship extended to at least 20–25 cases" plus routine prospective audit of personal outcomes during early adoption.

constraints: The estimate comes from a retrospective single-surgeon inception series and should be validated in larger multicenter cohorts before any prescriptive use; learning curves vary with prior proctologic experience, case selection, mentorship, and institutional setting

examples: CUSUM analysis of 51 consecutive cases identified an inflection at approximately case 23, more than twice the conventionally proposed 10 mentored cases

Instructor time to compile past examination questions aligned to knowledge domains

target_learning_goals: Preparation for licensing examination question formats

article_title: Exploring synchronous, asynchronous, and conventional online courses in higher education.
citation: Moon, Eunkyung and Shin, Won Sug. (2026). Exploring synchronous, asynchronous, and conventional online courses in higher education. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345955
title: Extended Information Systems Success Model integrating teaching presence and self-efficacy with system and information quality
description: The article extends the DeLone and McLean ISSM by adding teaching presence (TP) and self-efficacy (SE) alongside system quality (SQ) and information quality (IQ), to explain perceived usefulness, learning satisfaction, and continuance intention. It states the model "extends the original ISSM by incorporating key psychological factors (SE, TP) alongside the traditional system factors of SQ and IQ." In this framework, quality perceptions and psychological variables influence PU, which affects LS and ultimately CI. The model was applied to compare how synchronous, asynchronous, and conventional online courses engage these mechanisms differently.
requirements: Measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar) must hold before cross-group latent mean comparison
constraints: Service quality was excluded because all participants used the same LMS within a single institutional context
target_learning_goals: learner satisfaction and continuance intention in online learning
examples: Applied with latent mean analysis and multi-group SEM to survey data from 795 undergraduates

article_title: Preparing House Officers for Emergencies in a Psychiatric Setting with Simulation-Based Learning.
citation: Matthew Tennant, Maggie Meeks, Ben Beaglehole, Chris Frampton, Jane Foley, Emily Ide, Dylan Hill, Carol Dean. (2025). Preparing House Officers for Emergencies in a Psychiatric Setting with Simulation-Based Learning. Academic Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40596-025-02217-4
title: Experiential learning theory explains the value of immersive simulation followed by reflective debriefing
description: The article uses experiential learning theory to account for the perceived value of realistic, immersive simulation with debriefing. "In experiential learning theory, learners are exposed to a novel experience that involves risk", learners actively experiment with the concrete experience, and afterwards "critical reflection mediates meaningful learning". The authors argue that experiencing the emergency as novel and risky heightens house officers' attention, and debriefing consolidates the learning.
requirements: A debriefing stage in which learners critically reflect on the simulation
constraints: Simulations are performed in a contained environment rather than real clinical settings
target_learners: house officers participating in simulation training
target_learning_goals: reflecting on emotional responses to emergencies
examples: Debriefs led by a simulation educator, consultant psychiatrist, registrar, and senior nurse let participants imagine scenario changes and talk through how these would affect management

article_title: Investigating Hip Arthroplasty Femur Preparation Training Using a Haptic-Enabled Virtual Reality Simulation.
citation: Duncombe Justin M.T., Camaly de Brosses Pierre, Kassam Al-Amin M., Harris David J., Buckingham Gavin. (2026). Investigating Hip Arthroplasty Femur Preparation Training Using a Haptic-Enabled Virtual Reality Simulation. Surgical Innovation, 33(2), 169-180. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506251383830
title: Provide extended familiarisation with VR technology and haptic devices before procedural skill assessment to reduce device-related cognitive load
description: The article recommends that VR surgical training studies build in a dedicated pre-training phase with the virtual environment and haptic interface before assessing procedural skills. It argues, via Cognitive Load Theory, that "Difficulties arising from the software or haptic devices result in the allocation of additional cognitive resources to master the technology, thereby increasing cognitive load and hindering performance". In this study, one hour of familiarisation may have been insufficient for learners to overcome the initial cognitive burden of the haptic devices, potentially masking training benefits.
requirements: Dedicated time for participants to become comfortable with the haptic interface and virtual environment navigation before focusing on surgical skill development
constraints: The article states the limited familiarisation time provided in this study (one hour) may have been insufficient to overcome the initial cognitive burden of learning to use the haptic devices
examples: The study provided only a single live demonstration of the VR module and a 60-minute training session, after which participants were assessed without additional familiarisation with the haptic devices.

title: Course design grounded in experiential learning theory and situated learning theory
description: The pilot course’s design was explicitly grounded in two named theoretical frameworks. Experiential learning theory “views learning as a cycle of concrete experience, reflection, conceptual understanding, and active experimentation,” which the authors align with immersive, scenario-based virtual patient simulation and feedback-supported reflection. Situated learning theory is invoked for “the crucial importance of authentic contexts and social participation in developing professional competencies,” justifying immersive simulations in which students progress from observation to active decision-making within authentic clinical contexts.
requirements: Structured design of virtual simulation tasks with scaffolded language and communication challenges
Debriefing activities to support reflection and knowledge transfer
constraints: The authors state these theories supported the design; the study itself did not test the theoretical mechanisms
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in multicultural, trilingual cohorts
examples: Pre-session vocabulary reviews, guided feedback and reflective debriefings were described in the Discussion as aligning with Kolb’s experiential learning model

citation: Xie Lichun, Mo Yongkang, Ma Jiejia, Xiao Yubin, Wu Xiaojia, Ma Xilun, Sun Danmiao, Ke Dongping, Mei Wei, Huang Ruibin. (2025). Rapid-cycle deliberate practice with an ex vivo porcine model of intussusception improves radiology residents' competence in air enema reduction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08339-5
title: Ex vivo porcine model of colonic intussusception for air enema reduction training
description: A high-fidelity training model built from a fresh porcine colon segment: the distal end is narrowed with a rubber band to simulate the anal entrance, the middle portion is invaginated to create the morphology of intussusception, and the proximal end is lanced to prevent gas leakage. Used with a gastrointestinal fluoroscopy machine and a computer remote control enema rectifier, it "effectively demonstrates the gradual withdrawal technique for reduction of intussusception, supported by dynamic visualization under X-ray fluoroscopy". The authors report it was proven cost-effective and efficient in preliminary research.
requirements: Used with a gastrointestinal fluoroscopy system and an air enema rectifier device as in the study setup
constraints: Assessment of the model's fidelity and implementation was reported in a previous study, not verified within this trial
target_learning_goals: performing air enema reduction of pediatric intussusception
examples: Both study groups trained on this model; unlike prior doll-and-tube simulators, it replicates progressive intussusception reduction under fluoroscopy

citation: Mellinas-Martínez Irene, Pecci-Lloret María Pilar, Pecci-Lloret Miguel Ramón, Adánez-Martínez María Gracia, Guerrero-Gironés Julia. (2025). Clinical simulation as an effective teaching model in the Special Needs Dentistry course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07882-5
title: Expert-validated assessment checklists completed by three independent evaluators
description: Student performance was assessed with standardized checklists "designed by the research team for each simulation scenario", covering "both technical and non-technical competencies such as decision-making, teamwork, communication, and prioritization of care". Checklist content was "validated by an expert panel composed of 11 faculty members from six Spanish universities", and three evaluators recorded Yes/No ratings item by item at both assessment points.
requirements: Expert-panel validation of checklist items using Likert-type importance and relevance ratings, consensus refinement, and piloting before formal use
Three independent evaluators completing each checklist item by item, with session recordings available to improve evaluation accuracy
constraints: The checklists offered no “partially completed” option, forcing a done-or-not-done choice even when a task was partially or inadequately executed
target_learning_goals: evaluating clinical performance including decision-making, teamwork, communication and prioritization of care
examples: Evaluations from the three instructors were compiled into Excel spreadsheets, one per scenario, recording Yes/No ratings for PRE and POST

title: ExpandTPT simplified training protocol with simulation models (sausages for application, silicone induration models for reading)
description: ExpandTPT is a program begun in April 2023 with the Brazilian Ministry of Health coordination, REDE-TB and McGill University to expand access to tuberculosis preventive treatment. It promoted professional training, "incorporou ferramentas inovadoras, como o protocolo simplificado para aplicação e leitura da prova tuberculínica", implemented virtual quality control of test application, and used sausages for application practice and silicone models with varying indurations for reading practice by all trainees.

title: Exocad-based preclass 3D digital tooth morphology module
description: An instructional component in which a clinical instructor introduces tooth morphology (the permanent maxillary right first molar) using Exocad dental CAD/CAM design software and interactive 3D modelling, followed by student self-directed practice with the 3D models on mobile or desktop devices. The article selected Exocad because it is "a dental CAD/CAM platform widely adopted by laboratories and clinics in over 150 countries" with a user-friendly interface suitable for educational use. In the trial this module preceded the traditional hands-on carving session.

constraints: The module was evaluated over a 3-week intervention at a single institution; the article states generalizability is limited
target_learners: second-year dental technology students at a junior college
target_learning_goals: understanding of permanent maxillary right first molar morphology
preparation for hands-on plaster tooth carving
examples: In Week 1 the experimental group received a 90-minute digital course introducing PM1M morphology with Exocad and interactive 3D modelling; in Week 2 students practised self-directed with the provided 3D models outside scheduled class hours.

citation: Xiang Y, Wei C. (2025). The performance of ChatGPT on medical image-based assessments and implications for medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07752-0
title: Keep human oversight and expert validation central whenever large vision-language models are used to generate or explain medical instructional content
description: Across both the assessment and the instructional explorations, the article holds that AI-generated medical content requires expert checking before use: "human verification and correction remain essential", and ensuring "the clinical validity, cognitive appropriateness, and pedagogical alignment of AI-generated content remains a critical challenge". The authors recommend integrating such tools with faculty-led review and revision mechanisms to preserve instructional reliability.
requirements: Faculty-led review and revision mechanisms integrated into any deployment of LVLM-generated medical teaching content
constraints: Errors remain in nuanced clinical contexts involving medical images even when model reasoning shows high coherence

article_title: Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research.
citation: Lazarus Michelle D., Sarkar Mahbub, Palermo Claire, Soh Sze‐Ee, Farlie Melanie K. (2025). Expanding worldviews on psychometric analysis of measurement tools in health professions education and research. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70053
title: Researchers should explicitly state which worldviews they engaged and at which stage of the research process, in all psychometric studies
description: The article calls for researchers to be "upfront and transparent about their worldviews and research approaches in all (not just some) psychometric studies," also acknowledging the qualitative studies upon which scales were built. The rationale is that worldviews have historically been implied as tied to positivism, that worldview–method tension can cause misinterpretation or dismissal of others' work, and that explicit statements reduce assumptions about the research process. The authors also urge readers to "refrain from placing a value judgment on the quality and rigor of research simply based on the worldview applied."
requirements: Explicit researcher statements about which worldviews were engaged and at which stage in the research process each was applied, regardless of methods used
constraints: The article notes such statements can only be assumed today when authors do not state their worldviews, as in its uncertainty tolerance scale example
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation and application of psychometric literature in HPE
examples: The article suggests a researcher could state that a physician uncertainty tolerance scale was developed using CTT from a positivist worldview, a statement currently only assumable

citation: Manav Esra Yildirim, Akbiyik Sema Yazici, Ceylan Aydan Büşra, Çakiroğlu Ayfer Ezgi Yilmaz, Tuncer Duygu. (2025). Effects of virtual reality and layered tooth model training on manual dexterity in preclinical dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07622-9
title: Provide extended and equalized simulation practice time, since short two-day exposure may limit measurable gains on complex skills
description: The article's discussion and limitations converge on training-time design for simulation-based psychomotor training. Citing prior work, it notes that "Studies suggest that repeated simulation exposure over a period of 3 to 4 weeks, with at least 3 to 5 sessions, is often necessary to achieve measurable improvements in psychomotor skills and knowledge retention among novice dental students." The study's own compressed two-day schedule is offered as a likely reason non-depth parameters showed no differences, and unequal exposure across groups is flagged as a potential dose-effect confound.
requirements: Future comparative studies should equalize total hands-on training time across groups when comparing instructional strategies
constraints: The article notes cost-effectiveness and long-term skill retention could not be addressed due to short study duration and institutional constraints; extended protocols are recommended to determine optimal frequency and spacing
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill development and knowledge retention in simulation-based training
examples: The trial's 20–25 minute sessions over two consecutive days produced depth gains but no differences in outline, retention form, or overall quality, which the authors attribute partly to limited exposure

article_title: Explore your brain: A randomized controlled trial into the effectiveness of a growth mindset intervention with psychosocial and psychophysiological components.
citation: Janssen, T. W. P., & van Atteveldt, N. (2025). Explore your brain: A randomized controlled trial into the effectiveness of a growth mindset intervention with psychosocial and psychophysiological components. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 280–302. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12572
title: Three mindset-based motivational profiles: Fixed, Growth non-competitive, and Growth competitive
description: Using Latent Profile/Transition Analysis on eight indicators (growth mindset, effort beliefs, four goal orientations, external regulation, intrinsic motivation), the article identifies three profiles. The Fixed profile showed "less growth mindset endorsement (more towards the fixed side of the mindset scale), less positive effort beliefs and less mastery goals". Both growth profiles endorsed growth mindset and positive effort beliefs more, but differed in goal orientation: Growth non-competitive students showed low performance goals and high mastery goals, while Growth competitive students endorsed both performance and mastery goals. This extends mindset theory by capturing naturally occurring combinations at the individual level.
requirements: Measurement invariance of profile indicator thresholds over time, checked by comparing constrained and unconstrained models
constraints: Profile differences on external regulation and intrinsic motivation were unstable at T2, so the authors urged caution interpreting those indicators
target_learners: Dutch 7th-grade secondary school students (vocational to pre-university tracks)
target_learning_goals: Growth mindset and related motivational constructs: effort beliefs, goal orientation, academic motivation

Explore your brain: A randomized controlled trial into the effectiveness of a growth mindset intervention with psychosocial and psychophysiological components. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 280–302. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12572
title: Combine psychosocial mindset teaching with an experiential psychophysiological component (EEG neurofeedback) to make growth mindset messages convincing
description: The article argues that modest effects of prior growth mindset interventions may stem from overly theoretical techniques, and addresses this by pairing lessons on brain plasticity and mindset with a neurofeedback lesson giving "a convincing experience of influencing one's own brain activity". Experiencing control over one's brain activity was expected to help internalize the theoretical growth mindset messages. In the RCT this combination produced relatively large effects on mindset and math grades compared to meta-analytic averages, which the authors attribute to synergetic effects of the two components.
requirements: Mobile EEG equipment and a neurofeedback application; exercises in which students can genuinely lower theta/beta index relative to baseline
constraints: The reading exercise failed because students found it too difficult to focus on text and auditory feedback simultaneously; T3 assessment was dropped due to COVID-19 drop-out
target_learning_goals: Growth mindset endorsement, protection of math achievement, motivation
examples: In the RCT, lesson 3 had students influence a brain correlate of focused attention (theta/beta index) with mobile EEG neurofeedback, and 91.7% indicated they were more convinced they could influence their own brain afterwards

citation: Kronner, N., Strebl, M., Lenk, J., Gebauer, B., Schweizerhof, O., Frisch, A., Wintergerst, C., Uller, W., de Bucourt, M. & Can, E. (2025). Simulator training for enhanced interventional radiology education. Scientific Reports 15, 10861. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-95828-8

It also invokes the ICAP hypothesis (Interactive, Constructive, Active, Passive) of Chi and Wylie (2014), under which deeper engagement levels yield enhanced learning. citation: Bruen Catherine, Illing Jan, Daly Ronan, Meagher Frances, Delany Caroline, Offiah Gozie, Doherty Sally, Stuart Ellen, Crehan Martina, Kelly Helen. (2025). Medical student experiences of Case-Based Learning (CBL) at a multicultural medical school. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06585-7
title: Experience Based Learning (ExBL) model as a framework of affective, pedagogical and organisational support
description: The Experience Based Learning model, developed by Dornan et al. and adapted here for CBL, organises how learning experiences support students through three supports. Affective support "is about relating to others", including emotions such as "anger, anxiety, empathy and compassion"; pedagogical support covers modelling good practice and structuring discussion; organisational support "brings all aspects of the case together" including real patient cases, resources, debriefing and summing up. This study used the three themes as its analytical framework, deriving results under each.
requirements: Facilitators who understand and can operationalise all three supports during CBL sessions
constraints: The model was developed initially to understand clinical placements and was adapted for CBL in this study
target_learners: First-year undergraduate medical students in a multicultural school

citation: McDaniel Mark A., Cahill Michael J., Frey Regina F., Limeri Lisa B., Lemons Paula P. (2022). Learning Introductory Biology: Students' Concept-Building Approaches Predict Transfer on Biology Exams. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-12-0335
title: Exemplar-based versus abstractor-based concept-building framework
description: Cognitive-science framework holding that for a given conceptual learning challenge, learners construct one of two qualitatively different representations: exemplar-based representations built on "memorizing the individual training examples," or abstractor-based representations built on "the abstract regularities (e.g., rules) that capture the relations among the training examples." The framework holds these tendencies are relatively stable across very different conceptual-learning tasks and only modestly related to working memory and fluid intelligence. The article applies it to predict which biology students will transfer instructed concepts to novel exam questions.
requirements: Learners must meet a learning criterion on the classification task (final training block MAE < 10) before their concept-building approach can be diagnosed
constraints: Classification was possible for only 67 of the participating students; slightly more than 50% of assessment completers could not be classified
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory biology courses
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding of core biology concepts
transfer of learned concepts to novel problems
examples: Students were classified via a Mars-organism function-learning task in which they predicted Beros release from Zebon absorption following an inverted-V function

article_title: EBCOG position statement - Simulation-based training for obstetrics and gynaecology during the COVID-19 pandemic.
citation: Zimmerman Erin, Martins Nuno N., Verheijen René H.M., Mahmood Tahir. (2021). EBCOG position statement – Simulation-based training for obstetrics and gynaecology during the COVID-19 pandemic. European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejogrb.2020.12.002
title: Expand simulation-based training across the obstetrics and gynaecology curriculum, from basic tool handling to subspecialty skills
description: The article recommends that, to maintain a high standard of training across Europe, "simulation-based training should be expanded to support the learning of a wide variety of skills". It specifies a skill range from basic tool handling to pathology identification and performing different procedures, aligned with the EBCOG PACT core skills. Simulation is positioned as a pillar of a well-rounded training system that should remain in place post-COVID to support equitable training across geographic and socio-demographic lines.
requirements: Simulators and well-defined training standards, as the article states simulators along with well-defined training standards can help facilitate pan-European knowledge exchange
constraints: Simulation equipment and models are expensive and not universally available in the areas of Europe where they are most needed
simulation training is usually done in groups, which might not be possible during COVID-19 time
target_learning_goals: subspecialty skills such as embryo transfer
examples: The statement lists PACT core skills suitable for simulation: transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound, diagnostic and therapeutic hysteroscopy and laparoscopy, open surgical training such as suturing, placement of IUD, and subspeciality skills such as embryo transfer.

article_title: Clinical study of skill assessment based on time sequential measurement changes.
citation: Yamaguchi Tomoko, Nakamura Ryoichi, Kuboki Akihito, Otori Nobuyoshi. (2022). Clinical study of skill assessment based on time sequential measurement changes. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-10502-7
title: Extended surgical feature parameter set including acceleration, jerk, bimanual angle and bimanual distance 2
description: The element is the set of surgical feature parameters quantified from surgical log data (instrument tip position, rod orientation, instrument type, time stamp at 5 Hz). Beyond the velocity, rotation, relative velocity and bimanual distance 1 used previously, the study "added acceleration and jerk, which are often used in surgical technique evaluation to evaluate finer parts of the movement of surgical instruments", and added "the bimanual angle and bimanual distance 2 were added as indicators of the positioning of the two surgical instruments", capturing the instrument–lesion–camera relationship.
requirements: Surgical log data from an optical position measuring device (surgical navigation system) with point-based registration and reference markers, sampled at 5 Hz
constraints: A new coordinate system relative to nasal anatomy must be manually set per patient because nasal cavity size varies
target_learners: surgical residents in endoscopic sinus surgery training
target_learning_goals: quantitative skill assessment of instrument handling and positioning during surgery
examples: The added parameters enabled detection of a new error type related to the positional relationship of the surgical instrument that a previous study did not detect

article_title: Artificial intelligence in laparoscopic simulation: a promising future for large-scale automated evaluations.
citation: Belmar Francisca, Gaete María Inés, Escalona Gabriel, Carnier Martín, Durán Valentina, Villagrán Ignacio, Asbun Domenech, Cortés Matías, Neyem Andrés, Crovari Fernando, Alseidi Adnan, Varas Julián. (2022). Artificial intelligence in laparoscopic simulation: a promising future for large-scale automated evaluations. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-022-09576-1
title: Expand AI automated assessment to additional basic laparoscopic exercises as a preliminary framework
description: The article concludes that this first use of AI in basic laparoscopic skills simulated training assessment "shows promising results, providing a preliminary framework to expand the use of AI to other basic laparoscopic skills exercises". The principle is to build automated assessment incrementally: validate agreement with expert evaluators on selected exercises first, then extend to the remaining exercises of the training program as more videos are collected and the algorithm is refined.
requirements: Continued collection of training videos, since the algorithm was developed using less than 500 sample videos for each exercise and could be modified to improve accuracy further
constraints: Fallen-object labeling has technical limitations, especially in the bean drop exercise, and the algorithm does not replace experts' feedback
target_learners: surgery trainees in laparoscopic simulation training programs
target_learning_goals: scalable, automated assessment of basic laparoscopic technical skills
examples: The authors report that modifications to the digital platform are being developed to automatically incorporate the algorithm outputs and avoid manual pass/fail categorization

article_title: Immersive virtual reality simulated learning environment versus role-play for empathic clinical communication training.
citation: Sapkaroski Daniel, Mundy Matthew, Dimmock Matthew Richard. (2021). Immersive virtual reality simulated learning environment versus role‐play for empathic clinical communication training. Journal of Medical Radiation Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1002/jmrs.555
title: Expert-panel-scored MRI empathic communication scenario tool with nine scaffolded steps and 1–3 response scoring
description: A guided, pre-scored communication scenario developed by a panel of three clinical experts using annotated feedback from anxious and claustrophobic MRI patients. It asks participants to explain an MRI scan to a patient in nine scaffolded steps (five examination-related, four coping-related), and "each statement was assigned a score from one to three according to the quality of the empathic language used and clinical relevance". It served both as the training content in both delivery formats and as the scored assessment instrument administered on-screen after training.
requirements: A panel of clinical experts to author and score the statements, and patient-derived annotated feedback to ground the scenario
constraints: The scores associated with responses are not shown to users because the scenario is used as an assessment tool in current and future teaching syllabuses
target_learning_goals: selecting empathic verbal statements when explaining MRI procedures to anxious patients
examples: The same scenario questions were covered in both delivery formats, with role-play participants receiving scripted and prompting questions from a clinical tutor

article_title: WeChat as a Platform for Problem-Based Learning Among Hematological Postgraduates: Feasibility and Acceptability Study.
citation: Luo P, Pang W, Wang Y, Liu M, Liu S, Zhang X, Liu L, Liu Y, Zhou F. (2021). WeChat as a Platform for Problem-Based Learning Among Hematological Postgraduates: Feasibility and Acceptability Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/16463
title: Use examination after each PBL class to drive learning and monitor progress, because examination affects what and how students learn
description: The article argues that assessment is necessary in learner-centered PBL because self-regulated learning skills vary: "Some students are highly self-disciplined, whereas others are not." It states that "Examination drives learning, and it affects not only what students learn but also how they learn," and reports observing an obvious correlation between examination scores and more active participation. Accordingly, all participants completed a tutor-graded quiz after each class, with progress displayed to the group and poorly performing students monitored.
requirements: Quizzes graded by the tutor immediately after each class
Tutor monitoring of students who perform poorly
constraints: The reported correlation between examination scores and participation is an observation, not a tested statistical result
target_learners: postgraduate medical students in PBL groups
examples: In the study, students were assessed by performance in the WeChat-PBL group, completion of work, and a quiz after each class

article_title: Competences in the training of nurses to assist the airway of adult patients in urgency and emergency situations.
citation: Miranda Fernanda Berchelli Girão; Alves Gerson Pereira-Junior; Mazzo Alessandra. (2021). Competences in the training of nurses to assist the airway of adult patients in urgency and emergency situations. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.3380.3434
title: Involve experts throughout construction and validation of competence-based training and assessment material
description: The article concludes that expert participation across all phases — workshop construction, Delphi validation, content analysis with CVI calculation, and simulated-workshop EPA validation — was essential to the material's relevance. As the authors state, "The participation of experts in the construction and validation of this material was essential to guarantee the theoretical and practical relevance of the result." Experts were selected by snowball sampling against Fehring's adapted criteria.
requirements: Experts meeting adapted Fehring criteria (experience, specialization, research or publication in the area) at each phase
constraints: The study notes limitations regarding the number of experts participating in each phase
target_learners: nursing students in urgency and emergency training
target_learning_goals: valid, theoretically and practically relevant competence frameworks and assessment tools
examples: A workshop of experts built the frameworks; 15 then 13 nurses validated them via Delphi; nine experts validated the EPAs in simulated ALS workshops

title: Course-specific app for anamnesis and physical examination used as blended-learning preparation and review material
description: The intervention tool is "an app specifically created for the anamnesis and physical examination course", a smartphone application letting students view learning content organized by organ system, with each organ system's examination divided into inspection, auscultation, palpation and interpretation of unusual findings, and explained with descriptive images. It served as pre- and post-course material replacing paper handouts, and students reported satisfaction with its usability and design. The authors note advantages of offline availability and updatable content.
requirements: Students needed an "iPhone" or "iPad" to participate, since the app ran only on Apple devices
constraints: At the time of the study the app did not include android support; the authors state expansion to android devices and addition of interactive content, videos, and regular updates is planned

examples: Used as pre- and post-material in a bedside clinical examination course on heart, lungs, abdomen, and lymphatic system

article_title: The tension-free vaginal tape operation: Is the inexperienced surgeon a risk factor? Learning curve and Swedish quality reference.
citation: Nüssler EK, Löfgren M, Lindkvist H, Idahl A. (2021). The tension‐free vaginal tape operation: Is the inexperienced surgeon a risk factor? Learning curve and Swedish quality reference. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. https://doi.org/10.1111/aogs.14033
title: Experience-group learning-curve method with an experienced-surgeon quality reference for assessing surgical trainees
description: The article devises learning curves by categorizing trainee operations into "experience groups" where all trainees share the same operation count ("all first TVT operations labeled as “experience = 1,”" and so on), plotting outcomes operation by operation against the averaged results of Sweden's most experienced surgeons with 95% confidence intervals, and additionally comparing group averages for operations 1–10 and 11–50. The experienced surgeons' averaged results are labeled a "quality reference" and regarded as a desirable goal for trainees. This method handles wide intra- and interindividual scattering of individual learning curves.
requirements: A prospectively collected register of operations with surgeon identity, allowing trainee operations to be ordered chronologically and compared with a defined experienced-surgeon reference group
constraints: The article reports only averaged results, noting learning curves for particular persons can show wide disparities, and incomplete information on supervised operations per trainee limits general recommendations about a minimum number of operations
target_learners: surgical trainees learning a new procedure
target_learning_goals: acquiring surgical competence in a standardized procedure
examples: Learning curves for all 163 Swedish TVT trainees' first 50 operations were plotted against the experienced surgeons' averaged results for 14 quality variables

article_title: Self-regulated learning in a competency-based and flipped learning environment: learning strategies across achievement levels and years.
citation: Zheng, Binbin, Ward, Amy, & Stanulis, Randi. (2020). Self-regulated learning in a competency-based and flipped learning environment: learning strategies across achievement levels and years. Medical Education Online, 25(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2019.1686949
title: Explicitly teach monitoring strategies when moving students into flipped, self-directed learning environments
description: The article's central design recommendation is that when a curriculum shifts responsibility for pre-class learning to students, educators cannot assume students bring monitoring strategies with them and must instead provide explicit instruction. The authors state that "When the learning structure changes, new learning strategies must be explicitly taught and practiced for students to be successful," reinforcing prior work suggesting that without specific instruction of self-monitoring, students would not improve acquisition. Planning, monitoring, and reflecting are described as integrated phases, so instruction should address how to apply an appropriate strategy in different contexts.
requirements: Curriculum developers and faculty who design explicit instruction and repeated practice for monitoring strategies during curricular transitions
constraints: Evidence base is one cohort of 26 students at a single medical school; the authors state findings may not be generalizable to other learning contexts
target_learners: medical students in flipped, competency-based curricula
target_learning_goals: self-monitoring of understanding during independent pre-class learning
examples: Even second-year students rarely reported monitoring strategies, and the authors interpreted this as showing students need more explicit instruction in how to monitor their own learning

article_title: How important is distractor efficiency for grading Best Answer Questions?
citation: Puthiaparampil Thomas, Rahman Mizanur. (2021). How important is distractor efficiency for grading Best Answer Questions? BMC Medical Education, 21:29. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02463-0
title: Expert review of examination items is obligatory even when psychometric performance is excellent
description: The article holds that psychometric indices alone must not replace expert judgement of item quality. The authors state that "although psychometrics are important, expert review of questions is obligatory" and recommend "an expert review of all items despite excellent to acceptable psychometric performance", noting their recommendation is consistent with that of McCoubrie. This guards against reusing items whose statistics look acceptable but whose content is flawed.
requirements: A panel of subject experts available to review vetted examination questions alongside item-analysis data
constraints: The article does not specify procedures or criteria for the expert review itself
target_learning_goals: quality assurance of high-stakes multiple-choice assessment
examples: All questions in the study's examinations were newly written and vetted at the department and faculty levels

article_title: Experiential Learning Program to Strengthen Self-Reflection and Critical Thinking in Freshmen Nursing Students during COVID-19: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Cheng Yi-Chuan, Huang Li-Chi, Yang Chi-Hsuan, Chang Hsing-Chi. (2020). Experiential Learning Program to Strengthen Self-Reflection and Critical Thinking in Freshmen Nursing Students during COVID-19: A Quasi-Experimental Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17155442
title: Experiential learning as a cycle from experience through reflection and discussion to internalized meaning
description: The article defines experiential learning as a sequence that "begins with experience, followed by reflection, discussion, and analysis, re-experience and evaluation, and ends with the construction of internalized meaning and value". It stems from Dewey's philosophy of learning by doing, emphasizing participation, reflection, and sharing in practice, and treats learning as conversion of experience into knowledge, skills, and attitudes. The ELP operationalizes this by pairing embodied experiences with journals and group discussion.
requirements: Personal experience must be followed by structured reflection, discussion, and analysis for experience to convert into knowledge, skills, and attitudes
examples: Students cared for a real intelligent baby for two days, wore a pregnancy dress for 2 h, and wore elderly assistive appliances for 4 h, then wrote journals and joined group discussion

International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17155442

article_title: Training and transfer effects of extensive task-switching training in students.
citation: Zhao Xin, Wang Haien, Maes Joseph H. R. (2020). Training and transfer effects of extensive task-switching training in students. Psychological Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-018-1059-7
title: Extensive (overtraining) task-switching protocols enhance trained-task efficiency but do not produce far transfer
description: The article shows that extending task-switching training to 21 sessions, implicating overtraining, strengthened trained-task and near-transfer gains but did not yield benefits on far-transfer tasks. The authors conclude that "the lack of beneficial far-transfer effects is in line with previous cognitive training studies employing fewer training sessions, suggesting that the extent of training is not critical for (not) finding transfer effects". Designers should therefore not expect longer training alone to broaden transfer.
requirements: An active control group to rule out non-specific practice and expectancy effects
constraints: Non-adaptive task difficulty and low working-memory demands of the cued task may have limited far-transfer potential, per the authors' limitations section
examples: Trained group performed the cued switching task on 21 successive weekdays (about 20 min per session, 4473 mixed-task trials) while controls made sand paintings

article_title: Supervisors' intention to observe clinical task performance: an exploratory study using the theory of planned behaviour during postgraduate medical training.
citation: de Jonge Laury P. J. W. M., Mesters Ilse, Govaerts Marjan J. B., Timmerman Angelique A., Muris Jean W. M., Kramer Anneke W. M., van der Vleuten Cees P. M. (2020). Supervisors' intention to observe clinical task performance: an exploratory study using the theory of planned behaviour during postgraduate medical training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02047-y
title: Extended Theory of Planned Behaviour model adding past behaviour, social pressure and modelling to predict supervisors' intention to perform direct observations
description: The article extends Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour — in which behavioural, normative and control beliefs yield attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control that form behavioural intention — with three additional measures: past behaviour, perceived social pressure, and modelling. The article states: "With the addition of these extra measures we composed an extended TPB model to explore and predict supervisors' intentions to engage in DOs of trainee performance in the clinical workplace (Fig. 1)." The model was operationalised in a 56-item questionnaire and tested via hierarchical regression in postgraduate GP training.
requirements: Application follows the five-stage manual by Francis and colleagues (2004): defining the behaviour, identifying participants and context, instrument development, data collection, and statistical analysis.
Belief items must be elicited from the target population; beliefs here came from three audio-recorded focus groups with 21 GP supervisors.
constraints: The article notes the TPB is a continuum model that "typically do[es] not account for the postintentional phase in which goals are translated into action"; intention was measured rather than actual behaviour.
target_learners: Postgraduate GP supervisors in workplace-based medical residency training
target_learning_goals: Increasing supervisors' intention to perform direct observations of trainee clinical task performance and provide feedback
examples: The extended model was tested with a four-step hierarchical regression in which demographics, indirect measures, direct measures and past behaviour were entered sequentially, explaining 45% of intention variance at the final step.

article_title: Using Food Models to Enhance Sugar Literacy among Older Adolescents: Evaluation of a Brief Experiential Nutrition Education Intervention.
citation: Santaló María Isabel, Gibbons Sandra, Naylor Patti-Jean. (2019). Using Food Models to Enhance Sugar Literacy among Older Adolescents: Evaluation of a Brief Experiential Nutrition Education Intervention. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu11081763
title: Pair brief didactic nutrition lectures with hands-on experiential activities using visual food models to build sugar literacy
description: The article's intervention design combines short lectures with experiential learning activities in which students manipulate food models, following the recommendation that effective adolescent food literacy interventions use "innovative teaching aids, including opportunities for experiential or 'hands-on' learning" and incorporating behavior change techniques from the COM-B model. Each 45-minute session paired a brief lecture (diet quality, then sugar content and label reading) with group activities visualizing diets and sugar content with the models. The trial showed this pairing significantly improved knowledge, label-reading confidence and intention.
requirements: Food model kits and real nutrition fact labels for the hands-on activities
Delivery within school Physical and Health Education class time
constraints: Follow-up immediately after the second lesson meant behavior frequency and self-efficacy did not change; longer-term effects were not assessed
target_learners: Older adolescents (high school students) in Physical and Health Education classes
target_learning_goals: Sugar literacy: knowledge, awareness, skills and intention to limit added sugar
examples: Two 45-minute sessions: session 1 covered Canada's Food Guide servings with menu-design activities; session 2 covered WHO sugar recommendations with teaspoon-conversion and label-reading activities

article_title: "They cared about us students:" learning from exemplar clinical teaching environments.
citation: Gamble Blakey Althea, Smith-Han Kelby, Anderson Lynley, Collins Emma, Berryman Elizabeth, Wilkinson Tim. (2019). “They cared about us students:” learning from exemplar clinical teaching environments. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1551-9
title: Five-theme framework of exemplar clinical teaching practices
description: A thematic framework describing the practices of two clinical areas voted best by students: ongoing welcome, collective responsibility, relationship, teacher values supporting student learning, and teaching students' values for professional practice. The authors state the framework is "useful, clear and transferrable to other clinical teaching contexts" and that specific pedagogic method or theoretical standpoints were not reported as important. It combines fundamentally logistic and personal factors rather than specific teaching techniques.
requirements: Staff assign time and resources to deliberately make provision for students' arrival, including a daily deliberate welcome
Responsibility for teaching is shared between multidisciplinary and support staff who understand how to use teachable moments
Teachers create opportunities to develop a healthy relationship with students sufficient to understand their specific learning needs
constraints: Practices were reported by proxy through students and staff rather than observed first hand
The study assumes that supportive experiences mean helpful for student learning, which survey data cannot fully distinguish
target_learners: fifth-year medical students on clinical rotations
target_learning_goals: professionalism and values for clinical practice
engagement and belonging in clinical teams
examples: Exemplar staff displayed student ID photos before arrival, introduced students to all staff on day one, and held a daily focus on which student does what
Staff shared tasks including organising rosters, supervising tasks, giving tutorials, and reassuring students they could seek assistance from any staff member

article_title: The Mediating Role of Self-Concept between Sports-Related Physical Activity and Mathematical Achievement in Fourth Graders.
citation: Dapp Laura C., Roebers Claudia M. (2019). The Mediating Role of Self-Concept between Sports-Related Physical Activity and Mathematical Achievement in Fourth Graders. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16152658
title: Exercise and self-esteem model cascade extended to mathematical achievement
description: The article applies Sonstroem's exercise and self-esteem model, in which "engaging in PA increases the physical self-concept, which, in turn, results in an increased general self-concept", which then supports the academic self-concept and finally achievement. Exploratory serial mediation analyses in Appendix A tested this cascade within a multidimensional self-concept, finding significant paths from structured PA through physical, general, and mathematical self-concept to mathematical achievement, with a significant indirect effect and an insignificant direct effect.
requirements: A multidimensional self-concept framework distinguishing physical, general, and academic (mathematical) self-concept, measured with the respective SDQ-I subscales
constraints: The serial mediation is exploratory and the study's cross-sectional design limits conclusions to correlational ones
examples: Appendix A reports a Maximum Likelihood serial mediation with latent variables in which structured PA predicted physical self-concept (b = 0.46), physical self-concept predicted general self-concept (b = 0.61), and the chain continued to mathematical achievement with a significant indirect effect

title: Extend flipped classroom intervention duration to improve long-term retention of EBN knowledge
description: The article recommends extending the intervention period because a brief 5-hour flipped classroom course produced immediate gains that faded within one month. The authors state that "One way of overcoming this issue is to extend the intervention period to improve the long-term impacts of flipped classroom on EBN knowledge accumulation and practice performance." This principle applies to short-course professional training contexts where durable knowledge retention is a goal.
requirements: Sufficient intervention duration to produce lasting effects, as the article identifies the 5-hour course length as a limitation on long-term impact
constraints: The article's evidence is limited to a single 5-hour course; the optimal duration for long-term retention is not established
target_learners: Practicing nurses in hospital in-service training
examples: The study's 5-hour flipped classroom EBN course produced immediate knowledge gains that were not sustained at one-month follow-up

article_title: Exploring Biology: A Vision and Change Disciplinary First-Year Seminar Improves Academic Performance in Introductory Biology.
citation: Wienhold Caroline J.; Branchaw Janet. (2018). Exploring Biology: A Vision and Change Disciplinary First-Year Seminar Improves Academic Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-08-0158
title: Cohorts-in-large-course design: large lecture plus ~20-student discussion sections builds disciplinary community while serving large numbers
description: Exploring Biology serves ~200 students per semester using a cohorts-in-large-course design: all students meet in large lecture for the first hour, then split into small discussion sections of ~20 students. According to the article, this "creates communities of students with common interests, which enhances opportunities for networking among peers and informal interactions with faculty, and promotes retention in the discipline through an increased sense of belonging." The design combines small-group learning benefits with large-course capacity.
requirements: A faculty-led instructional team spanning career stages and campus professionals to populate the network of support
constraints: Availability of a dedicated course director and teaching fellow instructors may be limiting at other institutions
target_learners: first-year undergraduate students intending to major in biology

develop networking and academic navigation skills

article_title: Exploring Biology: A Vision and Change Disciplinary First-Year Seminar Improves Academic Performance in Introductory Biology.
citation: Wienhold Caroline J.; Branchaw Janet. (2018). Exploring Biology: A Vision and Change Disciplinary First-Year Seminar Improves Academic Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-08-0158
title: Vision and Change core concepts used as a conceptual learning framework in a disciplinary first-year seminar
description: The course organizes biology learning around the five Vision and Change core concepts: "1) evolution; 2) information flow, exchange, and storage; 3) pathways and transformations of energy and matter; 4) structure and function; and 5) systems." Students also use a scale-versus-concept framework as a visual tool to organize knowledge, exploring each topic through multiple core concept lenses and at multiple scales. The article states frameworks lead to greater and faster learning gains by developing students' abilities to organize, connect, and relate concepts.
requirements: Instructional team develops topics each semester based on team expertise while core concept learning goals remain constant
constraints: Further studies are underway to assess whether students' conceptual understanding improves after engaging with the framework
target_learning_goals: think about and learn biology conceptually
organize, connect, and relate biology concepts
examples: Eight topic examples address multiple scales and/or core concepts in the scale-versus-concept framework table

article_title: Developing and evaluating a course programme to enhance existential communication with cancer patients in general practice.
citation: Hvidt EA, Ammentorp J, Søndergaard J, Timmermann C, Hansen DG, Hvidt NC. (2018). Developing and evaluating a course programme to enhance existential communication with cancer patients in general practice. Scandinavian Journal of Primary Health Care. https://doi.org/10.1080/02813432.2018.1459235
title: Existential philosophy and psychology framework for the course
description: The course's theoretical base lies "within the tradition of existential philosophy and psychology that deal with questions relating to the most basic questions of existence: the meaning of one's being, freedom, isolation and death". In this framework these conditions are inescapable givens of human existence and also catalysts for existential distress and growth; reaching authentic being requires actively addressing existential questions such as meaninglessness, loneliness and fear of death. During illness, meaning breaks apart, and new or renewed meaning orientations, possibly religious or spiritual, may be needed. The article uses this framework to ground the course's knowledge, reflection and communication elements.
requirements: Reflection on existential questions is treated as a critical process in preparing health professionals to care for others
target_learning_goals: Understanding existential dimensions of illness such as meaning-making, freedom, isolation and death

article_title: Medical students preference of problem-based learning or traditional lectures in King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
citation: Ibrahim Nahla Khamis, Banjar Shorooq, Al-Ghamdi Amal, Al-Darmasi Moroj, Khoja Abeer, Turkistani Jamela, Arif Rwan, Al-Sebyani Awatif, Musawa Al-anoud, Basfar Wijdan. (2014). Medical students' preference of problem-based learning or traditional lectures in King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Annals of Saudi Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5144/0256-4947.2014.128
title: Expand hybrid-PBL curricula and increase PBL share while retaining lectures, to improve attitudes, skills and learning outcomes
description: The article recommends that medical faculties combine problem-based learning with traditional lectures, increasing the amount of PBL because students preferred it for most learning-outcome domains. It states the faculty "needs to provide more integration between PBL and traditional lectures, with an increase amount of PBL", and that "Introducing hybrid–PBL curriculum in all Saudi universities is highly recommended." The recommendation rests on student perceptions rather than tested outcome differences.
requirements: Students must experience both methods in a hybrid curriculum so preferences and domain-specific strengths can be assessed.
constraints: The recommendation is based on students' expressed preferences and perceptions, not on objective measures of gained knowledge or skills; the study itself found no significant difference in recalled basic knowledge between the methods.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in hybrid-PBL curricula
target_learning_goals: Professional skills such as critical thinking, communication and teamwork
examples: The study surveyed 460 medical students in the hybrid-PBL curriculum at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, in 2011, using a stratified random sample by gender and educational year.
